levels.name: Change review
levels.description: Checks a diff or pull request: scope, size, compatibility, tests, and the description.

levels.name: Function audit
levels.description: Checks one file or function: names, errors, concurrency, and security at the call level.

levels.name: Module audit
levels.description: Checks a package or path: boundaries, state, dependencies, and the public surface.

levels.name: Service audit
levels.description: Checks one running service: its API, failure handling, limits, and security.

levels.name: System audit
levels.description: Checks a design that spans services: shared data, caches, migrations, and failure modes.

levels.name: Codebase audit
levels.description: Checks a whole repository: CI gates, dependencies, setup, and conventions.

levels.name: Production audit
levels.description: Checks a release or launch: rollout, rollback, alerts, and load.

levels.name: Incident audit
levels.description: Checks an incident and its follow-up: evidence, guards, and owned actions.

cards.applies_when: The repo builds a web UI and has an automated test suite.
cards.tool_gate: This card is the gate: axe (through `@axe-core/playwright` or similar) against rendered pages in the test step; `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` in the lint step for JSX code.
cards.note: Rule backed by USWDS (axe and pa11y on every change, failing merges blocked), Microsoft Playwright (the test verifies there are no violations), and Deque axe-core (axe calls in existing functional tests, example throws on violations); the JSX lint (jsx-eslint only) and merge blocking in CI (USWDS only) sit in Why; GDS found the best of 13 automated tools caught 40% of planted barriers
cards.rule: Run an automated accessibility check, such as axe on rendered pages, in the automated tests, and fail the test on a violation.
cards.why: A violation that nobody sees at review ships. A failing test catches the missing label or `alt` on the pull request that adds it, and run in CI on every pull request it blocks the merge. A JSX lint such as `jsx-a11y` catches some of the same problems earlier, in the editor. Either way it is a floor: tools find only part of the problems, so a person still tests with a keyboard and reviews the results the engine marks "incomplete".
cards.counterpoint: "Tools only catch a minority, and we have a backlog, so a failing check would turn every build red." The check catches the cheap failures at no review cost, which frees the manual pass for what only a person can judge. For the backlog, exclude the known violations by name (`disableRules`, `exclude`, or a fingerprint of each known issue) and fail on anything new. Remove each exclusion once it is fixed.

cards.applies_when: Auditing whether the reasons behind significant design choices are recorded.
cards.rule: Keep a short written record for each significant design choice (datastore, framework, deviation from a pattern) that states the context, the decision, the options ruled out, and its consequences.
cards.why: Without a record, the next reader reverses a decision blindly or cargo-cults it. A record that weighs only the chosen design, its strengths or its flaws, is not a trade-off analysis, so say why each ruled-out option lost. Give each record a status (proposed, accepted, superseded). Do not edit an accepted record: write a new one that supersedes it and keep the old one. If review finds an undocumented decision, write its record then.
cards.counterpoint: ADRs rot and become paperwork. Keep each to a page, write them only for hard-to-reverse choices, and mark superseded ones.

fail.code: Repo uses Kafka for one 10-msg/day job. No record why; nobody dares remove it.

pass.code: docs/adr/0007-queue.md: context, decision, consequences, status, and the 2 options ruled out.

cards.applies_when: A pull request was written in whole or part by an AI tool.
cards.tool_gate: PR template checkbox for AI assistance; commit trailer check.
cards.rule: Disclose AI assistance in the PR, and have a human author who can explain and defend every changed line without the tool.
cards.why: Reviewers calibrate by who wrote the code. An undisclosed generated change gets the wrong scrutiny, and an author who cannot explain it leaves the reviewer to do the author's job.
cards.counterpoint: "Disclosure stigmatises tool use." The rule is about scrutiny, not blame: disclosed work is reviewed the same way and merged on the same terms. The agent never signs off or certifies origin; the human does.

fail.code:
PR description: "Add retry logic."
(500 generated lines; asked why a 3rd retry, the author says "the model chose it")

pass.code:
PR description: "Add retry logic. Drafted with <tool>; I read and tested every line.
 Tests: test_retry.py. Not covered: jitter."
Trailer: Assisted-by: <tool>

cards.applies_when: The repository has a build, a packaging, or a release step.
cards.tool_gate: Build twice in clean containers and compare checksums; `diffoscope` shows where two artifacts differ.
cards.note: Rule backed by Google (Bazel hermeticity), Airbnb (Gradle tasks could touch the whole file system, Bazel sandboxes each action to its declared inputs) and Slack (a build step must use only the inputs it is given and give the same output for them); Dropbox lists hermetic, reproducible builds as a Bazel benefit; pinned toolchains (Google only) sit in Why
cards.rule: Build from declared inputs only, so that the same source revision gives the same artifact.
cards.why: A build that reads whatever is installed on the machine gives different output on different machines, so a bug cannot be reproduced and a release cannot be checked against its source. Tools are inputs too: pin the compiler and toolchain versions, and do not call host binaries. Undeclared shared files also break builds at scale, for example two tasks that clean and use the same `/tmp` directory race each other.
cards.counterpoint: "Bit-identical builds are overkill." Full reproducibility is the ceiling. Declared inputs, pinned tools, and a recorded revision are the floor, and they cost little. [[code-dependency-pinning]] covers dependency pins.

fail.code:
steps:
  - run: make               # uses whatever gcc, node and protoc the runner has
  - run: date > BUILD_ID    # the clock is an undeclared input

pass.code:
container:
  image: ghcr.io/acme/builder@sha256:4b1e...   # toolchain pinned by digest
steps:
  - run: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$(git log -1 --format=%ct) make   # timestamps come from the commit

cards.applies_when: Auditing which checks must pass before a change merges.
cards.tool_gate: Branch protection with required status checks.
cards.rule: Require review and passing build, tests, lint, and type checks on the default branch before merge, and leave nothing mechanical to reviewer vigilance.
cards.why: Any rule that depends on someone remembering will be skipped. Components where changes merge unreviewed or without discussion tend to ship more post-release defects. Changes reach the branch only through a pull request, and force-push and branch deletion are blocked, so what was reviewed is what ships.
cards.counterpoint: Gates slow small teams, and flaky tests train people to override. Keep gates few and reliable, fix flakes instead of overriding them, and let the gates own the mechanical checks so review time goes to design.

fail.code: Default branch: no protection. Force-push allowed. CI optional.

pass.code:
Protected main: pull request required, 1 approval + required checks (build, test, lint, types).
Force-push and branch deletion blocked.

cards.applies_when: Auditing whether one concern is solved in several incompatible ways across the repo.
cards.tool_gate: Lint rules that ban the deprecated pattern once a standard is chosen.
cards.note: Spotify, Uber, Cabify and Stripe back one standard per concern; tracking old variants has 2 (Stripe, Spotify), so it is in Why
cards.rule: For each recurring concern (errors, config, HTTP clients, logging), make one pattern the standard instead of leaving several as equal peers.
cards.why: Each extra variant is another thing to learn, test, and secure, and drift accumulates through changes that each looked locally fine. Two limiters built two ways enforce the same quota differently. List the older variants and count them, so the migration shows progress and a new one shows up in review.
cards.counterpoint: "Forcing one way can block a better tool." Allow change through a proposal that updates the standard and the migration list, not through a quiet second pattern. Consistency breaks ties. It does not outrank a measured reason to switch.

fail.code:
Three HTTP clients (requests, urllib3, httpx) with three timeout conventions;
no document says which is current.

pass.code:
docs: "use httpx via net/client.py". Lint bans direct requests imports;
legacy sites listed in MIGRATION.md.

cards.applies_when: Auditing for code, flags and files that nothing uses.
cards.tool_gate: An unused-code linter in CI (vulture, knip, or deadcode); allowlist each intentional exception with a reason.
cards.note: Unreachable code (CMU SEI, Lockheed Martin JSF, NVIDIA), commented-out code (Lockheed Martin JSF, JetBrains, TUM) and the flag's definition and configuration (Microsoft, GitLab, Uber) each have three organisations, so they sit in the Rule. Orphaned files (no source) sit in the Why. Palantir's page loads and backs only the commented-out-code case. Version-control history as the reason to delete has two organisations (Google, JetBrains), so it stays in the Why. Unused imports have two (NVIDIA, Go), so they sit in the Why. JetBrains and Statsig are vendors.
cards.rule: Delete unreferenced functions and variables, unreachable code, commented-out code, and expired feature flags with their branches and configuration.
cards.why: Dead code costs reading time, misleads searches, and gets "fixed" and tested for no benefit. The same holds for unused imports and files nothing links to: delete them too and let version control remember.
cards.counterpoint: Code may be called by reflection, plugins, or external users. Check with the detector's config and a grep of consumers. For public API, deprecate first (see `chg-expand-contract`).

    render_legacy()
# if USE_CACHE: warm()     # commented-out code, kept "just in case"
return result
log.info("done")          # unreachable

pass.code:

The unused-code linter reports 0 symbols, or each is allowlisted with a reason.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo whose docs, READMEs or design notes describe code that has since changed or gone.
cards.tool_gate: A freshness check (last-reviewed date or owner per page) that fails or flags pages untouched past a threshold.
cards.note: Google (eng-practices), the Linux kernel and GitLab state it for docs of removed or never-shipped code. Whole-section retirement (MDN) and a deprecate-then-delete delay (Fuchsia) are partial
cards.rule: Delete the docs for code or features that were removed or never shipped, instead of leaving or hiding them.
cards.why: A wrong page is worse than none: readers trust it. A design doc left as a living doc after the code ships drifts the same way, so archive it as a decision record. Version control keeps the history, so deleting loses nothing. Docs known to be wrong go for the same reason.
cards.counterpoint: "Old docs may still help someone." Version control keeps them. The kernel guide allows an outdated-warning banner on a page you cannot fix yet. Mark a still-useful record `superseded` and link the replacement so nobody mistakes it for current.

fail.code: docs/design-auth-v1.md   # describes a login flow removed two releases ago, no status line

pass.code: docs/adr/0004-auth.md    # status: superseded by 0009; the old design doc is deleted

cards.applies_when: Auditing what third-party code the repo ships and under which terms.
cards.tool_gate: A vulnerability scanner such as OSV-Scanner or Dependabot alerts; an SBOM generator such as Syft.
cards.note: SBOM backed by OWASP, NIST and GitHub; scan by OWASP, OpenSSF, GitHub and Cabify (Trivy at build, running images rescanned every 6 hours); the licence allowlist is team policy, unsourced
cards.rule: Generate an SBOM, and scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities on every change or on a schedule, and raise an alert when a new vulnerability applies. Each ask is judged separately: name which one failed on the FAIL line.
cards.why: Without an inventory, a team cannot answer a disclosed vulnerability quickly. CI is the usual place for both steps: the SBOM then matches what was built, and the scan runs without anyone remembering it. Team policy: also fail the build on a dependency whose licence is not on the approved list.
cards.counterpoint: SBOMs and scanners create noise that nobody triages. Tune severity thresholds and assign an owner, since an ignored report is worse than none. The licence list is team policy, not a universal rule. Drop it if your team has no licence constraints.

fail.code: No SBOM anywhere, no scanner in CI, and dependency alerts turned off.

pass.code:
CI: generate SBOM, run vulnerability scanner, fail on high severity;
release artifacts attach the SBOM; a new advisory for a shipped component raises an alert.

cards.applies_when: Auditing how the repo resolves third-party packages.
cards.tool_gate: Lockfile-required install in CI; dependency-update bot config present.
cards.note: Install must fail on a stale lock, not re-resolve (npm ci errors when the lock and package.json disagree; pip --require-hashes rejects unhashed requirements). The Go and uv/poetry equivalents are the same rule applied to their tools; the sources name npm and pip only
cards.rule: Commit a lockfile with hashes and install from it in CI.
cards.why: Unpinned versions make builds non-reproducible and let a compromised release flow straight into production. Updates should arrive as reviewed, staged changes, not silently. Run an update bot (Dependabot, Renovate or an autoroller) so the lock does not go stale and updates arrive as pull requests. [[code-workflow-supply-chain]] covers CI action pins.
cards.counterpoint: Pinning delays security patches. A pin plus an update bot with a defined cadence beats floating versions, because the lock makes the update visible and revertable.

fail.code: requirements.txt:  requests>=2   (no lockfile; CI runs pip install -U)

pass.code:
requirements.lock with hashes; CI: pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.lock
Update bot opens PRs; changes are rolled out in stages.

cards.applies_when: Auditing docs, READMEs or doc comments that contain code samples.
cards.tool_gate: Rust `cargo test --doc`, Go example functions, Python `doctest`, or a build step that includes samples from files that CI compiles.
cards.note: Rust, Go (Google) and Elixir state running doc examples as tests. Including examples from a file that CI builds has two (Kubernetes, Microsoft), so it sits in the Why
cards.rule: Run each code example in the docs as a test.
cards.why: A pasted example drifts from the API it shows, and readers copy it. A tested example fails the build when the API changes. Including the sample from a source file that CI builds, instead of pasting it, gives the same protection.
cards.counterpoint: "Some samples are fragments that cannot run." Mark those as fragments and keep them short. The rule is for samples a reader will copy and run.

pass.code: README.md: the sample is the body of tests/test_quickstart.py, run by `pytest --doctest-glob`

cards.applies_when: Auditing docs, READMEs or comments that restate a guide, spec or page that already exists elsewhere.
cards.note: Google, GitLab, Mozilla (MDN) and Kubernetes state it. Chromium and Go are Google. README-per-directory and minimum-viable-docs have only Google behind them
cards.rule: Link to the existing page or guide instead of rewriting or restating it.
cards.why: Each copy is one more page to keep current, and the copies drift apart. A link has a single owner who fixes it once.
cards.counterpoint: "A link breaks and the reader has to leave the page." Run a link check (see `code-docs-refs-resolve`) and quote only the one line the reader needs here.

fail.code: README.md: a 40-line "How to use git rebase" section copied from the team wiki

pass.code: README.md: Rebase and branch rules are in [the contributing guide](docs/contributing.md#branches).

cards.applies_when: A diff adds or edits a link in documentation, a README or a user-facing message.
cards.tool_gate: markdownlint `MD059` (descriptive link text) or a regex for "here" and "click here" link text.
cards.note: Google, GitLab, Microsoft and Kubernetes state it in their docs style guides
cards.rule: Write link text that says where the link goes, never "here", "this page" or "click here".
cards.why: Readers scan links on their own, and screen readers list them out of context. "Here" tells neither what they will find.
cards.counterpoint: "Short link text reads better." The descriptive phrase is usually the words already in the sentence, so it costs no length.

fail.code: For the deploy steps, click [here](docs/deploy.md).

pass.code: Follow the [deploy steps](docs/deploy.md).

cards.applies_when: A diff adds documentation text that points to other content or to something on screen.
cards.tool_gate: A Vale rule (`Google.WordList`, `Microsoft.Avoid`) or a regex for "above", "below", "left" and "right" in docs.
cards.note: Google, Microsoft, Mozilla (MDN), GitLab, Elastic and Red Hat state it. Docker only maps the words in a table
cards.rule: Do not point to content with "above", "below", "left" or "right"; name it or link to it.
cards.why: A screen reader gives those words no meaning, and the page reflows on a phone. A reorder of the page also turns "the table below" into a false pointer.
cards.counterpoint: "Readers understand 'below'." Most do, until the section moves. A link survives a reorder, and "the following" works where a link is too heavy.

fail.code: See the example above, and the options in the table below.

pass.code: See [the retry example](#retry-example) and [the options table](#options).

cards.applies_when: A diff adds text to published documentation that describes a feature, release or date that is not shipped.
cards.note: Google, Kubernetes and GitLab state it. Comments and TODOs fall under `fn-comments-survive-context`; this card covers published docs
cards.rule: Do not promise unreleased features, versions or dates in published docs.
cards.why: A promise in the docs reads as a commitment. When the plan changes, the page is wrong, readers have planned around it, and nobody owns the fix.
cards.counterpoint: "Users want a roadmap." Keep one, outside the reference docs. Link the issue, which says what is planned without a date.

fail.code: Bulk export will arrive in the next release.

pass.code: Bulk export is not supported. Track the request in issue #482.

cards.applies_when: A diff adds documentation text that describes a task or a step.
cards.tool_gate: A Vale rule (GitLab `SubstitutionWarning`, Google `WordList`) or a regex for "simply", "just", "easily" and "obviously".
cards.note: Django, GitLab, Google, Docker and Elastic state it
cards.rule: Do not call a step "simple", "easy", "just" or "simply" in docs.
cards.why: What is easy for the author is not easy for a newcomer. A reader who fails at an "easy" step blames themselves, and the word adds nothing to the instruction.
cards.counterpoint: "'Just' softens the tone." Cut the word and keep the instruction. If a step really is optional, say so.

fail.code: Simply run the migration, then just restart the worker.

pass.code: Run the migration, then restart the worker.

cards.applies_when: A diff renames, moves or deletes a published documentation page.
cards.tool_gate: A redirect-file check in CI that fails when a page is removed and no redirect names it.
cards.note: Redirect on move or delete: GitLab, Cloudflare, Microsoft, TYPO3, MDN and GitHub. In the same change: Cloudflare, Microsoft and TYPO3 (reviewers ask for it). GitLab implies it through merge requests; MDN allows adding it later
cards.rule: Add a redirect from the old URL in the same change that moves, renames or deletes a documentation page.
cards.why: Links in issues, search results and other docs keep pointing at the old address. Without a redirect they land on a 404, and the broken links are found one reader at a time.
cards.counterpoint: "Internal docs have few outside links." Then the redirect is a one-line file. Skip it only for a page that was never published.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo whose README, guides or AGENTS.md cite file paths, anchors or other pages.
cards.tool_gate: A link checker in CI, such as lychee (`lychee --offline --include-fragments docs README.md`) or mdBook linkcheck.
cards.note: GitHub docs, GitLab docs and the Rust dev guide each run a link check on every change. Whether the documented commands run is a different rule
cards.rule: Run a link check in CI over the docs, so that every relative link and anchor they cite resolves.
cards.why: A rename or a deleted file leaves docs that point at nothing. Readers and agents then follow a dead path, and nobody notices until someone trips on it. A machine finds a dangling reference on the pull request that causes it.
cards.counterpoint: "External links flake, so the job will be red half the time." Check local paths and anchors on every change, where the result is stable. Run the external links on a schedule, so a dead site never blocks a merge.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo whose application reads settings from .env files.
cards.tool_gate: A secret scan on push; a CI check that `git ls-files` lists no .env.local or .env file with real values.
cards.note: Laravel (.env should not be committed; commit a .env.example with placeholders), Symfony (.env.local should be ignored by git), Next.js (default template ignores all .env files; you almost never want to commit them) and Vite (add *.local to .gitignore). Symfony, Next.js and Vite commit a non-secret .env of defaults, so the rule names the local files and the secrets, not every .env
cards.rule: Git-ignore local environment files that hold real values; commit only a template with placeholders.
cards.why: An `.env` file with real credentials, once committed, sits in every clone and in history, and deleting it later does not recall the copies ([[code-secrets-not-plaintext-in-repo]]). A committed template with placeholder values still tells the next developer which variables the app needs.
cards.counterpoint: Frameworks such as Symfony and Next.js commit a `.env` of non-secret defaults, and an encrypted env file can be committed too. Both are fine: the check is that no file in the repo holds a real credential in plaintext, and that local override files are ignored.

pass.code:

              .env.*.local

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo for files that have grown past comprehension.
cards.tool_gate: Pylint too-many-lines (C0302, max-module-lines default 1000), ESLint max-lines, or Checkstyle FileLength, with an allowlist for generated files.
cards.note: a documented file-length limit - Pylint (default 1000), ESLint (default 300; recommendations "usually range from 100 to 500"), Checkstyle (default 2000), RuboCop (class and module length, default 100) and PMD (size and complexity caps); the numbers differ, so the Rule asks for a limit and not for 1,000
cards.rule: Set a file-length limit in the linter (Pylint and SonarSource default to 1,000 lines), keep hand-written files under it unless a listed exception says otherwise, and split larger files by knowledge owned, not by execution order.
cards.why: Huge files hide unrelated decisions, attract merge conflicts, and cannot be understood in one read. Linters ship a default for this because a file that passes it is "hard to understand" (Checkstyle). The defaults differ from 300 to 2,000 lines, so pick one and enforce it.
cards.counterpoint: Ousterhout favours deep modules and a long file can be coherent. Splitting for its own sake adds shallow pieces. 1,000 lines is a trigger for a look, not a verdict. The fix is to separate decisions (his information-leakage and temporal-decomposition flags).

  4,812 src/utils.py
  3,105 src/app.py

pass.code: pylint: max-module-lines = 1000; no hand-written file over it; generated files listed in an allowlist.

cards.applies_when: Auditing how the codebase handles tests that pass and fail on the same code.
cards.note: report and route flaky tests - Dropbox (Quarantine Keeper removes tests that fail too often and files a bug against the owner), Shopify (retries a failed test up to three times and notifies developers of every pass after a retry); rerun-verified fix - Dropbox only (100 or more CI runs); causes - Shopify (fixed pauses instead of waits), Cabify (state kept between tests), Dropbox (short timeouts, leftover state); only 2 orgs back the Rule
cards.rule: Report every test that passes only on retry, move it to a quarantine with a named owner and a ticket, and return it to the merge gate only after it passes many reruns.
cards.why: A test that fails at random on unchanged code teaches people to rerun until green, and then a real regression looks like noise. Dropbox removes tests that fail too often from the main pool and files a bug against the owner. Its fix workflow then runs the test 100 or more times in CI before the fix lands. Give the ticket a due date, so a quarantined test gets fixed or deleted instead of sitting there for good. Shopify retries a failed test but tells developers about every pass after a retry. The usual causes are a fixed pause where the test should wait for an element (Shopify) and state left behind by an earlier test (Cabify, Dropbox).
cards.counterpoint: "Retries keep the build green, and quarantine hides coverage." Shopify's data backs retries: a slightly slower build beats an engineer rerunning it by hand. Retries are fine when each pass after a retry reaches someone. A quarantined test still runs outside the gate, and its owner and ticket stop it from staying there for good. Skipping or deleting a flaky test in a diff is a separate FAIL. See [[chg-no-silenced-diagnostics]]. For the merge gate itself, see [[code-ci-gates]].

fail.code:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
- run: pytest --reruns 3          # a pass on retry counts as a pass, and nobody hears about it

pass.code:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
- run: pytest --reruns 3 -m "not quarantine" --junitxml=report.xml
- run: python tools/flaky_report.py report.xml   # opens a ticket per pass after retry, owner from CODEOWNERS
# nightly.yml: a quarantined test rejoins the gate after 100 clean runs
- run: pytest -m quarantine --count 100

cards.applies_when: Auditing a codebase that adopted a linter, a quality gate or an architecture rule after most of its code existed.
cards.tool_gate: A baseline or frozen violation store with CI set to read it but not rewrite it (ArchUnit `FreezingArchRule`, a linter baseline file).
cards.rule: Gate CI on new or modified code, and track pre-existing violations in a separate store without letting a build add to it.
cards.why: A gate that fails on thousands of old findings gets switched off, and a gate with no record of them lets the debt grow unseen. Failing only on new findings keeps the gate on and stops the debt growing, and the store shows what is left to pay down.
cards.counterpoint: "A baseline hides real problems." It lists them in a file under version control, in plain view, and a change that touches a baselined spot is held to the full rule. Pair it with a plan to shrink the store.

cards.applies_when: The repo has a performance target (bundle size, page metrics, latency under load, or a benchmark) that matters to users.
cards.tool_gate: Lighthouse CI assert, size-limit, k6 thresholds, Gatling assertions, or a benchstat comparison in CI.
cards.rule: Write the performance budget down as a CI check that fails the build when it is exceeded.
cards.why: Performance regresses a few percent at a time, and no reviewer sees a 3% slowdown in a diff. A budget that only warns becomes a log line nobody reads.
cards.counterpoint: "Benchmarks in CI are noisy and flake." They are when a gate trusts one run. Gate on a stable budget, compare repeated runs (benchstat wants 10 to 20), and keep the threshold above the noise. On a site with much room to improve, a tight budget only turns every build red, so set it at today's level and lower it later.

k6 script with no thresholds block

k6: thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"] }        # non-zero exit fails the job

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo with several packages, modules or self-contained components.
cards.tool_gate: A CI check that every package root holds a README (a glob test, or a docs linter).
cards.note: Google (with Chromium), Microsoft (Azure SDK) and HashiCorp (Terraform) state it. None says every subdirectory, so the Rule stops at the package, module or component root
cards.rule: Give each package, module or self-contained component a README at its root that says what it holds and how to use it.
cards.why: A reader landing in a directory from search or a stack trace has no other place to learn what the code is for. The README is the one file everyone opens first.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a test suite in which many tests share an expensive setup (a database schema and seed data, a container, a loaded application context).
cards.tool_gate: A CI job timeout plus a slowest-tests report in the build log (pytest or Django --durations, Gradle build scan).
cards.note: build once - Django (setUpTestData), Spring (context cache), Laravel (RefreshDatabase skips the migration), Microsoft (create and seed "exactly once"), Alloy.ai (migrate once per suite), GitLab (let_it_be); reset by rollback - Django, Rails, Spring, Laravel, Ecto, SQLAlchemy, Microsoft, Alloy.ai, GitLab; truncate for tests that must commit - Django, Microsoft
cards.rule: Build an expensive fixture once per test run, and reset state between tests with a rollback or a truncate, never a rebuild.
cards.why: A fixture that takes 20 seconds costs 20 seconds times the number of tests that rebuild it, and adding tests adds that cost again. One team measured about 10 seconds to drop, recreate and migrate a database per test and a 14-minute suite for 78 integration tests; wrapping each test in a rolled-back transaction cut it to 8 minutes. A slow suite then gets skipped locally, and changes arrive in larger, riskier batches.
cards.counterpoint: "A shared fixture breaks test isolation and blocks parallel runs." It does when the shared part is mutable or when tests commit. Keep the shared part read-only, undo each test's writes by rollback, give each parallel worker its own database, and give the few tests that must commit a separate database. A database kept between runs goes stale after a schema change, so rebuild it when the migrations change.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a repo whose layout or CI report separates unit, integration and end-to-end tests, so a reviewer can count tests per tier. Without that split there is no count to fail, so mark the card N/A.
cards.tool_gate: A CI report that prints the number of tests per tier next to the run time.
cards.note: Google gives a very rough 80/15/5 mix, GitLab says most tests should be unit tests, Microsoft (Azure Well-Architected) says use the pyramid as a guide; none sets a hard ratio
cards.rule: Keep most tests at the unit level, fewer at the integration level and fewest end-to-end.
cards.why: End-to-end tests are the slowest to run and the costliest to keep working, and a failure in one points at the whole system, not at a line. A suite that leans on them gives slow, flaky feedback. Unit tests run in milliseconds and locate the failure. The mix is a guide, not a quota.
cards.counterpoint: "Our service is a thin layer over a database, and a UI-heavy app gets little from unit tests." Fair: such systems get more value from integration tests, and the right mix is not fixed. Raise a finding only when end-to-end tests clearly dominate and the run is slow, and raise it for discussion, not as a defect.

cards.applies_when: A pull-request CI job runs a test suite that is slower than the team's feedback target for a pull request. Mark `N/A` when the full suite already fits the target.
cards.tool_gate: A PR job that runs the affected-tests command (`nx affected -t test`, Azure Test Impact Analysis, Develocity Predictive Test Selection), plus a full-suite job off the PR path.
cards.note: Meta, Microsoft, Shopify, Nx and Gradle (Develocity) select tests on the PR; Microsoft, Shopify and Gradle keep a full run before deploy or on a schedule (Meta's post does not say). Google's presubmit runs a team-chosen fast subset, not change-based selection
cards.rule: When the full suite is slower than the pull-request feedback target, run only the tests the change affects on the pull request, and run the full suite before deploy or on a schedule.
cards.why: A full suite on every pull request makes the queue wait for tests the change cannot break. Meta runs a third of the affected tests and reports catching more than 99.9 percent of regressions. Shopify runs the tests related to the change. Meta and Gradle pick them with a model trained on past results, not from what the change touches. The full run still happens, outside the pull-request gate.
cards.counterpoint: "Selection misses regressions." Shopify says a stale mapping let failing tests merge, about 0.06 percent of pull requests, and Shopify and Microsoft run every test when they cannot map or classify a change. Keep the full run, fall back to all tests when the mapping cannot decide, and do not present the pull-request run as full coverage. The selected tests gate the merge, as [[code-ci-gates]] asks; the full run comes before deploy or on a schedule.

cards.applies_when: Auditing a test suite, or reviewing a diff that adds or changes a test that waits for something to happen.
cards.tool_gate: Grep the test directories for sleep calls (`time.sleep`, `Thread.sleep`, `cy.wait(<number>)`) and fail CI on a new one.
cards.note: Google (small tests may not sleep or do I/O), Microsoft (avoid sleeps in unit tests) and Cypress (no arbitrary waits) back the sleep clause. The I/O half has Google and Microsoft only, with GitLab descriptive, so it sits in the Why
cards.rule: Do not wait in a test on a fixed delay; wait for the condition you need, or inject a clock.
cards.why: A delay that is long enough on a fast machine is too short on a loaded CI runner, so the test turns flaky, and it adds its whole length to every run even when the thing it waits for finished at once. A sleep also often means the code reaches a dependency the test should have replaced. For the same reasons, small unit tests do no real network, database or file-system I/O.
cards.counterpoint: "Some systems give no signal to wait on, so polling with a sleep is the only way." Poll with a short interval and a deadline, and return as soon as the condition holds, so the delay is a ceiling and not a cost. End-to-end and integration tests legitimately use real I/O and polling; the rule bans the fixed wait, not the poll.

cards.tool_gate: Dependabot or Renovate alerts with a severity SLA; OSV-Scanner or Scorecard `Vulnerabilities` in CI.
cards.note: Windows from OpenSSF (60 days for medium and above), CISA (two weeks for exploited CVEs) and GitHub (an SLA per severity). Risk acceptance is OWASP and GitHub only, so it sits in the Why
cards.rule: Write down how long a known-vulnerable dependency may stay unfixed and fix or upgrade it inside that window.
cards.why: A scan that finds a vulnerability and then sits unread protects nobody. An alert left open past its window is the failure, whatever the tool says. If a fix is not possible, record the accepted risk with the CVE, the reason, an owner and an expiry date that lapses on its own, so the open alert is a decision and not an oversight. cards.counterpoint: "Most alerts are not reachable in our code, so the window is busywork." Then triage the alert inside the window and dismiss it with the reason. Reachability is a finding to record, not a reason to skip the clock.

cards.applies_when: Auditing CI workflow files and release pipelines.
cards.tool_gate: OpenSSF Scorecard `Pinned-Dependencies` and `Dangerous-Workflow` checks; zizmor `unpinned-uses` audit.
cards.note: GitHub, OpenSSF and StepSecurity back the pin; GitHub, OpenSSF (Scorecard `Dangerous-Workflow`) and GitLab (protected runners keep untrusted code off deployment keys) back the untrusted-code boundary; OWASP's CI/CD cheat sheet is a reference only
cards.rule: Pin every CI action to a full commit SHA, and keep code from an unreviewed change out of any job that holds secrets or can deploy.
cards.why: The pipeline holds secrets and publish rights, so a compromised action or injected input owns the artifact. A privileged trigger that checks out a fork runs the fork's code with the base repository's token and secrets. Give workflows least-privilege tokens, keep untrusted event data out of `run:` and out of `pull_request_target` checkouts, and attach build provenance to releases. Review a change to the workflow file like any other code, because it can grant the next job anything. [[code-dependency-pinning]] covers dependency pins, and [[code-dependency-licence-sbom]] covers the inventory.
cards.counterpoint: "SHA pinning blocks automatic fixes and adds update churn." Let an update bot propose SHA bumps, so fixes still arrive as reviewed changes. Where the platform offers a lockfile for workflow dependencies, that lockfile is stronger than SHA pins and meets this check. A `pull_request_target` job can be safe when it never checks out or runs the fork's code, but splitting the privileged job from the untrusted one is easier to review than keeping them together.

cards.applies_when: A CI job or a service authenticates to a cloud provider.
cards.note: exchange for a short-lived credential backed by GitHub (no long-lived AWS secrets), Google (federated identities instead of a service account key) and Microsoft Entra (federation without managing secrets); pin the trust policy backed by GitHub (at least one condition, evaluate `sub`), Google (attribute condition) and GitLab (claims as condition keys in trust policies); GitLab's ID token page describes the token and its claims and does not argue against stored secrets
cards.rule: Exchange the platform's OIDC token for a short-lived cloud credential, and pin the trust policy to the workload.
cards.why: A cloud key stored as a CI secret stays valid until someone rotates it, and every job that reads it can use it elsewhere. An OIDC token is minted for one job, expires with it, and names the repository, branch or environment. The cloud side has to check that name. A trust policy with no `sub` condition lets any repository assume the role. Match on stable IDs, not names that can change, and check the audience too, so a token minted for another service or platform is refused.
cards.counterpoint: "Static keys work with every provider and every runner." Some providers and self-hosted setups cannot issue an OIDC token, so a scoped key is the fallback. If a key is unavoidable, scope it to the one deploy action, keep it in the platform's secret store rather than in the repository, rotate it, and keep the deploy job away from pull request code. Where OIDC is available, use it and pin the claim.

cards.note: state clause: W3C, Mozilla, Deque, Heydon Pickering; keys clause: W3C, Mozilla, Google web.dev; the accessible name has 2 orgs (W3C, Deque, both WCAG 4.1.2) and sits in Why; tool-gate rule names checked against the jsx-a11y README and the axe rule list

cards.why: A role only tells assistive technology what the element is. It adds no keyboard behaviour, and it says nothing about state. A `role="switch"` with no `aria-checked` is announced as a switch of unknown state. Wrong ARIA is worse than none, because it gives a screen-reader user a false picture. The widget also needs an accessible name, from its text or a label, or it is announced by role alone. An element that is not natively focusable also needs `tabindex="0"` to take part in the Tab order.
cards.counterpoint: "ARIA patterns are in the guide, so we copy them." Copy the keyboard table as well as the attributes. For a plain toggle, a `button` with `aria-pressed` is enough, and the label should stay the same when the state changes.

cards.applies_when: A function reads a file, a response or a request body through a reader that has a byte limit.
cards.tool_gate: Go lint rule against `io.LimitReader` on untrusted input; a test that feeds one byte more than the cap and expects an error.
cards.note: Google (Go) states the difference between a limit that ends with EOF and one that errors. Django raises an error at its cap, IETF defines 413 for a body over the cap, and OWASP says to reject instead of continuing with partial data. Python and Java readers that cut at n are not cited
cards.rule: When a size cap is reached, return an error; never hand back the first N bytes as if they were the whole input.
cards.why: A reader that stops at the cap reports a normal end of input. The code then parses half a JSON document, saves a truncated file, or hashes a prefix, and nothing says the data was cut. The failure appears later as a corrupt record. Check for bytes beyond the cap, or use a reader that errors.
cards.counterpoint: "We only need the first part, like a preview." Then say so in the name and the return value, such as `readPrefix` returning a `truncated` flag. The card fails a function that presents the prefix as the full content.

cards.applies_when: Styles or markup show an error, a required field, a status, or a link using colour.
cards.tool_gate: none; view the page in greyscale, or run a browser colour-vision emulation.
cards.rule: Pair every colour that carries meaning with a second cue: text, an icon, a shape, or an underline.
cards.why: Colour-blind users, glare, greyscale mode, and a screen reader all remove colour. A red border on a bad field, or a link that differs from body text only by hue, tells those users nothing.
cards.counterpoint: "Colour is the quickest cue, and the icon clutters the design." Colour can stay as the fast cue. The rule asks for a second one, not for removing the first. A text prefix such as "Error:" costs a few characters. A link in body text can also pass with 3:1 contrast against the text around it plus a non-colour cue on hover and focus. The underline is the simpler fix.

cards.applies_when: A comment sits next to code, or the code needs one to be understood.
cards.note: 4 orgs back the Rule (Google, Mozilla, Apache Flink; PEP 8 agrees). Google, the Linux kernel and Refactoring.Guru say to rewrite before commenting, so that point sits in the Why
cards.rule: Write comments that give a reason, a constraint, or a trade-off, and never restate what the next line does.
cards.why: A restating comment rots silently and adds nothing. A missing reason makes the next person delete the code that mattered. Rename or extract a step before you comment how the code works.
cards.counterpoint: "Good names make comments unnecessary." Names carry *what*. They cannot carry why a branch exists, a unit, or what callers may rely on, and a missing reason costs more than a slightly stale one. Rename first, then comment what the name cannot say. A stale comment is a defect either way. The test is whether the comment adds information that the code cannot carry.

cards.tool_gate: PMD CyclomaticComplexity (reports 10 or more), RuboCop Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity (configured Max), Microsoft CA1502 (default 25).
cards.rule: Set a cyclomatic complexity limit in the linter and keep every function under it.
cards.why: Each `if`, loop, `and` and `or` adds a path that a reader must follow and a test must cover. A function with 20 paths needs about 20 test cases, and nobody holds them all in mind at once. Set the limit in the linter so the count is not a matter of opinion. Common limits run from 10 to 25. Pick one and enforce it. Split a function that passes it into helpers that each do one job.
cards.counterpoint: "A flat `switch` over 30 cases is simple, and the split makes it worse." Agreed: one flat dispatch is easy to read, and a hard cap can force a bad split. Treat the limit as the point where a reviewer looks, and let a flat dispatch pass with a short note in the config or the code. Split by job, not to hit a number.

cards.applies_when: Code opens, reads, writes or deletes a file whose name or path includes request data.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `py/path-injection` (CWE-22) or the equivalent query for your language.
cards.rule: Resolve the final path and check that it stays inside the intended base directory before using it.
cards.why: A name like `../../etc/passwd`, or its percent-encoded form, walks out of the upload folder. Stripping `../` fails against `....//` and double encoding. The reliable check works on the resolved path. Better still, map a user choice to an ID and build the path in code.
cards.counterpoint: "We already strip `..`." String stripping is a blocklist and gets bypassed. Resolve first, compare second. Resolving catches a symlink that already points outside, but a symlink swapped in between the check and the open still escapes. For trees that untrusted users can write to, use a rooted open such as Go's `os.OpenInRoot`, which refuses any escape at open time.

fail.code: return send_file(os.path.join(UPLOADS, request.args["name"]))

cards.applies_when: Code compares a caller-supplied API key, token, signature, MAC or CSRF value with a stored or computed secret.
cards.tool_gate: Semgrep or CodeQL rules for `==` on secrets; Bandit has no rule for this, so grep for `==` next to names such as `token`, `signature`, `api_key`, `digest`.
cards.note: fn-csprng-for-secrets covers generating the value; this card covers checking it. A password hash check goes through the hash library's verify call (fn-password-slow-hash)
cards.rule: Compare a secret, token or MAC with the platform's constant-time function, never with `==` or `!=`.
cards.why: Ordinary equality stops at the first differing byte, so the response time tells an attacker how many leading bytes were right. Repeated requests recover the value one byte at a time. The constant-time call costs one line and no performance anyone will notice.
cards.counterpoint: "Network jitter hides the difference." Attackers average thousands of samples, and the jitter shrinks when they sit in the same cloud region. Also, some constant-time functions need equal lengths (Node throws; Go returns 0 at once, and Python's `compare_digest` can leak the length); compare fixed-length digests, or check the length first, since the length of a MAC is not secret.

pass.code:
def verify(body: bytes, header_sig: str, key: bytes) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(key, body, "sha256").hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected.encode(), header_sig.encode())   # bytes: a non-ASCII header raises no TypeError
# Go: subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(a, b) == 1
# Node: crypto.timingSafeEqual(bufA, bufB) after checking the lengths match

cards.applies_when: Code generates a token, session ID, password-reset code, API key, nonce or IV.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B311 (`random`) for Python; elsewhere a grep for `Math.random` and `rand()` in code that builds tokens or keys.
cards.rule: Draw every security-relevant random value from the platform CSPRNG.
cards.why: A general-purpose PRNG is predictable from a few outputs, so an attacker who sees two tokens can guess the next. A value built from the clock or another narrow range is just as guessable, and so is a CSPRNG seeded with one. UUIDv1 is time-based and also not secret. The API call is the whole fix, so it is cheap to demand.
cards.counterpoint: "Math.random is fine for a short-lived code." Short-lived codes still get brute-forced, and predictable ones need no brute force. Use the CSPRNG for anything an attacker gains from guessing.

fail.code:
token = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_letters, k=32))
reset = str(int(time.time()))

pass.code:
token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)           # os.urandom under the hood
# JavaScript: crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32))

cards.applies_when: A diff marks a function, class, option or setting as deprecated.
cards.tool_gate: A deprecation helper that requires `since` and `replacement` arguments, or a lint on `@deprecated` without both.
cards.note: Oracle (Java) and WordPress state both halves in the doc comment; Django requires a warning class that names the removal version, and says the upgrade path goes in the docs. Python, Angular, Node.js and Rust state parts of it
cards.rule: Say in a deprecation notice which version deprecated it and what replaces it.
cards.why: A bare "deprecated" tells callers to stop but not what to do. The version lets them judge how long they have, and the replacement is the migration. Name the removal version too when you have one.
cards.counterpoint: "We don't know the removal date." Then name the version it was deprecated in and the replacement, and leave the removal version out until it is decided.

fail.code: /** @deprecated Use something else. */

pass.code: /** @deprecated Since 3.2, use {@link #fetchAll()}. Removed in 4.0. */

cards.applies_when: A handler deletes user data, spends money, or sends something that cannot be recalled.
cards.tool_gate: none; a test that triggers the action and asserts a confirm step or an undo path exists.
cards.note: 4 orgs (NN/g, Apple, W3C, Shneiderman) for undo or confirm. Naming the outcome on the buttons and not defaulting to Cancel has 2 (NN/g, Apple), so it is in Why. Norman's undo chapter is a table of contents only, so topic only
cards.rule: Make a destructive action reversible with undo, or ask the user to confirm it before it runs.
cards.why: People click the wrong thing. If the action cannot be reversed and nothing stops it, one slip deletes their work. Undo costs a successful user nothing, while a dialog on every click trains them to click through. A dialog works best when its buttons name the outcome, such as "Delete project" and "Cancel", because "OK" and "Are you sure?" say nothing about what happens next. Always include Cancel as the clear, safe way out. Payments and legal commitments need the same care as deletes.
cards.counterpoint: "Confirm everything to be safe." Frequent prompts are dismissed without reading, so they protect nothing. Use undo for common actions and reserve the dialog for rare, irreversible ones. Do not make Cancel the default button.

fail.code: <button onClick={() => api.deleteProject(id)}>Delete</button>

cards.applies_when: A component opens a modal dialog, drawer, or menu that covers the page.
cards.tool_gate: none; a component test that opens the dialog, presses Tab and Escape, and asserts `document.activeElement`.
cards.note: Focus into the modal, Tab kept inside: W3C APG, Mozilla, GitHub (Primer). Escape is in W3C APG and WebAIM. Return focus to the opener is in W3C APG, WebAIM and GitHub (Primer), so it is in the Rule. Inert background is W3C APG and MDN (2 orgs), so it is in Why
cards.rule: When a modal opens, move focus into it and keep Tab inside it. Make Escape close it. When it closes, return focus to the control that opened it or, if it is gone, to the next logical control.
cards.why: Without it, a keyboard user keeps tabbing through the page behind the dialog, or gets stuck inside it with no exit. Content behind a modal must be inert, so neither keys nor the pointer reach it. Focus that falls to the top of the page after close makes them start over.
cards.counterpoint: "Our library handles it." Check, because a library that traps focus but never restores it is common. Prefer the native `<dialog>` with `showModal()`, which makes the page inert, closes on Escape and restores focus to the opener in current browsers, so the `onclose` handler above is belt and braces. A dialog built from generic elements must recreate each of those.

fail.code:
{open &&

Delete?

}

pass.code: Delete project?

cards.applies_when: Markup or a component hides content behind a `<details>`, an accordion, a "Show more" link, or an "Advanced" toggle.
cards.note: Not hiding what most users need: NN/g, GOV.UK, Appian. No organisation states that a closed disclosure must not hide the primary action, so that part is out of the Rule. The two-level cap is NN/g's alone, so it sits in Why
cards.rule: Do not hide a required field or information most users need behind a disclosure that starts closed.
cards.why: Users who never open the disclosure must still be able to finish the task. A closed `<details>` that holds the delivery date, or an "Advanced" section that holds a required field, sends most users hunting. Disclosure is for what only some users need. A field that appears because of the user's own answer, such as a follow-up field shown after they pick "Yes", is a conditional reveal, not a disclosure, and passes. Nesting adds its own cost. NN/g counts the first view as level one, so a disclosure inside a disclosure is already level three, and NN/g found designs past two levels lose people as they move between levels. In a step-by-step flow, such as picking a make and then a model, Appian says to disable fields that are not ready yet rather than hide them.
cards.counterpoint: "Hiding fields makes the form shorter." It makes the first view shorter, but required content still has to be found. Measure who opens the disclosure. If most users open it, the content belongs on the default view.

fail.code:
<details>
  <summary>Delivery options</summary>
  <label for="address">Delivery address</label>
  <input type="text" id="address" required>
</details>

pass.code:
<label for="address">Delivery address</label>
<input type="text" id="address" required>
<details>
  <summary>Add an order reference</summary>
  <label for="ref">Order reference</label>
  <input type="text" id="ref">
</details>

cards.applies_when: A function takes two or more arguments of one primitive type that mean different things (ids, amounts, units).
cards.tool_gate: Type checker with a newtype or branded-type pattern.
cards.note: one vendor's engineering guidance (opinion), from pstack principle-type-system-discipline
cards.rule: Give arguments with different meanings distinct types, so a call that swaps them fails to type-check.
cards.why: Two `str` ids compile in either order. The swap passes review and fails in production, often as a "not found" that looks like missing data.
cards.counterpoint: "Wrapper types add ceremony." A newtype costs one line and no runtime. Where the types differ only by argument position and the function has two arguments with obvious names, keyword-only parameters can be enough.

fail.code:
def refund(user_id: str, order_id: str) -> None: ...
refund(order.id, user.id)   # accepted

pass.code:
UserId = NewType("UserId", str)
OrderId = NewType("OrderId", str)
def refund(user_id: UserId, order_id: OrderId) -> None: ...

cards.applies_when: A public function can raise or throw, panic, or has a safety precondition the caller must meet.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff `DOC501` (pydoclint rules) or the language's doc lint.
cards.note: Rust, Google (Python) and Microsoft (.NET) state it. numpydoc makes Raises optional and Kotlin sets no expectation, so the Rule limits itself to exceptions a caller can cause or must handle
cards.rule: Document in the doc comment each error a public function can raise, each condition that makes it panic, and each precondition a caller must meet to call it safely.
cards.why: A caller reads the doc, not the body. An undocumented exception reaches production as an unhandled one, and an undocumented precondition becomes a crash or a memory bug.
cards.counterpoint: "Exceptions change and the list goes stale." That argues for a lint that checks it, and for listing only what callers can cause. Listing every exception from every callee is not what the rule asks.

pass.code:
def port_for(name):
    """Return the port for a service name.

    Raises:
        KeyError: If the name is not in PORTS.
    """
    return PORTS[name]

cards.applies_when: A diff changes the parameters of a function that has a doc comment, or adds a doc comment that lists parameters.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff `D417` (missing argument descriptions), `DOC102`, Checkstyle `JavadocMethod`, or the compiler's doc warning (C# `CS1572`, `CS1573`).
cards.note: Drupal, Microsoft (.NET) and Python PEP 257 state it. Google's guide only says to list each parameter, which is coverage
cards.rule: Make the parameters a doc comment lists match the function's signature, by name and in number.
cards.why: Callers pass keyword arguments by the documented name. A renamed, added or removed parameter left out of the doc sends them to a name that no longer exists.
cards.counterpoint: "Obvious parameters need no description." Then leave the list out. The rule is against a list that disagrees with the signature, not against a short one.

fail.code:
def send(to, subject, body):
    """Send a message.

    Args:
        recipient: Who gets it.
    """

pass.code:
def send(to, subject, body):
    """Send a message.

    Args:
        to: Who gets it.
        subject: The subject line.
        body: The message text.
    """

cards.applies_when: A function, class or module has a doc comment or docstring.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff `D205` and `D415` (pydocstyle), Checkstyle `SummaryJavadoc`, or the language's doc lint.
cards.note: Python PEP 257, Swift, Rust, Google, Drupal, WordPress, OpenStack and NumPy each state it. The exact form varies (sentence or fragment, one line or two), so the Rule keeps only what they share
cards.rule: Open each doc comment with one short summary line, then a blank line before any detail.
cards.why: Tools and readers show only the first line in indexes, hovers and search results. A summary that wraps, or that starts with detail, shows up cut off or empty.
cards.counterpoint: "A one-line docstring is enough for a trivial function." It is, and the rule is met: the summary line is the whole comment. The rule only applies the moment a second line appears.

pass.code:
def fetch(url):
    """Return the page body, following up to five redirects.

    Raise FetchError when the server keeps redirecting.
    """

cards.applies_when: A function checks an error or edge case, then continues with the main path.
cards.tool_gate: Pylint no-else-return (R1705), clang-tidy readability-else-after-return.
cards.rule: Handle the error or edge case first and return early, so the main path is not nested.
cards.why: Nesting the main path inside `if ok:` pushes the real work to the right and puts the failure case far from its check. Exiting early keeps the success path in one straight line down the page, and each failure sits next to its test. An `else` after a `return` adds a level of indentation for nothing.
cards.counterpoint: "A single exit point is easier to reason about." That holds when the function must release something on every path. Use `try`/`finally` or a context manager for that, and return early otherwise. Two symmetric branches of equal weight can stay as `if`/`else`.

cards.applies_when: The project has a written language policy, or its code may be read by people outside one language group.
cards.tool_gate: Spell-check or non-ASCII identifier lint.
cards.note: no source makes English universal; PEP 8 and LLVM give the rule, PEP 3131 the counter-view, so the card stays a project-policy check
cards.rule: Write identifiers and comments in English, unless the project policy names another language.
cards.why: Mixed languages split search, break naming conventions, and exclude readers. The tools, libraries, and error messages the code touches are already in English.
cards.counterpoint: "Domain terms have no English word." Keep the local term, once, in a glossary, and comment it ([[mod-one-name-per-concept]]). Python itself allows non-ASCII identifiers so that teams can name things in their own language (PEP 3131). If the code will never leave one language group, a team may choose that language. Write the choice down so the check can pass.

fail.code: def calcular_precio_total(carrito): ...   # next to total_price() and cart.items

pass.code: def calculate_total_price(cart): ...

cards.applies_when: A diff writes a message for a person or an API caller that reports a failure, outside form validation.
cards.note: GCC, Google (AIP-193), Atlassian and Apple state it; GitLab Pajamas says the same for forms. `fn-error-says-what-and-how` covers form validation
cards.rule: Say in an error message what went wrong and what the reader can do about it.
cards.why: A message that stops at "failed" leaves the reader to guess the cause and the fix, and sends them to a search engine or a support ticket.
cards.counterpoint: "Some causes are unknown." Then say what is known and where to look, such as a log id. Keep the cause and fix in the message and put internals in a details field.

fail.code: Error: request failed (code 4021)

pass.code: The export was cut off because the file is over 100 MB. Choose a shorter date range and try again.

cards.applies_when: Code builds the message shown when user input fails validation.
cards.tool_gate: none; a rendered check that submits each invalid field.
cards.rule: Show each validation error next to its field, in plain words that name what is wrong and how to fix it.
cards.why: "Invalid input" or an error code leaves the user to guess which field and what to change. A message at the top of a long form, or in a toast that fades, sends a magnifier user searching. Naming the fix is the shortest path to a valid form.
cards.counterpoint: "Detailed messages leak information." For a login, that is true: say "Email or password is wrong". For ordinary fields, the specific message is the fix. Hold back the suggestion only where it would weaken security.

fail.code: Error 422: invalid data

pass.code: Error: Enter a date of birth in the past, such as 27 3 1986

cards.applies_when: Code builds an error or diagnostic string that callers wrap, print after other text, or show next to other tool output.
cards.tool_gate: Go `staticcheck` `ST1005`, `revive` `error-strings`, Rust `clippy` has no rule; a regex check otherwise.
cards.note: Google (Go review comments and style decisions), Rust (rustc-dev-guide and API guidelines) and LLVM state it. It is for developer-facing and wrapped strings; user-facing UI text follows sentence case with a period
cards.rule: Start an error string in lowercase and end it without punctuation when it is wrapped or printed after other context.
cards.why: Wrapped errors join into one line ("open config: read file: permission denied"). A capital or a full stop in the middle reads as a typo and breaks the chain.
cards.counterpoint: "Messages shown to users should be proper sentences." They should, at the UI layer. Keep the wrapped error lowercase and format the user text where it is shown.

fail.code: return fmt.Errorf("Failed to read config.")

pass.code: return fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err)

cards.applies_when: Code renders a form again after validation fails.
cards.tool_gate: none; a rendered check that submits an invalid form and looks for the summary.
cards.rule: After a failed submit, show a summary at the top of the page that lists every error and links each one to its field.
cards.why: On a long form, an error below the fold goes unseen, and a screen reader user hears none of it until they reach the field. A summary at the top shows the whole problem at once and lets the user jump to each field. Show it even when there is only one error. Keep the message next to each field too; see [[fn-error-says-what-and-how]].
cards.counterpoint: "The summary repeats the per-field messages and adds noise." It repeats them on purpose: the summary is for finding the errors, and the field message is for fixing one. The cost is one short list.

fail.code: Enter a valid date

pass.code:
There is a problem

  • Enter an email address
  • Enter a valid date of birth
...

cards.applies_when: A diff writes or edits a message shown to a person when something fails.
cards.tool_gate: A regex or Vale rule for "please", "sorry", "oops" and "you forgot" in message strings.
cards.note: GOV.UK, Atlassian, Apple and Microsoft state it. Microsoft and Google allow narrow exceptions: a serious product fault, or asking permission
cards.rule: Do not blame the user, and do not pad error text with "please", "sorry" or "oops".
cards.why: The padding does not help the reader fix anything, and blame makes them stop reading. Say what happened and what to do, in neutral words.
cards.counterpoint: "A sorry shows empathy." For a serious fault that is ours, say so once and plainly. For input the user got wrong, the shortest fix reads as the kindest.

fail.code: Oops! You forgot to enter your email. Please try again, sorry for the trouble.

pass.code: Enter your email address.

cards.applies_when: The code changes the case of a string that a program reads (an identifier, header name or protocol key), in a runtime whose default depends on the machine's locale, such as Java, Kotlin or .NET.
cards.note: Oracle, Google (Android) and Microsoft back the case-change Rule. Number formatting and parsing has Google and Microsoft only, so it sits in the Why. Rust's to_lowercase is locale independent, so the rule does not apply there
cards.rule: Change the case of a machine-read string with an explicit root or invariant locale, never the default one.
cards.why: The default locale is whatever the machine or user has set. In Turkish, `"TITLE".toLowerCase()` gives `"tıtle"` in Java, so a header lookup or a key match that works on one host fails on another. The same applies to numbers: formatting a number with the default locale writes a decimal comma on some machines, and the program that reads the file cannot parse it. Use the locale of the person only for text shown to that person.
cards.counterpoint: "Our users and servers are all in en-US." The default is a property of each host, and a laptop, a container image or one customer in Istanbul is enough to change it. The explicit argument costs one word. For text a person reads, such as a name in a heading, the user's locale is the right one.

fail.code: String header = name.toLowerCase();

pass.code: String header = name.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);

cards.applies_when: A function queries a database or an API and then filters, counts, or sums the result in application code.
cards.rule: Filter, count, and aggregate in the query, and select only the columns the code uses.
cards.why: Loading every row to count it, or every column to read one, moves data across the network and through memory for nothing. `SELECT *` also rules out an index-only scan.
cards.counterpoint: "Pushing logic into the database makes it the bottleneck." It does for formatting and business rules. Filtering and aggregation are what the database is built for, and moving them out usually ships far more data than it saves.

fail.code:
total = sum(o.amount for o in Order.objects.all() if o.status == "paid")
n = len(Order.objects.filter(user=u))        # loads every row
emails = [u.email for u in User.objects.all()]   # loads every column

pass.code:
total = Order.objects.filter(status="paid").aggregate(Sum("amount"))["amount__sum"]
n = Order.objects.filter(user=u).count()
emails = User.objects.values_list("email", flat=True)

cards.applies_when: A type holds a set of independent options that can be combined, such as permissions or render options.
cards.tool_gate: .NET analyzers CA1027 (mark flag enums with FlagsAttribute) and CA2217 (do not mark other enums with it).
cards.rule: Model a set of independent flags with the language's or ecosystem's flags type (a `[Flags]` enum in C#, the `bitflags` crate in Rust, `EnumSet` in Java), and do not use a plain enum for it.
cards.why: A plain enum holds one value. Code that ORs its members together gets numbers that match no member, which print as a bare integer and fail an equality check. A flags type defines the combination, its printing, and the "no flags" value.
cards.counterpoint: "A plain enum with a `List<Access>` is simpler." For two or three options it can be. Once callers combine and test flags, a list loses the one-value set operations and the compact storage a flags type gives.

cards.applies_when: Styles or script change `outline`, `:focus`, or `:focus-visible`.
cards.tool_gate: Stylelint `declaration-property-value-disallowed-list` with `outline: ["none", "0"]`.
cards.note: SC 2.4.13 (AAA, size and contrast of the indicator) is not required here; the 3:1 figure comes from web.dev and SC 1.4.11. Focus hidden under a sticky bar (SC 2.4.11) has 2 orgs (W3C, Google), so it is in Why, not the Rule
cards.rule: Keep a visible focus indicator on every focusable element. Never set `outline: none` without a replacement.
cards.why: A keyboard user finds their place by the focus ring. Remove it and they navigate blind. A sticky header that covers the focused link has the same effect once they tab down the page. `scroll-padding-top` on `html`, as tall as the header, keeps the focused element in view.
cards.counterpoint: "Designers dislike the ring on mouse clicks." `:focus-visible` shows the ring for keyboard focus and hides it for most mouse clicks. Restyle the ring if you must. Do not remove it.

fail.code:
*:focus { outline: none; }
a:focus { outline: 0; }

pass.code: :focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1a56db; outline-offset: 2px; }

cards.applies_when: Markup or a component renders an input, a select, or a textarea.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint `jsx-a11y/label-has-associated-control` and axe `label`.
cards.note: Label tie: W3C, MDN, A11y Project, jsx-a11y. A placeholder is not a label: Deque, GOV.UK, WebAIM. USWDS covers only fieldset and legend
cards.rule: Tie every form control to a visible `<label>`, with `for` and a matching `id` or by wrapping it. A placeholder is not a label.
cards.why: A screen reader announces a bare field as "edit text". Voice-control users cannot say its name. A label also enlarges the click target. A placeholder vanishes when the user types, so it fails every user who looks away and comes back. Hints and examples vanish with it, so keep them out of the placeholder too.
cards.counterpoint: "The design shows a floating placeholder label." A floating label is a real label if it stays visible and is wired to the input. Use `aria-label` only where the purpose is already visible, such as a search field next to a Search button.

fail.code: Name

pass.code:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" autocomplete="email">

<label>Name <input type="text" name="name" autocomplete="name"></label>

cards.applies_when: Code calls `decodeURIComponent` or `decodeURI` on a query parameter, a hash, a path segment or other input a user controls.
cards.note: MDN lists the URIError and shows a try/catch; Node's querystring.unescape falls back to a decoder that does not throw
cards.rule: Wrap `decodeURIComponent` on user input in a `try`/`catch`, or parse with `URLSearchParams`, so that a malformed `%` sequence cannot throw.
cards.why: `decodeURIComponent("%E0%A4%A")` throws a `URIError`. A link with a stray `%` in its query then breaks the page script for that visitor, and anyone can craft such a link.
cards.counterpoint: "Only our own links reach this code." The address bar accepts anything, and other sites, chat apps and crawlers produce broken links. A guard costs three lines.

fail.code:
const q = decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1));
render(q);

cards.applies_when: Code starts a promise that can reject, such as `fetch`, `navigator.clipboard.writeText` or an async function, and does not return it.
cards.tool_gate: typescript-eslint `no-floating-promises`.
cards.note: MDN (Mozilla), web.dev (Google), typescript-eslint and Node.js each state the practice or its effect. Node.js ends the process by default on an unhandled rejection
cards.rule: Handle the rejection of every promise you start: `await` it inside `try`/`catch`, end the chain with `.catch()`, or return it to a caller that does.
cards.why: A browser API such as `writeText` rejects when the page lacks permission. With no handler the failure surfaces only as an `unhandledrejection` event, the user sees nothing, and the next step runs as if the call worked. In Node.js 15 and later the same rejection ends the process by default.
cards.counterpoint: "A global `unhandledrejection` handler already logs everything." It logs after the fact and cannot tell the user what to do. Only the call site knows which message and which fallback fit. Keep the global handler as a net, not as the handling.

cards.applies_when: A handler puts a request-derived value into a response header, such as `Location` or `Set-Cookie`.
cards.tool_gate: A test that sends `%0d%0a` in the echoed parameter and asserts a 400 or an encoded value; Node and Django throw at runtime, which is a guard rather than a linter.
cards.note: fn-redirect-target-allowlist checks where a redirect points; this card checks how the value is written. Both clauses have IETF (RFC 9112 names header-writing APIs that filter bad octets), MITRE, OpenJS and Django
cards.rule: Set every response header through the framework's header API, never by writing to the connection, and reject or encode CR and LF in any request-derived value.
cards.why: A header value is one line. Bytes that end the line start a new header, so a value the attacker controls can add a header or a second response. The browser follows the attacker's redirect, stores the attacker's cookie, or reads the attacker's body under your origin. Filtering `%0d%0a` at one decode step is not enough, because a second decode or a charset change puts the bytes back.
cards.counterpoint: "The framework rejects newlines, so this cannot happen." It does reject them, for headers set through its API. The failure sits in the code that writes the status line or the whole response itself, such as a proxy, a websocket handshake, or a hand-rolled error page. Keep those on the API path too.

fail.code:
u = request.query["u"]                    # %0d%0a arrives as CR LF
conn.write(f"HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /next?u={u}

")

pass.code:
u = request.query["u"]
resp = Response(status=302)
resp.headers["Location"] = "/next?u=" + quote(u, safe="")   # quote() encodes CR and LF; the header API rejects any that remain

cards.applies_when: Markup or a component renders a title or a section heading.
cards.tool_gate: axe `p-as-heading` (experimental) flags a bold paragraph styled as a heading; axe `heading-order` flags skipped levels.
cards.note: 3 orgs (W3C, Mozilla, A11y Project) for real heading elements. No skipped levels has 2 (W3C, A11y Project), so it is in Why. The one-`h1`-per-page rule is the A11y Project's alone, so this card does not require it
cards.rule: Mark every heading with a real `<h1>` to `<h6>` element, not a styled `div`, `span`, or `p`.
cards.why: Screen-reader users jump from heading to heading to scan a page. A `div` styled as a heading is invisible to that. Pick the level from the outline, not from the size you want: a skipped level, such as `h2` to `h4`, makes the outline look as if a section is missing.
cards.counterpoint: "The design needs a small `h2`." That is a CSS problem. Keep the level that matches the outline and set the size in the stylesheet. Jumping back up a level, such as `h4` to `h2`, is fine when a section ends.

fail.code:
Account

Billing

Invoices

pass.code:
Account

Billing

Invoices

cards.applies_when: The code runs a long-lived loop, a background task or request-scoped work in a language with a cancellation mechanism (context, token, interrupt, coroutine or asyncio task).
cards.note: Each clause has its own organisations. Check the signal between steps - Google (Go), Microsoft (.NET), Oracle (Java) and JetBrains (Kotlin). Re-raise a caught cancellation - Python, Google (Android Kotlin) and JetBrains
cards.rule: Take a cancellation signal in long-running work and check it between steps; when a handler catches a cancellation, finish the cleanup and re-raise it.
cards.why: A caller that timed out or gave up still has its work running unless the work looks at the signal, so abandoned requests keep holding connections and threads. Cancellation is cooperative: nothing stops the code that does not check. A handler that swallows the cancellation turns a stop request into a task that carries on, and timeouts built on cancellation then misbehave.
cards.counterpoint: "Some steps must not be interrupted, such as a commit or a write-ahead flush." Let that step finish and check the signal after it; the rule asks for a check between steps, not an abort in the middle of one. A deliberately detached task that must outlive the request should say so and carry its own owner and stop condition.

cards.applies_when: Markup or a component renders an image, an icon, or a chart.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint `jsx-a11y/alt-text` and axe `image-alt` catch a missing `alt`. Only a person can judge whether the text is accurate.
cards.note: 5 orgs back the rule; no tool can check that the text is right
cards.rule: Give every `` an `alt` attribute: text that serves the image's purpose, or `alt=""` when the image is decorative.
cards.why: A screen reader has nothing to say about an image with no `alt`, and often reads the file name instead. An informative image with an empty `alt` hides its content. A decorative image with a long `alt` adds noise to every page view. Words such as "image" or "chart", and file names, say nothing about what the image is for.
cards.counterpoint: "A linter already checks `alt`." It checks that the attribute exists, not that the text fits the image or the context. Review the text itself. For a chart, give a short `alt` plus the data nearby as text.

cards.applies_when: A function awaits or calls several I/O operations that do not depend on each other.
cards.note: Start independent work together: Python, Mozilla, Go (errgroup). Sequence only when one call needs another's result: Mozilla, Microsoft (a vendor), Apple (a vendor); the cursor/plugins skill is opinion and supports it
cards.rule: Start independent I/O together and wait for all of it; run calls in sequence only when one needs the result of another.
cards.why: Sequential awaits add their latencies. Three 200 ms calls take 600 ms in a row and 200 ms together.
cards.counterpoint: "Parallel calls load the dependency harder and complicate errors." Cap fan-out with a semaphore or pool, and use a task group so one failure cancels the rest. Waiting for all of it still has to surface a failure: `errgroup`'s `Wait` and `Promise.all` report the first error, so check it. A deliberate order, for rate limits or ordering, is a valid reason. Write it down.

fail.code:
user = await get_user(uid)
orders = await get_orders(uid)       # does not use `user`
prefs = await get_prefs(uid)

pass.code:
user, orders, prefs = await asyncio.gather(
    get_user(uid), get_orders(uid), get_prefs(uid))

cards.applies_when: A function builds a string from pieces in a loop whose length depends on input.
cards.tool_gate: Linter rule for string concatenation in a loop (for example pylint `consider-using-join`).
cards.rule: Build a string from a loop with a builder or a join, never with repeated `+=`.
cards.why: Strings are immutable in Python, Go, Java, and .NET, so each `+=` copies everything built so far. Over n pieces the total cost grows with the square of the output length.
