cards.counterpoint: "CPython optimises `+=` in place." Sometimes: only in CPython, and only while nothing else holds a reference to the string. Code that leans on it turns quadratic on other runtimes. A small fixed number of pieces is fine with `+` or an f-string, which read better. The rule covers loops over input-sized data.

pass.code: out = "".join(f"{row.id},{row.name}\n" for row in rows)

cards.applies_when: Code accepts a JWT as proof of identity or permission.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `js/jwt-missing-verification`; a grep for `verify_signature": False` and for `jwt.decode(` calls with no `algorithms=`.
cards.rule: Verify the signature against a fixed list of accepted algorithms, and check `iss`, `aud`, and `exp`, before reading any claim.
cards.why: If the verifier takes the algorithm from the token header, an attacker picks `none` or turns an RSA public key into an HMAC secret. Claims read before verification are attacker text. Pinning the algorithm and binding each key to one algorithm closes both. Leave `none` out of the list, and never mix HMAC and public-key algorithms in it. Pick the key by `kid` from the issuer's published key set. Requiring `exp` means a stolen token stops working.
cards.counterpoint: "Our gateway already verifies the token." Then the service trusts a header that any internal caller can forge. Verify at each trust boundary, or prove that only the gateway can reach the service.

fail.code:
claims = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})
claims = jwt.decode(token, key)               # PyJWT 1.x: algorithm taken from the header

pass.code:
claims = jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"],
                    issuer=ISSUER, audience=AUD,
                    options={"require": ["exp", "iss", "aud"]})

cards.applies_when: A form handler or component re-renders after a failed validation or a failed submit.
cards.tool_gate: none; a test that submits an invalid form and asserts the entered values are still there.
cards.note: GOV.UK says validate on submit and Baymard says validate when the user leaves a field; this card takes no side on timing. Shneiderman's rule 8 is about re-entry across screens and is related, not the same.
cards.rule: After a failed validation or submit, show the form again with every value the user entered, correct or not.
cards.why: A form that wipes its fields turns one typo into ten minutes of retyping, and some users give up. The user fixes one field, not the whole page.
cards.counterpoint: "Clear a password or card number on error for safety." That is a fair exception for secrets, and the message should say so. Everything else the user typed stays.

cards.applies_when: Markup or styles lay out a form field and its visible label.
cards.note: 4 orgs put the label above a text field (GOV.UK, Atlassian, NN/g for mobile and short forms, W3C as one of two conventions). The checkbox and radio order is W3C's alone, so it sits in Why. W3C also says the choice depends on nearby fields, so the severity is discuss. Nothing between label and field has only Atlassian and NN/g, so it sits in Why
cards.rule: Put the visible label of a text input, select, or textarea directly above it.
cards.why: A label sitting below a field, or halfway between two fields, gets read as the label of the wrong one. W3C notes that a label above the field cuts sideways scrolling for low-vision and phone users, who can lose a side label off the edge of the screen. Hint and error text can go between the label and the field. A help link, a button, or another field cannot. Placeholder text is not a label: it vanishes when the user types. Checkboxes and radios are the exception: W3C puts the control first and its label to the right, in left-to-right languages.
cards.counterpoint: "Labels to the left fit our long desktop admin form better." Labels beside the field are an accepted convention for very long desktop forms. Accept a left label on such a form if it stays next to its own field at every breakpoint. A wrapping label, as in the `fn-form-control-has-label` PASS, passes when CSS sets the label text to `display: block` so it sits above the field. A label below the field is still a `FAIL`. This card covers placement only. `fn-form-control-has-label` covers the code tie between label and field.

fail.code:
<input type="text" id="town">
<label for="town">Town or city</label>

pass.code: For example, SW1A 2AA

cards.applies_when: A function has grown past the length limit the project sets, or the project has no limit yet.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint max-lines-per-function (default 50), Pylint too-many-statements (R0915, max-statements default 50), Checkstyle MethodLength (default 150), RuboCop Metrics/MethodLength (default 10), PMD NcssCount (methodReportLevel default 60). PMD CognitiveComplexity (default 15) and Microsoft CA1505 (maintainability index threshold 10) measure complexity, not length.
cards.note: length is a signal, not a defect. ESLint, Checkstyle, Pylint, RuboCop and PMD ship a size gate. Google (about 40 lines, no hard limit), the Linux kernel, Pylint and Microsoft CA1505 back the split clause and keep a long simple body, so the card asks for an inspection when a function passes the limit
cards.rule: Split a function that passes the project's length limit (about 40 lines if it sets none) unless its body is one simple operation or one flat dispatch.
cards.why: A long body hides its steps. Validation, pricing, a charge, the order write and the receipt become one block, and a reader cannot test, skip or reorder one of them. Linters ship a limit because a long method is hard to understand and does too many things, so set one in the project's linter. The number is where the inspection starts, not a verdict. A body that is one flat dispatch can stay long, because its reader follows one dispatch rule.
cards.counterpoint: "A long function is one operation, and the split scatters the sequence." Length alone does not decide. A hard limit can force bad splits, which is why Google sets none, so treat the limit as a prompt to inspect. Keep the function when its body is one simple operation or one flat dispatch table. Split when the lines serve different jobs, and let each new function own one of them.

cards.applies_when: A URL taken from remote JSON, a query parameter or stored data is written to `href`, `src`, `location` or `window.open`.
cards.note: OWASP says URL properties need URL validation even where React blocks javascript: URLs; Angular sanitizes URL bindings. fn-no-raw-html-sink covers HTML sinks, and fn-redirect-target-allowlist covers server redirects
cards.rule: Parse a URL that comes from data and allow only `https:` (and `http:` or `mailto:` where needed) before you set it as a link target.
cards.why: A `javascript:` URL in an `href` runs script in your origin when clicked, and a data feed or an API you do not fully control can supply one. Some frameworks block it, but the check belongs to the app, because the next sink may not be covered.
cards.counterpoint: "The feed is ours, so it is trusted." It is trusted until a third party writes into it or someone breaches it. The check is two lines and does not depend on who owns the source.

fail.code:
const item = await (await fetch("/feed.json")).json();
link.href = item.url;

cards.applies_when: A function handles an error by logging it and also returning or rethrowing it.
cards.tool_gate: A linter for log-and-return (Go `errorlint` patterns, SonarQube `S2139`), or a review check.
cards.note: Google (Go best practices), Uber (Go style guide) and Kubernetes (logging guide) state it
cards.rule: Handle an error once: return it or log it, not both.
cards.why: Each caller up the stack repeats the same log line, so one failure fills the log with copies and hides the real order of events. The caller knows if the error is expected and can log it once, or retry.
cards.counterpoint: "I want the log at the point of failure." Add context with wrapping and log once at the boundary that decides the outcome. A top-level handler is where logging belongs.

cards.applies_when: A CLI command, admin page or debug view prints stored configuration that can include tokens, API keys, or URLs with embedded secrets.
cards.tool_gate: A test that seeds a fake token, runs the list/show/debug command, and asserts the full value is absent from stdout and stderr.
cards.note: sys-secrets-and-errors covers secrets in errors and logs; this card covers a command whose purpose is to display configuration. svc-no-secrets-in-url covers secrets in request URLs
cards.rule: Mask credentials in list, show and debug output (keep only the last four characters), and print a full value only behind an explicit flag.
cards.why: Output gets pasted into tickets, chat and CI logs, and screen-shared. A webhook URL that carries its token, or an API key shown whole by `config show`, becomes a leak the first time someone asks for help. Masking keeps the output useful for telling two credentials apart.
cards.counterpoint: "Users need the value to copy it." Then give them an explicit reveal flag that is off by default, so the copy is a deliberate act and the default output is safe to paste. Never ask users to scrape the full secret out of a listing.

cards.applies_when: The code measures how long something took, or waits until a deadline, inside one process.
cards.note: Go, Oracle (Java), Android and Mozilla state it as a rule; Python and Rust describe the monotonic clock without telling you to prefer it, so they are extra sources. In Go, time.Now carries a monotonic reading, so subtracting two Time values is already safe
cards.rule: Measure elapsed time and timeouts with a monotonic clock, never by subtracting wall-clock readings.
cards.why: The wall clock jumps when the system clock is corrected, set by hand or resumed after a pause, so a difference of two readings can be negative or hours long. A timeout built on it fires at once or never. A monotonic reading only moves forward, but it means something only inside one process: a deadline saved to a database or sent to another host still uses wall time.
cards.counterpoint: "The drift is tiny, and the wall clock is what the logs show." Corrections of seconds happen on any host that syncs its time, and one negative duration breaks a rate limiter or a retry loop. Keep wall time for what people read, such as a log line or a created-at field, and take the elapsed time from the monotonic clock.

fail.code:
start = time.time()
do_work()
elapsed = time.time() - start
deadline = time.time() + 30

pass.code:
start = time.monotonic()
do_work()
elapsed = time.monotonic() - start
deadline = time.monotonic() + 30

cards.applies_when: An `if` or `while` joins three or more terms in one expression.
cards.rule: Name each compound condition by assigning its sub-conditions to booleans that say what they mean.
cards.why: Dense conditions force the reader to simulate them. A name states the intent and gives a place to put the next clause.
cards.counterpoint: "More variables, more state to track." These are immutable one-use names, and they replace a comment you would otherwise write. If the names turn out vague (`flag1`), the condition probably mixes two concepts. Fix that instead.

fail.code: if u.active and not u.banned and (u.plan == "pro" or u.trial_days > 0) and not u.locked:

cards.applies_when: A component handles a click or tap, or navigates.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint `jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events` and `jsx-a11y/no-static-element-interactions`; `jsx-a11y/anchor-is-valid` for `href="#"`.
cards.note: 4 orgs; Norman's perceived-affordance essay is context only
cards.rule: Use `<button>` for an action and `<a href>` for navigation. Do not attach a click handler to a `div`, `span`, or `a` with no `href`.
cards.why: A `div` is not in the tab order, has no role, and ignores Enter and Space. A keyboard or screen-reader user cannot reach or operate it. A fake link also loses open-in-new-tab and copy-link. A native element gives all of that with no code.
cards.counterpoint: "Native buttons are hard to style." They are not: reset `border`, `background`, and `font` on the element. Rebuilding the keyboard, role, and focus behaviour by hand costs more and fails more often. Where a custom widget is unavoidable, follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices pattern for it. A `div` that must take a click needs `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, and Enter and Space handlers; the role alone does not make it operable.

fail.code:
Save
Menu navigate("/billing")}>Billing

pass.code: Billing

cards.applies_when: Code nests conditions or loops several levels deep.
cards.tool_gate: PMD AvoidDeeplyNestedIfStmts (problemDepth 3), Pylint too-many-nested-blocks (R1702, max-nested-blocks 5).
cards.rule: Keep control-flow nesting shallow.
cards.why: Each level of nesting adds a condition the reader must keep in mind while reading the lines inside it. Deep code is harder to read and easier to break. Flatten it with early exits (see [[fn-early-return-no-else]]), and set a limit in the linter. The linters above stop at 3 levels of `if` or 5 nested blocks by default.
cards.counterpoint: "Some data is nested, so the code must nest too." Walking a tree or a grid needs the loops. Move the inner body into a named function, or hide the walk in a generator, so each function stays flat.

cards.applies_when: Markup or CSS hides an element that can take keyboard focus.
cards.tool_gate: axe `aria-hidden-focus`.
cards.rule: Never put `aria-hidden="true"` on an element that can take focus, or leave an element visually hidden while it has focus.
cards.why: Keyboard focus still lands on the element, but a screen reader is told to skip it. The user tabs onto something that is not announced, or never reaches a control that does work. To hide a control, hide it for everyone, or remove it from the tab order too. A `role="presentation"` on a focusable element conflicts the same way: browsers ignore the role there, so the control is still announced, and axe flags it.
cards.counterpoint: "The icon button is decorative, so hide it." If it takes focus, it does something, and it needs a name. Hide the icon inside the button, not the button.

fail.code: Help Skip to content

pass.code:
Help
Admin
Skip to content

cards.applies_when: Code runs on an event loop or an async runtime (asyncio, Node.js, Tokio, ASP.NET async handlers).
cards.tool_gate: Linter rule for blocking calls in async functions (for example ruff ASYNC); asyncio debug mode flags slow callbacks.
cards.rule: Never make a blocking I/O call or run long CPU work directly in async code; use the async API or hand the work to a thread or worker.
cards.why: An event loop runs one callback at a time. A `time.sleep`, a synchronous HTTP call, or a big hash inside a handler stalls every other request on that loop, not just the slow one.
cards.counterpoint: "This call is fast enough." A short read from a local SSD can be quicker synchronously. Measure it with asyncio debug mode or the runtime's equivalent. A call that crosses the network, or that waits on anything outside the process, is never in that class.

fail.code:
async def handler(req):
    data = requests.get(url).json()          # blocks the loop
    digest = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw, salt, 600_000)

pass.code:
async def handler(req):
    data = (await client.get(url)).json()    # httpx.AsyncClient
    digest = await asyncio.to_thread(hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac, "sha256", pw, salt, 600_000)

cards.applies_when: A function writes to a parameter or to an object the caller still owns, such as a list, map, state object or shared configuration.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint no-param-reassign with props true (the default props false misses param.field = value); Pylint dangerous-default-value (W0102) for a mutable default.
cards.note: parameters and caller-owned objects only; module and class state belongs to mod-no-module-mutable-state, and a fresh local object may be mutated before it is returned
cards.rule: Do not mutate a parameter or an object the caller owns, unless the function is documented as mutating it.
cards.why: The caller still holds the old reference, so the change lands at a distance. A list passed to one function changes under the next loop, a shared default collects values across calls, and a mutated state object never triggers a re-render. Return a new value or a copy: the change shows at the call site and the old value stays safe to compare. A fresh local object is different. Nothing else references it yet, so build it in place and return it.
cards.counterpoint: "Copying on every update is expensive, and an in-place reducer is simpler." Copy only the part you change and share the rest, which keeps the cost low for wide objects. An in-place API is honest when its name says it mutates and its caller owns the object, as with a builder or a buffer. The failure is a quiet change to something the caller still uses. A linter set to catch only reassignment will miss a field write, so turn on the property check too.

cards.applies_when: Code reads shared state, yields (await, I/O, a lock release), then writes based on the earlier read.
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Make check-and-write one atomic operation where the state lives, and never split it across a suspension point.
cards.why: Another task runs at every yield. Two withdrawals both read 100, both pass the check, and the balance goes negative. In SQL, read the row with a locking read (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) or use serializable isolation, because a plain read takes no lock.
cards.counterpoint: "A lock fixes it." A process-local lock covers one process. With two workers or two hosts, you need a transaction, an atomic statement, an idempotency key, or optimistic concurrency. Name the other readers and writers of that state.

cards.applies_when: Code runs `eval`, `exec`, or `new Function`, or compiles a template, and some of the text comes from a request, a file, a database row, or model output.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B307 (`eval`) and B102 (`exec_used`); CodeQL `py/code-injection` and `py/template-injection`; ESLint `no-eval` and `no-implied-eval`.
cards.note: overlaps fn-no-shell-with-input (commands, not code) and fn-no-raw-html-sink (HTML, not templates); ASVS 1.3.2 and 1.3.7
cards.rule: Never pass untrusted text to `eval`, `exec`, `new Function`, or a template compiler. Pass it to a fixed template or a parser as data.
cards.why: Each of these turns a string into code that runs with the server's rights, so one field becomes remote code execution. A template engine counts: `render_template_string(request.args["msg"])` lets `{{ config }}` or worse run on the server. An expression language, such as SpEL, carries the same risk. Parse the data format instead (`json.loads`, `ast.literal_eval`), and keep templates in files the author wrote, with user values passed as variables. Better still, avoid run-time code generation where a parser or a lookup does the job.
cards.counterpoint: "Users need formulas, so we need `eval`." Write or adopt a small expression parser that knows only numbers and the operators you allow. A sandbox around `eval` loses to the next escape someone publishes.

fail.code:
total = eval(request.args["expr"])
html = render_template_string("Hello " + request.args["name"])

pass.code:
data = json.loads(request.get_data())
html = render_template("hello.html", name=request.args["name"])

cards.applies_when: Code reads or writes an attribute or field by a dynamic key when the name is known at write time.
cards.tool_gate: ruff B009 / B010
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Use plain field access, and reserve dynamic access for genuinely dynamic names.
cards.why: Dynamic access defeats rename tools, type checking, and grep. A rename misses it, and it fails at runtime.
cards.counterpoint: "I loop over field names." That is fine when the set of names is the data (a mapping from column names, a serializer). If the names are fixed, unroll the loop.

fail.code: value = getattr(order, "total")

pass.code: value = order.total

cards.applies_when: A test body contains if, for, while or switch, or a table test branches on its case.
cards.tool_gate: none; a review check for control flow inside test functions.
cards.rule: Keep `if`, `for`, `while` and `switch` out of test bodies.
cards.why: A test with logic can be wrong itself, and nobody tests the tests. A loop that skips a case or an `if` that skips an assertion turns a failure into a pass. A table test that branches on its case means the cases do not share one expectation.
cards.counterpoint: "A loop over many inputs is shorter." A parameterised test is just as short and reports each case separately. Cases that need different checks are different behaviours, so each gets its own test.

cards.applies_when: A literal string or number carries meaning the reader must guess (status codes, mode names, limits).
cards.tool_gate: none (partial: ruff PLR2004)
cards.rule: Give every meaningful literal a name: an enum member or a constant.
cards.why: Literals drift. `"canceled"` in one file and `"cancelled"` in another is a silent bug, and nobody can grep for what `3` means.
cards.counterpoint: "A constant used once is noise." True for self-evident values (`0`, `1`, `""`, an index into a pair, a default value). A literal that is itself the abstraction, such as a coefficient in a formula, needs no name either. The rule is for literals whose meaning is not visible at the use site, or that appear twice. The failure is two spellings of one concept, not the literal itself.

fail.code:
if resp.status == 404 or retries > 3:
    mode = "fast"

pass.code:
if resp.status == HTTPStatus.NOT_FOUND or retries > MAX_RETRIES:
    mode = Mode.FAST

cards.applies_when: A handler copies request fields into a model, ORM entity or settings object.
cards.tool_gate: A custom Semgrep rule for `Model(**request.json)`; tests that post extra fields such as `is_admin` and assert they are ignored or rejected.
cards.rule: Bind request data to a DTO or an explicit field allowlist, never straight onto the model.
cards.why: When the model has `is_admin`, `balance` or `owner_id`, a client that adds those keys to the JSON body sets them. A blocklist fails the day someone adds a new sensitive column. The allowlist still needs the object-level check from [[fn-object-level-authz]].
cards.counterpoint: "A DTO per endpoint is boilerplate." Generate DTOs from the API schema. The boilerplate costs less than one privilege escalation.

fail.code:
user = User(**request.json)          # body {"name": "a", "is_admin": true}
user.save()

pass.code:
class UserIn(BaseModel):            # only editable fields exist here
    name: str
user = User(**UserIn(**request.json).model_dump())

cards.applies_when: Code turns bytes or text from outside the process into objects.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B301 (`pickle`) and B506 (`yaml_load`), CodeQL `py/unsafe-deserialization`; a grep for `ObjectInputStream`, `BinaryFormatter` and `unserialize` elsewhere.
cards.rule: Parse untrusted input with a data-only format, never with a native object deserialiser.
cards.why: `pickle`, `ObjectInputStream`, `BinaryFormatter` and full-power YAML loaders can run attacker-chosen code while they load, so validating after the call is too late. JSON cannot instantiate arbitrary classes. Validate the parsed data against a schema afterwards, as the PASS does.
cards.counterpoint: "The data comes from our own queue." Anyone who can write to the queue can run code on every consumer, so the queue is a trust boundary. Signing the payload, or a Java serialisation filter that allowlists classes, narrows the risk while you migrate. The call still fails this check until it reads a data-only format.

fail.code:
obj = pickle.loads(request.data)
cfg = yaml.load(body, Loader=yaml.Loader)

pass.code:
obj = Model.model_validate_json(request.data)
cfg = yaml.safe_load(body)

cards.applies_when: Markup sets `tabindex`, or a layout reorders content with CSS.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint `jsx-a11y/tabindex-no-positive`; axe `tabindex`.
cards.note: 4 orgs (W3C, Google, WebAIM, A11y Project); both tool-gate rule names checked against the jsx-a11y README and the axe rule list
cards.rule: Write the DOM in reading order and never set `tabindex` above 0.
cards.why: A positive `tabindex` jumps those elements to the front of the tab order, ahead of everything else on the page. Each new control then needs a new number, and the order stops matching what the user sees. CSS that moves items visually without moving them in the DOM does the same thing.
cards.counterpoint: "The visual layout puts the sidebar first, but the main content comes first in the DOM." Reorder the DOM to match, or accept the difference only if the order still makes sense to a keyboard user. Do not patch it with numbers.

fail.code:
<input name="last" tabindex="2">
<input name="first" tabindex="1">
<button tabindex="3">Save</button>

pass.code:
<input name="first">
<input name="last">
<button>Save</button>
<!-- tabindex="0" only to add a custom widget to the order; tabindex="-1" to focus it from script -->

cards.applies_when: JavaScript or TypeScript code merges, clones, or assigns properties whose key names come from JSON, a query string, or other untrusted input.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `js/prototype-pollution-utility` and `js/prototype-polluting-assignment`.
cards.note: ASVS 15.3.6; fn-no-mass-assignment covers the same input setting fields on a model instead of the prototype
cards.rule: Never write an untrusted key into a plain object. Use a `Map`, an object from `Object.create(null)`, or an allowlist of keys.
cards.why: `obj[key] = value` with `key` set to `__proto__` writes to `Object.prototype`, so every object in the process gains that property. An attacker who sets `isAdmin` or a template option there can skip checks or reach code execution. The bug sits in generic helpers such as deep merge, deep clone and path setters, so one bad helper exposes every caller. Blocking `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` inside a deep merge helps, but a blocklist misses obfuscated keys, so treat it as a stopgap.
cards.counterpoint: "Just freeze `Object.prototype` at startup." That helps, but it can break libraries that patch prototypes, and it leaves `constructor.prototype` paths in class instances open. Fix the merge, and add the freeze on top if your dependencies allow it.

cards.applies_when: Code writes a string into a page, a template or a rendered model-output view.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint (`no-unsanitized/property`, `no-unsanitized/method`, `react/no-danger`) and template-engine autoescape checks.
cards.rule: Write untrusted text through an encoding sink (`textContent`, auto-escaped template), never through a raw HTML sink.
cards.why: One `innerHTML` of a username or of model output runs the attacker's script with the victim's session. Encoding must match the context: body, attribute, script string and URL each differ. Framework escape hatches such as `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` have the same effect.
cards.counterpoint: "We need to render rich text." Then sanitise with a maintained library such as DOMPurify at render time and add a CSP as a second layer. A CSP alone is not a fix, because it is defence in depth. Where the browser supports Trusted Types, enforce them through the CSP, so HTML sinks reject plain strings and take only the sanitiser's output.

fail.code:
el.innerHTML = comment.body;
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: reply }} />

cards.applies_when: Code starts a process and some part of the command comes from a request, a file or model output.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B602 (`subprocess_popen_with_shell_equals_true`) and B605 (`start_process_with_a_shell`) for Python.
cards.rule: Start processes with the program and each argument as separate list items, and never through a shell string.
cards.why: A shell reads `;`, `|` and `$()` as commands, so a filename of `a; rm -rf ~` runs. Argument arrays skip the shell. A library call skips the process too, so it is better still when one exists. The values still need validation, since an argument beginning with `-` becomes an option; end options with `--` where the tool allows it.
cards.counterpoint: "We need shell features like pipes." Chain two `subprocess` calls in code, or use the library that does the job. If a shell is unavoidable, build the string only from constants.

fail.code:
os.system("convert " + upload_name + " out.png")
subprocess.run(f"git log {branch}", shell=True)

pass.code:
subprocess.run(["convert", upload_path, "out.png"], check=True)   # upload_path is a server-generated name
subprocess.run(["git", "log", branch], check=True)   # branch checked against an allowlist

cards.applies_when: A handler loads, changes or deletes a record by an ID that comes from the request.
cards.tool_gate: Authorization tests that call each endpoint as a second user; no static gate catches a missing check.
cards.rule: Check that the caller may act on the specific record before returning or changing it.
cards.why: A login proves who the caller is, not which records they own. Without a per-object check, changing `id=41` to `id=42` reads or edits another user's data (IDOR, also called BOLA). Random IDs only hide the problem.
cards.counterpoint: "The IDs are UUIDs, nobody can guess them." A UUID leaks through logs, links and shared screenshots, and it is not an access check. Keep it as a second layer. Scope the query itself (`WHERE owner_id = :me`) so the check cannot be forgotten on the next endpoint.

fail.code:
order = db.get(Order, request.args["id"])     # any logged-in user, any order
return order.to_json()

cards.applies_when: A function or constructor signature takes more parameters than the project's limit allows, or the project has no limit yet.
cards.tool_gate: ESLint max-params (default 3), Pylint too-many-arguments (R0913, max-args default 5) and too-many-positional-arguments (R0917, default 5), Checkstyle ParameterNumber (default 7), RuboCop Metrics/ParameterLists (default 5), PMD ExcessiveParameterList (minimum default 10).
cards.note: the defaults range from 3 to 10, so the card asks for the project's limit; Checkstyle lets a project ignore an overridden method whose signature it does not control
cards.rule: Set a parameter-count limit in the project's linter, and keep signatures within it.
cards.why: Every positional value is a fact the caller must remember and a slot that can take the wrong one, especially when several share a type. `create_user(name, email, street, city, zip, country, plan, trial_days)` cannot be read at the call site and is easy to call in the wrong order. A named record or a builder gives the values names and lets the compiler and the reader check them. Group only values that already travel together, and keep required fields required.
cards.counterpoint: "A parameter object just moves the fields into another class and can hide required ones." A record that groups values with one owner is not hiding them, and a builder that names each required value at the call site is clearer than eight slots. The failure is a bag object with optional fields that may be missing. Do not introduce one. A signature the author cannot change, such as an override of a third-party method, is exempt, because the parameter count is not the author's decision. Keyword-only parameters fix the call-site order problem but still count toward the limit, so group the values that travel together.

fail.code:
def create_user(name, email, street, city, zip, country, plan, trial_days):
    ...

cards.applies_when: Code accepts a new password from a user, at sign-up, a change, or a reset.
cards.tool_gate: none; a test that submits a short password. ASP.NET Identity sets it with Password.RequiredLength.
cards.rule: Enforce a minimum password length on the server whenever a user sets a password.
cards.why: Length is the cheapest strength control: each added character multiplies the guesses an attacker needs. A check in the browser alone can be skipped by calling the API directly. NIST asks for 15 characters when the password is the only factor, and 8 when it is one of several. Framework defaults can be lower, so set the number on purpose.
cards.counterpoint: "Long minimums push users to reuse or write passwords down." Length without composition rules is easier to remember than a short mixed password, and a passphrase works. Pair the limit with a generous maximum of at least 64 characters, and never truncate silently.

cards.applies_when: Code stores or verifies a user password.
cards.tool_gate: Grep or SAST rule for `md5`, `sha1`, `sha256` near a `password` identifier.
cards.rule: Hash passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2) and a per-password salt from the library.
cards.why: A fast hash such as SHA-256 lets an attacker with the database try billions of guesses a second. A slow, salted, memory-hard hash makes each guess cost real time. A common baseline is Argon2id with at least 19 MiB of memory and 2 iterations. Check the current numbers when you review.
cards.counterpoint: "Argon2 is expensive at login." That cost is the defence; tune it to about a second on production hardware. Where FIPS compliance rules Argon2 out, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a high iteration count is the accepted fallback.

fail.code: stored = hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()

pass.code:
ph = argon2.PasswordHasher()            # salt and parameters stored in the hash string
stored = ph.hash(password)
ph.verify(stored, attempt)             # rehash when check_needs_rehash()

cards.applies_when: A diff adds a public module, class, function or method.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff `D100` to `D107` (pydocstyle), Checkstyle `MissingJavadocMethod`, Rust `missing_docs` (allow by default).
cards.note: Home Assistant, Python, Microsoft (Azure SDK), Apache Kafka and Drupal state it. Only Home Assistant says a linter enforces it, so the Rule leaves the gate to `tool_gate`
cards.rule: Give each public module, class, function and method a doc comment.
cards.why: The doc comment is the contract a caller reads. Without one, callers read the body and depend on what it happens to do. Keep it short: see `fn-comments-explain-why` for what it adds.
cards.counterpoint: "Getters and obvious one-liners get a restating docstring." Skip those, or give them a one-line summary that adds the unit or the failure case. A docstring that only repeats the name is worse than none.

cards.applies_when: A handler redirects to a URL taken from a query parameter, form field, header, or stored value, such as `?next=` after login.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `py/url-redirection`; ASP.NET Core `LocalRedirect` or `Url.IsLocalUrl`.
cards.note: ASVS 3.7.2 (allowlisted redirect hosts) and 1.2.2 (safe URL schemes); sys-ssrf covers the server following redirects, not sending users to them
cards.rule: Redirect only to a local path or to a host on a server-side allowlist, never to a URL taken from the request as is.
cards.why: A link such as `https://bank.example/login?next=https://evil.example` carries your domain, so users and mail filters trust it, and after login the user lands on a phishing page. When page script sets `location` from the same value, a `javascript:` URL runs as script. Parse the URL and compare its scheme and host. A `startswith("/")` check alone passes `//evil.example`, and browsers read `/\evil.example` the same way. Better still, accept a short name and map it to the URL on the server.
cards.counterpoint: "The redirect only matters after a successful login." That is when it hurts most: the user has just typed a password and trusts the next page. A phishing copy of the login form on that page collects the password a second time.

fail.code: return redirect(request.args["next"])

cards.applies_when: Styles or script add a transition, an animation, a parallax effect, or autoplay motion.
cards.tool_gate: Stylelint `a11y/media-prefers-reduced-motion` from the `stylelint-a11y` plugin. A browser run with reduced motion emulated.
cards.note: WCAG 2.3.3 is level AAA, so this is good practice and not an AA floor
cards.rule: Switch off or replace large, repeating, or interaction-triggered motion when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is set.
cards.why: Scaling, panning, and parallax can trigger nausea and dizziness for people with vestibular disorders. They have already told their device so. A page that ignores the setting makes them leave.
cards.counterpoint: "Motion carries meaning, such as a loading spinner." Keep what the user needs and make it gentler: swap movement for a fade. The rule is about decorative and large movement, not about every pixel that moves.

cards.applies_when: Code builds a regular expression or similar compiled matcher inside a loop or a function that runs per request.
cards.tool_gate: Linter rule for a regex constructor in a loop, where the language has one.
cards.note: 4 orgs back it; only the Rust docs state the loop rule outright, and Python and .NET cache recent patterns, so a few module-level calls are not a failure
cards.rule: Compile a regular expression once, at module or startup level, and reuse it.
cards.why: Compiling costs far more than matching and throws away reusable allocations. Inside a loop or a per-request function, the cost repeats on every call.
cards.counterpoint: "The library caches patterns." Python and .NET keep recently used patterns, so a few static calls are fine. A pattern built from input or an unbounded set of patterns defeats the cache.

pass.code:
var lower = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z]+$`)

func valid(s string) bool { return lower.MatchString(s) }

cards.applies_when: Markup or a component renders a radio group, a checkbox group, a value split across several inputs, such as a date or an address, or another set of related controls.
cards.note: 4 orgs (GOV.UK, W3C, USWDS, A11y Project). NN/g asks to tag groups for screen readers but does not name fieldset, so it does not count. No source gives a spacing threshold, so spacing stays out of the Rule. Only GOV.UK says the legend comes first, so that sits in Why
cards.rule: Wrap each radio group, checkbox group, and other set of related controls, such as day, month, and year, in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that names the group, often as the question.
cards.why: Each radio's own label says only "Yes" or "No". Without a group, a screen reader user hears the option but not the question it answers. Put the `legend` first inside the `fieldset`. It acts as the group's heading, so assistive technology can tie each option to its question. A set of related controls here means controls that answer one question together, so a sign-in form's two fields are not a set. The same holds for a date split into three boxes labelled "Day", "Month", and "Year". The visual group needs a matching code group, or the two drift apart.
cards.counterpoint: "A `fieldset` draws a border we don't want." Remove the border in CSS with `border: 0; padding: 0; margin: 0`. The grouping still reaches assistive technology. A `div` with `role="group"` and `aria-labelledby` is a fallback for a design system that cannot render a `fieldset`. VoiceOver on iOS ignores `fieldset` and `legend`. That is a reason to add `aria-labelledby` on each input as well, not to drop the group. A single checkbox, such as "I agree", needs no `fieldset`.

fail.code: Do you have a passport?

pass.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Do you have a passport?</legend>
  <input type="radio" id="pp-yes" name="passport" value="yes">
  <label for="pp-yes">Yes</label>
  <input type="radio" id="pp-no" name="passport" value="no">
  <label for="pp-no">No</label>
</fieldset>

cards.applies_when: A function or job changes state and can be run twice, or can be killed partway.
cards.note: second run - cursor/plugins, Uber, Stripe, Dropbox, GitHub, Netflix; crash at any step - cursor/plugins, Stripe, Dropbox (workers die mid-task and retries must stay correct), Netflix; derive from current state - cursor/plugins, Stripe, Netflix, GitHub; leftovers recognisable - cursor/plugins, Netflix (a marker tied to the backup timestamp, a size check against the manifest), GitHub (a review records done only after every removal succeeds)
cards.rule: Make a state-changing operation give the same result on a second run and after a crash at any step, by deriving each step from current state and making leftovers recognisable as stale.
cards.why: Jobs get retried and processes get killed. An append, a counter bump, or a lock file with no owner and time leaves the next run unable to tell finished work from half-done work. Record "done" only after the last step succeeds, so a crash leaves the work visibly pending. A long job should also save its progress, so a rerun resumes where it stopped instead of revisiting finished rows.
cards.counterpoint: "Retries are rare." Crashes are not. For API calls that cross a network, [[svc-idempotency-key]] covers the key-based form of this rule.

fail.code:
cur.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = %s", (amount, acct))  # a retry applies it twice
open("out.json", "w").write(data)                                                       # a crash leaves a truncated file

pass.code:
cur.execute("INSERT INTO applied_ops (op_id) VALUES (%s) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", (op_id,))
if cur.rowcount == 1:  # first run of this operation; same transaction as the update
    cur.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = %s", (amount, acct))
tmp = path.with_suffix(".tmp")
tmp.write_text(data)
os.replace(tmp, path)  # the reader sees the old file or the new one, never half of one

cards.applies_when: Code starts a task, thread, goroutine, or subprocess, or opens a handle (file, socket, connection).
cards.tool_gate: Leak detectors in tests (unclosed-resource warnings, goroutine leak checks).
cards.rule: Give every task and handle an owner that waits for it or closes it, on the error path too.
cards.why: A task started and forgotten outlives its caller. Its errors vanish, nobody cancels it, and its resources are never released, which shows up later as a leak or a stuck shutdown. Goroutines and threads are not garbage collected, so one blocked on a send or receive after its consumer stopped stays stuck unless it has a cancel signal.
cards.counterpoint: "Some work is fire-and-forget by design." Then a long-lived owner (a supervisor or worker pool) holds it, logs its failures, and stops it at shutdown. [[py-task-reference]] covers Python task references.

fail.code:
asyncio.create_task(send_metrics())     # nobody awaits it, nobody cancels it
f = open(path); data = f.read()         # leaked if read() raises

pass.code:
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:   # children finish inside this scope
    tg.create_task(send_metrics())
with open(path) as f:
    data = f.read()

cards.applies_when: A handler returns a stored object or entity to the client.
cards.tool_gate: Response-schema tests that fail on unlisted fields.
cards.rule: Return a response type that lists each field, never the stored model or a generic dump of it.
cards.why: A model gains `password_hash`, `internal_notes` or `email` and every endpoint that serialises it leaks the new field silently. Callers also start to depend on whatever is sent, so removing a field later is a breaking change. An explicit response type makes each exposed field a decision someone reviewed. The write side is [[fn-no-mass-assignment]].
cards.counterpoint: "A response type per endpoint duplicates the model." Derive it from the model with a field list. The duplication is one line per field and shows up in the diff when a field is added.

fail.code:
return jsonify(user.__dict__)
return user_model.to_dict()          # all columns

pass.code:
class UserOut(BaseModel): id: int; display_name: str
return UserOut.model_validate(user)

cards.applies_when: Code inside a database transaction enqueues a job, sends a message or email, calls another service, or clears a cache.
cards.tool_gate: A test that rolls the transaction back and asserts nothing was sent or enqueued; Rails `enqueue_after_transaction_commit = true` makes the safe form the default for jobs.
cards.note: After commit is backed by Django, Rails, Spring, Sidekiq and GitLab (GitLab says to keep jobs, emails and HTTP calls out of the transaction block). The outbox row is backed by AWS and Microsoft (the transactional outbox pattern), Spring (the event publication registry writes in the business transaction) and Rails (a queue in the same database joins the transaction). The lock-holding argument in the Why rests on GitLab alone
cards.rule: Start side effects only after the transaction commits, with an `on_commit` or `after_commit` hook, or record them as an outbox row written inside the same transaction.
cards.why: Inside the transaction, the worker can pick up the job before the row is visible, and it fails with "record not found". If the transaction then rolls back, the email or the message has already gone out for data that does not exist. A network call inside the transaction also keeps its locks open for as long as the call takes. After commit, the data is permanent and the effect follows it. Work that must not be lost, such as a payment event, needs the outbox form: a crash between the commit and the enqueue drops an after-commit hook, and an outbox row survives it.
cards.counterpoint: "An after-commit hook can be lost if the process dies right after the commit." True, which is why the Rule offers the outbox for work that must happen. For best-effort effects, such as a cache clear or a notification the user can live without, the hook is enough. A queue that stores its jobs in the same database already joins the transaction and meets the Rule; confirm that it does before you rely on it.

fail.code:
from django.db import transaction

def place_order(cart):
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(user=cart.user, total=cart.total)
        send_receipt.delay(order.id)   # may run before the commit, or after a rollback
    return order

pass.code:
from django.db import transaction

def place_order(cart):
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(user=cart.user, total=cart.total)
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.id))
    return order

cards.applies_when: Code catches exceptions in business logic.
cards.tool_gate: ruff BLE001 / E722 (Python)
cards.rule: Catch only the specific exception you can handle in business code.
cards.why: A blanket catch treats a mistyped attribute the same as a network blip. Real bugs get swallowed, logged as a warning, and retried. [[py-ruff-gate]] enforces this.
cards.counterpoint: "A worker loop must not die on one bad message." That is the one legitimate blanket catch: once, at the process boundary, with the traceback logged, playing the role that a web framework's error middleware plays for routes. Everywhere else, catch specific exceptions. The other exception is a security boundary: catch broadly there, log redacted, and deny (fail closed). See [[sys-secrets-and-errors]].

cards.applies_when: Script shows a message after an async action without moving focus, such as "Saved", a result count, or an error.
cards.tool_gate: none; a screen-reader pass, or a test that the region exists with a role before the text changes.
cards.note: 3 orgs (W3C, Mozilla, WebAIM); W3C technique ARIA22 is the W3C source for the region existing first, and MDN says role="alert" is announced even when injected. USWDS reports that VoiceOver on macOS does not support `role="alert"`, so test the target reader
cards.rule: Announce an async status message through a live region (`role="status"` or `role="alert"`), and put a `role="status"` or `aria-live` region in the markup before its text changes.
cards.why: A sighted user sees "Saved" appear. A screen-reader user hears nothing, because focus did not move. Most readers announce a change only in a region that existed first, so a status region created together with its message is often skipped. A `role="alert"` region is the exception: readers announce it even when script injects it. Add `aria-atomic="true"` when the whole region should be read out on every change, and leave it off otherwise. Use `assertive` only for urgent, time-sensitive messages, because it cuts into whatever the reader is saying.
cards.counterpoint: "Move focus to the message instead." Use that for a blocking error after submit, where the user must act. For a passive result, moving focus steals the user's place. Keep `assertive` and `role="alert"` for errors, because they interrupt speech.

cards.applies_when: Styles size a button, icon button, checkbox, or link that a pointer or finger operates.
cards.tool_gate: axe `target-size` (WCAG 2.2); a rendered check for the spacing exception.
cards.note: 3 orgs for the 24 CSS px floor and the spacing exception (W3C, Deque, Mozilla); Apple (44 pt) and web.dev (48 px) ask for more; the Material 48 dp page was not readable
cards.rule: Make each pointer target at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or space it so that a 24 px circle centred on it touches no other target and no other undersized target's circle.
cards.why: Small, tight controls cause mis-taps for anyone with a tremor, a large thumb, or a bumpy train. A mis-tap on "Delete" next to "Edit" costs more than a mis-tap on a menu item. Measure the size as the largest unobscured area of the target.
cards.counterpoint: "Inline links and dense tables are exempt." Targets inside a sentence are, and so are controls with an equivalent control that is big enough. A row of toolbar icons is neither, and nor are the action buttons on a table row. Touch platforms often ask for 44 px or more, so treat 24 px as the floor, not the goal.

fail.code: .icon-btn { width: 16px; height: 16px; margin: 0; }

pass.code: .icon-btn { min-width: 24px; min-height: 24px; padding: 4px; }

cards.applies_when: A test exercises a function, class, or module with callers.
cards.tool_gate: Refactor the code without changing what it does and run the tests; mutation testing shows whether they still catch real faults.
cards.note: Google (Software Engineering at Google, ch. 12), Microsoft Learn (.NET unit-testing best practices), Spotify engineering. Spotify keeps tests of internals for isolated, complex logic; the Rust book calls testing private functions a debate.
cards.rule: Assert what a caller can observe through the public interface, so a change that keeps behaviour does not break the test.
cards.why: A test tied to private calls, call order, or internal state fails when the code is restructured though nothing a caller sees changed. People then edit tests to match the code, and the suite stops protecting behaviour. It also pins whatever shape the code has today, including shapes that should change.
cards.counterpoint: "Some internals are complex enough to test on their own." Then give that logic its own unit with a public interface and test it through that. Testing a private function directly is a debated choice, so say why in the test.

fail.code:
def test_checkout():
    cart = Cart()
    cart.add(Item("pen", 300))
    cart._recalculate_totals = Mock()          # private call
    cart.checkout()
    cart._recalculate_totals.assert_called_once()

pass.code:
def test_checkout_charges_the_sum_of_item_prices():
    cart = Cart()
    cart.add(Item("pen", 300))
    cart.add(Item("book", 450))
    assert cart.checkout().total == 750

cards.applies_when: A test asserts on a computed value.
cards.tool_gate: Mutation testing.
cards.note: Google, Microsoft and Cursor each say to write the expected value out in the test, not compute it with logic that can share the bug
cards.rule: Take a test's expected value from the requirement, not from the code under test.
cards.why: An expected value computed by the code under test passes when the code is wrong. Likewise, a "not called" assertion passes when the spy is wired to the wrong target, so pair it with a case where the call happens.
cards.counterpoint: "Recomputing keeps the test short." It also repeats the bug. Use a literal from the spec or a worked example.

fail.code: assert total(items) == sum(i.price for i in items)   # re-implements the code

pass.code: assert total([Item(price=300), Item(price=450)]) == 750

cards.applies_when: The code stores, logs or sends a point in time (an instant), such as a created-at field, an event time or an API field.
cards.note: W3C, Django and Zalando back the store-and-send-in-UTC Rule. Only Django also says to convert to local time at the edge, so that half sits in the Why. The PostgreSQL wiki (use timestamptz) and Google AIP-142 (use Timestamp) are close but not counted
cards.rule: Store and send instants in UTC.
cards.why: Local times repeat or skip an hour when clocks change, and values written in different zones cannot be compared or sorted without knowing each zone. Keep the data in UTC and convert to a person's zone only where you show it to them. Scope: a calendar date (a birthday) is not an instant, and a future local event (a 09:00 meeting in Madrid) needs its zone name, because zone rules change before the event.
cards.counterpoint: "All our users are in one time zone." Daylight saving time still makes some local times ambiguous or missing twice a year, and the second time zone arrives after the data is in. Storing UTC costs nothing now and converting at display is one call; fixing mixed local times later means guessing what each row meant.

fail.code: created_at = datetime.now()          # naive local time, the zone is lost

pass.code: created_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

cards.applies_when: Code makes an outbound HTTPS, database or message-broker connection.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B501 (`request_with_no_cert_validation`), CodeQL `py/request-without-cert-validation`; a grep for `rejectUnauthorized: false` and `InsecureSkipVerify: true`.
cards.rule: Leave certificate and hostname verification on in every environment that ships, and check the certificate against the host you meant to reach, not a name the server supplies.
cards.why: With verification off, any on-path attacker presents a certificate and reads or changes the traffic. The flag is usually added to silence a dev-box error and then ships. Fix the trust store or pin a private CA instead. The client must supply the expected name itself, not take it from the certificate the server presents: set `ServerName` in Go, pass `server_hostname` in Python.
cards.counterpoint: "It is an internal network." Internal links get sniffed after one compromised host. A private CA gives you the same convenience with the check intact.

fail.code:

cards.note: GitLab and CockroachDB require an issue link; Envoy and OpenStack require an owner name. A TODO with a date or event is `fn-comments-survive-context`
cards.rule: Give each TODO an owner or a tracking issue, such as `TODO(alice)` or `TODO(#1234)`.
cards.why: An anonymous TODO has nobody to ask and nothing to close, so it stays for years. An owner or a ticket tells the next reader who knows the context and where the work is tracked.

cards.applies_when: A type or function models a value that is one of several variants or states.
cards.tool_gate: A type checker with exhaustiveness checking (`never` in TypeScript, `assert_never` in Python).
cards.note: one vendor's engineering guidance (opinion), from pstack principle-model-the-domain and typescript-best-practices
cards.rule: Model variants as a tagged union, and make every switch over it fail the build when a variant is unhandled.
cards.why: A bag of optional fields or booleans that must stay in sync allows states that mean nothing, and each reader has to know which combinations are legal. A new variant then slips past every switch that lacks an exhaustiveness check. A catch-all branch hides the same gap: Kotlin's `when` over a sealed type needs no `else`, and a C `switch` over an enum has a `case` for every member.
cards.counterpoint: "Two booleans are simpler." They are until a third state appears or the booleans disagree. For a true on/off flag with no related fields, a boolean is fine.

cards.applies_when: Code parses XML, SVG, SOAP, SAML, or an office document that a user or another system can supply.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `py/xxe`; Bandit B313 to B319 (stdlib XML parse calls) and B405 to B409 (XML imports).
cards.note: ASVS 1.5.1; sys-ssrf covers outbound fetches that XXE can also trigger
cards.rule: Parse untrusted XML with external entity resolution turned off, for example through a hardened parser such as `defusedxml`.
cards.why: A DTD can declare an entity whose value is `file:///etc/passwd` or an internal URL, and a parser that resolves it pastes that content into the document or makes the request for the attacker. Nested internal entities can also expand a small file into gigabytes. Where the parser allows it, also turn off DTDs, XInclude, and the parser's network access. Each parser has its own switches, so name them in the code instead of trusting the library default.
cards.counterpoint: "Recent Python XML modules already refuse external entities." Some do. The FAIL above opts back in, Java and .NET parsers have their own defaults, and a later change to the parser config reopens the hole. An explicit hardened parser makes the setting visible in review.

cards.note: Rule backed by Google (Go blog, SRE troubleshooting), Brendan Gregg (USE, flame graphs), GitLab, and Microsoft; "the same measurement after the fix" has 2 orgs (Google, GitLab) and sits in Why
cards.rule: Tie the performance fix to evidence that names the bottleneck: a profile, a trace, or a USE check.
cards.why: A guessed fix often speeds up code that was not slow, and the incident comes back. The profile that found the bottleneck is also the cheapest proof that the fix removed it, so take the same measurement again after the fix, under the same load ([[chg-perf-claim-evidence]]).
cards.counterpoint: "In an outage we mitigate first." Yes. Rolling back or adding capacity to stop the bleeding needs no profile. The rule covers the fix that closes the incident, which comes after the system is stable. Capacity kept as that fix, with no profile behind it, hides a code problem rather than removing it.

cards.applies_when: A postmortem, incident review or postmortem template is written or audited.
cards.note: Google, PagerDuty, Atlassian and Microsoft (Azure Well-Architected) each state it; Atlassian says the timeline may still name who made which change, so the Rule bans names as the cause, not names
cards.rule: Write a postmortem so that it names causes in the system and the decisions around it, never a person or team as the one at fault.
cards.why: People who expect blame stay quiet about what they saw and soften the timeline, so the contributing factors never reach the review. A cause of "someone was careless" also gives no action that prevents the next failure, while a cause such as "the schema accepted an empty list" does. The timeline may still say who made which change; only the verdict of fault is out.
cards.counterpoint: "Blameless means nobody is accountable." Each change stays in the timeline with its author, and each action has an owner. What the rule refuses is the finding that a person caused the outage, because that finding ends the inquiry at the person and leaves the system as it was. It says nothing about performance management, which is a separate process.

cards.applies_when: A runbook or incident response relies on rollback, failover, or a manual mitigation.
cards.note: exercising runbook mitigations is backed by Dropbox (monthly failovers), Slack (a restore runbook failed until drilled; use rollback tooling often), Cloudflare (regular cut tests; a kill switch SOP failed on a rule type it had never met) and Shopify (repeated Game Days); naming who may trigger the mitigation has no source and sits in Why
cards.rule: Exercise each mitigation that a runbook names (rollback, failover, flag off) on a regular schedule.
cards.why: Rollbacks fail on schema changes or removed artifacts, backups stop running without anyone noticing, and untested failover paths rot. After a drill finds a gap and you fix it, run the drill again to confirm the fix. People who rarely use a rollback tool hesitate to use it in an incident. The runbook should also say who may trigger each mitigation, so nobody waits for permission during the outage.
cards.counterpoint: "Drills are costly." Start with the mitigations an incident would need first, and drill again when a migration or release process changes. A drill is cheaper than finding out during an outage that the rollback is impossible.

pass.code: Runbook: rollback drilled monthly, last run 2026-10-01; schema is expand-only; on-call may trigger.

cards.applies_when: The repo or wiki holds an incident policy or runbook that covers major incidents. A repo with no such document has nothing to fail, so mark the card N/A.
cards.note: Google, PagerDuty and AWS name the commander role; Atlassian's handbook describes its own process and is not counted. Google and PagerDuty scope the role to major incidents
cards.rule: Name one incident commander for each major incident, who holds the overall state of the response and oversees the other roles.
cards.why: Without one person holding the whole picture, responders duplicate each other, change the system in parallel and wait for someone else to decide. The commander does not need to be the most senior or the most technical person present; the role is to keep the state and assign the work.
cards.counterpoint: "A role hierarchy is overhead for a small team or a small incident." Scope it to major incidents, and let one person hold several roles on a small team. The rule only asks that someone is named commander, so the question "who decides" has an answer before the page goes out.

cards.applies_when: A function computes something only from one object's own fields.
cards.note: Microsoft (entity methods own the invariants), PMD (DataClass, data-behaviour proximity) and DevIQ (anemic model) put the rule on the object; Microsoft and DevIQ also give the CRUD and functional exceptions
cards.rule: Put the invariants and calculations that read only one object's fields on that object.
cards.why: A rule about one object scattered across services makes every caller learn where the rule lives, and the object cannot enforce it. Microsoft says an entity's methods "take care of the invariants and rules of the entity instead of having those rules spread across the application layer". PMD calls a data holder whose behaviour lives elsewhere a sign of "poor data-behaviour proximity". DevIQ says model objects should "use encapsulation to manage their internal state and behavior".
cards.counterpoint: "Records, data classes and dataclasses are made to carry data." They are, and a carrier with no rules has nothing to move. The rule is about the calculation, not the declaration, so `total()` on a record does not stop it being a record. Keep the type a pure carrier when it holds only data. A simple CRUD context can keep a data-only model, and a functional design keeps behaviour in functions over data. The rule is for an object model.

cards.applies_when: A change adds imports or type references to a class, file or function that already depends on many others.
cards.tool_gate: Microsoft CA1506 (95 types, 40 members), Checkstyle ClassFanOutComplexity (20), eslint-plugin-import import/max-dependencies (10), PMD CouplingBetweenObjects (20) and ExcessiveImports (30).
cards.note: a documented limit on how many other types or modules a unit depends on - Microsoft (CA1506), Checkstyle, eslint-plugin-import, PMD; the defaults differ by a factor of ten, so the Rule asks for a limit and does not name a number
cards.rule: Set a limit on how many other types or modules one unit depends on, and split a unit that passes it.
cards.why: A unit that depends on many others breaks when any of them changes and is hard to test, because each dependency needs a stand-in. eslint-plugin-import says "a module with too many dependencies is a code smell, and usually indicates the module is doing too much". Microsoft's rule gives the same reason: high class coupling is "difficult to maintain". Count each type or module once, however many names a unit takes from it, and leave out built-in language types and generated code.
cards.counterpoint: "The entry point has to import everything to wire it up." It does, so allowlist the composition root and nothing else. Microsoft's own page says to suppress the rule when the type "is considered maintainable despite its large number of dependencies".

cards.applies_when: One class or type passes the project's size limit for fields, public methods or lines, or the project sets no limit. A long file that holds several units belongs to code-file-lines-ceiling, and a module that mixes concepts is judged for cohesion, not size.
cards.tool_gate: Pylint too-many-instance-attributes (R0902, max-attributes default 7) and too-many-public-methods (R0904, default 20), PMD NcssCount (classReportLevel default 1500) or GodClass, RuboCop Metrics/ClassLength (default 100).
cards.note: Pylint, PMD and RuboCop enforce a class-size limit but measure different things (fields, public methods, lines, NCSS); Pylint and PMD also give the rationale (a simpler class; split a god class). Microsoft CA1505 is a maintainability index, not a size gate, so it is not listed. The card asks for the project's limit and treats the result as a prompt to ask what the class owns
cards.rule: Split a class that passes the project's size limit for fields, public methods or lines, unless it is a data record.
cards.why: A class that owns too much has too many reasons to change, and the project's linter should carry a limit for it. Pricing, tax, invoicing, dunning and notification in one type means five sets of fields, five test setups and a constructor nobody can call correctly. The linters count different things: fields, public methods, lines, source statements or a maintainability index. Any of them is a prompt to ask what the class owns. A data record with many fields is a different case, and a wide but cohesive API can be justified.
cards.counterpoint: "Splitting a large class leaves shallow pieces that call each other." That happens when the split follows methods instead of knowledge. Move the state with the methods that use it, and keep one thin entry point for callers. If the pieces would only forward, the class is not too large. It is one concept with a wide surface, and the limit is the wrong signal. A data record is judged by its shape, not by this card.

cards.applies_when: A design-system module or theme defines foreground and background colour tokens.
cards.tool_gate: axe `color-contrast` on rendered components; a unit test that computes the ratio for each token pair. axe cannot see text on images or gradients.
cards.note: 3:1 for non-text parts (borders, icons, focus): A11y Project, web.dev, WebAIM. WebAIM's checklist restates WCAG 1.4.11; SC 1.4.11 was not read as its own page
cards.rule: Make every text and background token pair meet 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text, which is 18pt, or 14pt bold), and every border, icon, and focus colour meet 3:1 against its neighbour.
cards.why: Low contrast is invisible to the author on a bright monitor. Fixing it once in the tokens fixes every component. Fixing it per component means hunting through each one, and each new component can reintroduce it.
cards.counterpoint: "The brand colour fails." A logo is exempt. A brand-coloured button label or link is not. Darken the shade used for text and keep the brand shade for fills. The ratio is exact: 4.499:1 fails.

cards.applies_when: A new class or module is introduced, or an existing interface grows.
cards.note: a small interface, nothing more than callers need - Microsoft Framework Design Guidelines ("no more and no fewer" members), Rust API Guidelines (hide the representation, "promise less to the client"), Go review comments (do not define an interface before it is used); the "interface as complex as the implementation" test is Ousterhout alone and sits in the Why
cards.rule: Prefer a small interface that hides its implementation, and add a member only when callers need it.
cards.why: An interface with too many members is hard to learn and hard to implement, and a public detail is a commitment you cannot change later. A public field pins the representation and lets callers bypass any check, so keep fields private and expose them through methods. A shallow module, whose interface is nearly as complex as its implementation, charges the reader the cost of learning it and returns nothing. The complexity moves; it does not shrink.
cards.counterpoint: Ousterhout and Martin disagree. Martin favours many very small functions, and Ousterhout says that yields shallow, entangled pieces. Evidence is thin on both sides. Ask the local question: does the split help a reader here?

cards.counterpoint: "Generated code is awkward to read." A parity test gives the same safety with hand-written types. The rule fails only when neither derivation nor a check exists.

cards.applies_when: A reviewer sees long methods, feature envy, data clumps, primitive obsession, speculative generality, or divergent change.
cards.note: name the issue and give a reason, not taste - Google ("Aspects of software design are almost never a pure style issue"), GitLab ("Be explicit", "Offer alternative implementations"), Palantir ("Suggestion: extract method to improve legibility", "Critique the code, not the author"); the smell catalog itself comes from Fowler and Beck (persons) through Ousterhout's red flags
cards.rule: Name the smell, point to the line, and suggest the refactoring; do not file smells as taste.
cards.why: Smells are cheap to see and expensive to ignore, but a vague "this feels off" gives the author nothing to fix.
cards.counterpoint: "Smells are subjective." Yes: they signal; they do not prove. That is why the comment names the smell, the line, and the refactoring. "This is messy" gives the author nothing to act on.

cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Inject boundary collaborators through the constructor; do not construct them inside or reach for a global.
cards.why: Hard-wired collaborators force tests to patch module internals and tie the class to one environment.
cards.counterpoint: "Injection everywhere is enterprise bloat." Inject only the boundary (DB, HTTP, cloud, clock). Internal collaborators stay plain and real in tests.

cards.applies_when: A module has an intended public surface, with internal files, symbols or members.
cards.tool_gate: Import-boundary lint (import-linter, ESLint `no-restricted-imports`, package `exports`), Pylint protected-access (W0212).
cards.note: the import half has Google (Go internal packages and Bazel visibility), Cursor's design red flags and Microsoft (the `internal` keyword, a definition); the member half has Refactoring.Guru, PEP 8 and Pylint. A test may use a documented test-only export
cards.rule: Keep a module's internals unimportable and untouched from outside it. A caller uses the public surface, not a private file or member.
cards.why: Anything a caller can import becomes the interface, and a field a caller writes becomes part of the contract. A leading-underscore member is for its own class and its subclasses, yet a naming convention alone stops no one, and the module can no longer change its internals without breaking callers.
cards.counterpoint: "A boundary check is overhead for a small repo, and tests need internals." One lint contract is cheap, and the first outside import of an internal costs more. Tests may use a documented test-only export, and Java's qualified `exports ... to` or C#'s `InternalsVisibleTo` give them a door. For a single-file module, there is no inside to protect, so mark `N/A`.

cards.applies_when: A change adds a call chain that reaches through one object to use another, such as order.customer().address().city().
cards.tool_gate: PMD LawOfDemeter (trustRadius, default 1), JetBrains inspection LawOfDemeter.
cards.note: PMD, Google's Testing Blog (a heading only) and JetBrains state the rule. PMD's trustRadius (default 1) and JetBrains' LawOfDemeter inspection gate it with the same threshold: one call on an object another call returned; JetBrains notes the wrapper-method cost and calls the law a style guideline
cards.rule: Call methods on your direct collaborators, and do not call a method on an object that another call returned (a chain of two or more getters).
cards.why: A chain such as `order.customer().address().city()` ties the caller to the structure of three classes it does not own, so a change in any of them breaks it. PMD describes the rule as forbidding "fetching data from 'too far away'" to reduce coupling.
cards.counterpoint: "Fluent builders and stream pipelines chain by design." They return the same type or a value, so they do not expose structure. The rule targets getters that expose another object's parts. Every wrapper is code you now own. Pay that cost on the path that changes, and leave a stable library chain alone. The inspection ignores library calls by default. The law is a style guideline, which is why the severity is `discuss`. Use the project's tool setting as the threshold.

cards.counterpoint: "Three layers is ceremony for a CRUD app." For a ten-endpoint app, yes; fold them. The check applies once you have real logic. It asks only that dependencies not point outward, not that you build all three folders.

cards.applies_when: A change adds an import, dependency or project reference between modules, packages or build targets.
cards.tool_gate: eslint-plugin-import import/no-cycle, Pylint R0401 (cyclic-import), Nx @nx/enforce-module-boundaries, or ArchUnit slices().should().beFreeOfCycles().
cards.note: the language or build tool rejects a cycle - Go (an import cycle is illegal), Bazel (targets form a directed acyclic graph), Cargo (the resolver does not allow cycles, except dev-dependencies); lint rules - eslint-plugin-import, Nx, Pylint, ArchUnit; scope to the package boundary, because Python and Rust allow cycles between modules
cards.rule: Keep the dependency graph between modules or packages acyclic, and break a cycle by moving the shared part into a third module that both depend on.
cards.why: Two modules that import each other cannot be built, tested or understood alone, and a change in one can break the other. Go rejects the cycle at compile time, Bazel defines its dependency graph as acyclic, and Cargo tells authors to split a package so it "remains strictly acyclic". Where the language allows the cycle, it still ties the two modules into one.
cards.counterpoint: "Python lets you import inside the function, so the cycle works." That hides the cycle at run time and leaves the two modules coupled. Apply the rule at the package or module boundary, where the toolchain or a lint rule can check it, and allow a documented exception for generated code or a test-only dependency.

cards.applies_when: A module does anything at import or load time other than defining names.
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Keep I/O at the edges: importing a package must not touch the network, read files, or read the environment.
cards.why: Import-time effects make tests slow and order-dependent, break tooling that merely imports the module, and fail in places that had no reason to need a network. Opening a database connection or running heavy computation at import does the same damage.
cards.counterpoint: "Loading once at import is fast." Load once at startup, explicitly, where the caller controls it and tests can substitute it.

cards.applies_when: A constructor does work beyond assigning its arguments.
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Assign only in constructors, and put I/O, parsing, and heavy computation in a named factory.
cards.why: A constructor with side effects makes every instantiation, including in tests, read a file or call an API. You need a real resource or a patch just to build the object.
cards.counterpoint: "A factory per class is ceremony." For a value object with no I/O, there is nothing to factor out. The rule targets constructors that read, call, or parse. With the factory, the test builds the object in one line.

cards.applies_when: A module defines a value that changes after load: a module-level variable, a list, dict, counter, cache, client or singleton.
cards.note: Google Python guide 2.5 allows a rare internal global behind functions; the Uber Go guide and Microsoft CA2211 (public static fields) say to avoid mutable global or static state. Only Google names class attributes, so that point sits in the Why
cards.rule: Keep no mutable state at module level; hold it on an instance.
cards.why: Hidden global state leaks between tests, between requests, and between threads, and its order of mutation is unreadable. A mutable class or static field fails the same way, and the Google Python guide names class attributes as well. A frozen, load-once constant such as settings is the exception. A singleton used to dodge injection is not.
cards.counterpoint: "A module global is the simplest cache." It is also unbounded and shared by everything. If you need one, bound it (LRU or TTL), inject it, and tie its lifetime to what it caches. A rare, documented internal global behind functions can stay; say why in a comment.

cards.applies_when: A change to one rule, format or decision needs small edits in many classes or files.
cards.note: smell "Shotgun Surgery" (Fowler and Beck, through Refactoring.Guru); Microsoft says behaviour spread over several places is a frequent source of errors, and NDepend asks where the knowledge lives; Microsoft's warning about the wrong abstraction is the counterpoint
cards.rule: Keep one decision in one module, and when a single change needs edits in many classes, move the scattered parts together.
cards.why: One change repeats in file after file, and the copy you miss is the defect. Refactoring.Guru describes the smell as "a single responsibility has been split up among a large number of classes". Microsoft says behaviour spread over several places is "a frequent source of errors" and asks for one construct to own it. NDepend says knowledge should exist in one place. The test is concrete: the same rule changes in the same set of files every time.
cards.counterpoint: "A feature naturally touches many files." A new field does touch the model, the API and the UI. The smell is one internal rule that spreads. Duplication beats coupling to the wrong abstraction, and that is the limit: if the edits are unrelated decisions, merging them would create the wrong abstraction. The signal is that every change of this kind edits the same files.
