# the last two currency changes edited the same seven files

pass.code: Adding a currency edits: money.py   (rounding, formatting and tax rules live there)

cards.applies_when: The diff adds or grows a module named `utils`, `helpers`, `common`, or `misc`.
cards.rule: Put a helper in the module that owns the concept, or in a new module named after the concept.
cards.why: A grab-bag has no owner and no cohesion. It becomes the dependency of everything and the place where unrelated code accretes. The same goes for a `Helper` or `Util` class suffix: put the methods in the class they belong to.
cards.counterpoint: "Tiny helpers do not deserve a file." Then inline them where they are used (YAGNI applies). When one is shared, naming its concept is the work that makes it findable.

pass.code: dates.py, notifications.py, pricing.py, retry.py

cards.applies_when: A shared helper or base class has gained flags or conditionals so different callers can bend it.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff FBT001 and FBT002 (boolean positional arguments) catch the usual first sign.
cards.rule: Inline an abstraction that has grown flags for its callers.
cards.why: Extract an abstraction when real call sites need it ([[mod-yagni]]). A wrong one is harder to remove than the duplication it replaced, because each new caller adds a branch until nobody can say what the code is for. After you inline it, wait for the third similar caller before extracting again, so the new shape comes from real call sites.
cards.counterpoint: Sources disagree. Ousterhout lists repetition as a red flag (one fact in many places), and the AHA/Sandi Metz line prefers duplication to a wrong abstraction. They fit together: dedupe knowledge (a rule, a format, a constant), wait on shape, and extract only when the second real caller shows what is shared.

cards.applies_when: The change introduces or reuses names for domain concepts.
cards.note: the island.is and tum-esi conventions and Microsoft's Azure API guidelines ("use the same name for the same concept") back the same-name rule; Refactoring.Guru's alternative classes with different interfaces backs the two-class case, which sits in the Why
cards.rule: Use one name for one concept across the codebase.
cards.why: If `customer`, `client`, and `account` all mean the same thing, readers wonder whether they differ. A name that misdescribes behaviour is worse than a vague one. Follow the project glossary, and never choose a name that says something the code does not do. Two classes that perform the same job under different method names make a reader learn the operation twice.
cards.counterpoint: "Names are bikeshedding." Reviewers should not argue taste. They should check that the name is consistent and true. Vague names (names that could mean many things) are a design smell. Do not rename wholesale in a feature change; make the rename a separate change. An adapter at a boundary is exempt: its job is to present a different interface, and it should say which one it adapts.

cards.applies_when: Code creates a network or database client.
cards.rule: Build pooled clients once at startup and reuse them.
cards.why: A client per call defeats connection pooling, leaks sockets, and pays a handshake every time. When a client must be short-lived, close it when the work ends.
cards.counterpoint: "A throwaway client is simpler." For a one-off script, yes (scope it with `with`). On a server path it exhausts sockets under load.

cards.applies_when: A `.proto` file defines an enum.
cards.tool_gate: Protobuf linter (`buf lint`, ENUM_ZERO_VALUE_SUFFIX).
cards.note: a zero value with no real meaning has Google and Dropbox (UNKNOWN = 0); the _UNSPECIFIED name has Google only; Cabify lints for consistent zero values without naming the convention
cards.rule: Give every protobuf enum a zero value named `<ENUM>_UNSPECIFIED` with no real meaning.
cards.why: A reader that sees an unset or unknown field gets zero. If zero means a real state, such as `PAID`, a missing field reads as a payment.
cards.counterpoint: "Zero as the common default saves a field on the wire." The saving is a byte on a field already at its most common value, and the cost is a silent wrong state. Published enums keep their numbers, so the fix for an existing enum is a new unspecified name only if no value has to be renumbered.

cards.applies_when: More than one module, worker or process writes the same state.
cards.note: one writer at a time is backed by cursor/plugins, Netflix (an exclusive queue lets one worker evaluate a workflow at a time), Cabify (CI deploy runs that were not mutually exclusive reverted each other, replaced by one GitOps controller) and GitHub (writes to one reference are serialised); giving each writer its own state and merging on read has cursor/plugins and GitHub only, so it sits in Why
cards.rule: Let only one writer change a piece of state at a time, through a single owner, a queue that serialises the writes, or compare-and-swap, never by convention.
cards.why: A convention such as "only write your own field" is not concurrency control. Two workers writing different fields of one file still overwrite each other, and two deploy runs that overlap can undo each other's changes. Better still, split the state so that each writer owns its part and readers merge the parts: writers to different parts then never wait for each other.
cards.counterpoint: "A lock is simpler than a queue or an owner." A lock works only when the store rejects a writer whose lock has expired; see [[sys-lock-fencing]]. Without that check, a paused holder can wake up and write after another writer took over.

fail.code: worker A and worker B each load state.json, set their own key, and save the whole file

pass.code:
workers send updates to one queue; a single consumer applies them to state.json in order
or: state/a.json and state/b.json, one writer each; readers merge them

cards.applies_when: A private field is assigned and read inside one method, or every read of it follows an assignment.
cards.tool_gate: JetBrains FieldCanBeLocal, Sonar S1450, PMD SingularField (all private fields only).
cards.note: JetBrains, SonarSource and PMD flag a private field that is always assigned before it is read; PMD warns that threading can produce false positives. Refactoring.Guru's Temporary Field is a different smell (fields set only in some circumstances, fixed with Extract Class), so it backs the name and not the trigger
cards.rule: Make a field a local variable or a parameter when every method that uses it assigns it before reading it.
cards.why: The field looks like object state, so a reader expects it to survive between calls. It does not. It is one method's scratch space, so a reader looks for state the object never keeps. JetBrains, Sonar and PMD flag a private field whose every read follows an assignment, because a local variable says the same thing without the extra state.
cards.counterpoint: "The field carries state between calls." Then a read can happen before the next assignment, and the rule does not fire. The trigger is every read following an assignment in the same method. Caches, ORM models and serialisation models set attributes outside `__init__` on purpose, and their reads are not preceded by a fresh assignment, so they stay. In concurrent code a second thread can read between the assignment and the read, which is why PMD calls its rule threading-unaware; suppress it where another thread reads the field on purpose.

cards.applies_when: A module encrypts or decrypts data.
cards.tool_gate: A grep for `MODE_ECB`, `MODE_CBC` with no MAC, and nonces built from constants.
cards.rule: Encrypt with an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM, and never reuse a nonce under one key.
cards.why: Unauthenticated modes allow silent tampering, and ECB also leaks the structure of the plaintext. Reusing a nonce under one key breaks GCM completely: it leaks the XOR of the plaintexts and the authentication key. Take the call from a maintained library and never write your own cipher. Keys belong in a KMS or secrets manager, never in source; [[sys-secrets-and-errors]] covers where secrets live at runtime.
cards.counterpoint: "The library API is awkward, so a wrapper is safer." Wrap the vetted call, do not replace it. Review the wrapper only for nonce handling and key sourcing.

fail.code:
cipher = AES.new(KEY, AES.MODE_ECB)
ct = bytes(b ^ k for b, k in zip(msg, KEY * 99))

pass.code:
aead = AESGCM(key_from_kms)
ct = aead.encrypt(os.urandom(12), msg, aad)      # fresh nonce per message

cards.applies_when: The code adds or keeps an abstraction, parameter, hook or option.
cards.note: The MediaWiki architecture page labels itself a draft. The Microsoft playbook checklist may echo Google's wording and the extensibility guideline is indirect. Shopify and Microsoft ask for three or several uses, so no use count sits in the Rule.
cards.rule: Do not build an abstraction or capability for a need that does not exist yet; add it when the need appears.
cards.why: Speculative flexibility costs reading time every day and is usually the wrong shape when the need arrives. Reviewers cannot verify a use that does not exist.
cards.counterpoint: "But we will surely need it." Then add it when you do, in a change that has the real caller to shape it. Optimising for easy change means simple code, not built-in flexibility. The cost of waiting is low, and the cost of the wrong guess is not. When the need is certain and a retrofit would be costly, as for a public API that cannot change later, weigh that cost before waiting.

cards.applies_when: A new UI service or a major redesign is about to open to the public.
cards.tool_gate: none; a launch checklist item that links the audit report.
cards.note: 3 orgs for an audit with assistive technology (GOV.UK, W3C, Deque), but only GOV.UK ties it to before a public launch, which is the card's point; Section508.gov weak; the GOV.UK duty is a UK legal duty, so this card names WCAG 2.2 AA as the standard and claims no law elsewhere
cards.rule: Before a public launch, run an accessibility audit against WCAG 2.2 AA that includes assistive technology, and link the report in the launch checklist.
cards.why: Quick checks and automated tools are a first pass, not an evaluation. A page can pass both and still block a screen-reader user from finishing the task. Finding that after launch means fixing it under load and in public. The audit is not a one-off: test again, with automated and manual checks, when features change.
cards.counterpoint: "We have no budget for an external audit." The auditor can be in-house, if they are trained and did not build the service. Cut scope instead of the audit: audit the main task flows first, and say in the report which parts are not covered.

cards.applies_when: A service ships alert rules that page a person.
cards.tool_gate: A lint on alert rules that requires a description and a runbook annotation.
cards.note: Google SRE (every page should be actionable), Microsoft (alerts actionable and with context, an alerting process that defines owners, actions and scope), AWS Well-Architected OPS08-BP04 (create actionable alerts) and Datadog (context clarifies ownership and impact). Owner and runbook link have fewer than three organisations and stay in the Why; Grafana, Prometheus and Google Cloud only describe a runbook annotation field
cards.rule: Give every paging alert context a responder can act on: what it means and what to do next.
cards.why: A page that says only "metric X is high" makes the responder start from nothing at 3 a.m. The usual form is a one-line description, the owning team and a link to a runbook for the first checks and the mitigation. Written-down steps shorten recovery time, and an alert with an owner cannot be ignored by default. Alerts that need no immediate action belong in a ticket queue, not a page ([[prod-alerts-symptoms-golden-signals]]).
cards.counterpoint: "Runbooks go stale and nobody reads them." A stale runbook is a fixable defect, and the card asks only that the alert say what it means and where to start. Ticket-only and informational alerts need no runbook, so the rule covers rules that page.

cards.applies_when: A service ships alerts or dashboards.
cards.rule: Page on user-visible symptoms, such as error rate and latency, not on causes.
cards.why: Cause-based pages (CPU high) wake people without user impact. A mean hides the slow tail, and failed-request latency mixed with successes hides both. Require an error-rate alert to hold for a few minutes, so one blip does not page. Also cover latency, traffic, errors, and saturation, and page on saturation when a limit is about to be reached, not only after it is hit. Track latency as a distribution, and delete alerts that never fire.
cards.counterpoint: Cause alerts help diagnosis. Keep them as tickets or dashboard hints, not pages. The Honeycomb wide-event camp argues against pre-set metrics, while the SRE book favors simple metric-based paging, so this card does not ban events, only cause-paging.

cards.applies_when: A change, config or dependency update is rolled out to production.
cards.tool_gate: Deploy pipeline with canary stage and automatic abort.
cards.note: Canary: Google, OWASP, Microsoft (a vendor). Abort by rule: Google, AWS CodeDeploy (a vendor) and Microsoft (a vendor, halts on a health alert). Anthropic (a vendor) backs only staged rollout and says it has no circuit breaker yet; not a counted organisation
cards.rule: Roll out in stages behind a canary, and abort by rule, not by judgment.
cards.why: A 100% push exposes everyone to the bug. A canary must be large and long enough to be representative. Errors of 20% on 5% of traffic are only 1% overall, so tie the canary to your error budget. A feature flag does the same job inside one release: switch the change on for a small share of users, watch, then widen.
cards.counterpoint: "Hotfixes can't wait." Then keep the canary short, not absent. Fleet tools should also have velocity limits. A hermetic, reproducible build tied to one revision ([[code-build-hermetic]]) is the precondition for rollback to mean anything. [[prod-config-ships-like-code]] covers config and flag values.

cards.applies_when: A service has runtime configuration, feature-flag values or limits that can change in production.
cards.tool_gate: Production config store writable only by the deploy pipeline; the config repository requires review before merge.
cards.note: Google SRE (config changes lack the review and testing code gets; keep config in source control for history, rollback and review), Amazon Builders' Library (runtime config such as rate limits and feature flags ships in a dedicated pipeline with the same safety mechanisms as code) and Microsoft (a configuration or feature-flag update carries deployment risk and every deployment must follow a standard, automated pattern). OpenGitOps describes a method and is not counted
cards.rule: Change configuration and flag values through a reviewed commit and the same staged, automated pipeline as code, not by hand on a host or console.
cards.why: One configuration value can change behaviour as much as a code change, with less testing and review. A hand edit leaves no history, no second reader and no rollback, and it skips the canary that would catch the mistake ([[prod-canary-staged-rollout]]).
cards.counterpoint: "In an incident we need to change a value now." An out-of-band change is allowed when the pipeline is too slow, as long as a commit records the same value straight after, so the repository stays the source of truth. A fast config pipeline makes the exception rare.

cards.applies_when: A new risky feature or a dependency fallback is added.
cards.note: switch off without a deploy - Cloudflare (kill switches through global config), GitHub (Flipper rollout and rollback), Slack (feature flags with instant rollback), Dropbox (rollback for experiments and gates); exercise the fallback - AWS (tests with the cache disabled), Cloudflare (regular cut tests; an untested fail-open path), Shopify (repeated Game Days in production), Dropbox (monthly datacenter failovers); on a schedule - Cloudflare, Shopify, Dropbox; owned - FeatBit (long-lived kill switches need an owner and runbook), GrowthBook (document what it disables and its owner, test it in a game day) and Harness (the Ops team manages a kill switch); a runbook has FeatBit and GrowthBook only and stays out of the Rule; Cloudflare's overload tests are a stated plan; Anthropic (a vendor) also says "Changes behind feature flags can be disabled without deploying", not a counted third org
cards.rule: Make a risky feature switchable off without a deploy, give each kill switch that stays an owner, and exercise every fallback path in test or in production on a schedule.
cards.why: A deploy is the slowest way to stop a feature that is hurting users. An untested fallback fails exactly when you need it: a fail-open path that never ran under load can overload the systems behind it, and a kill switch applied to a case it never met can raise its own error. Run the service with the dependency turned off, such as the cache disabled, and check that the safeguards hold.
cards.counterpoint: "Flags add branches." True for release flags, so delete each one after the rollout. A kill switch is meant to stay: keep it, and exercise it with the fallbacks, so it still works the day you need it. For runbook steps that a person runs, such as a rollback or a failover, see [[inc-rollback-path-tested]].

cards.applies_when: A latency SLO, dashboard, or alert is defined for a service.
cards.tool_gate: Lint alert rules for avg() over latency or over pre-computed quantiles.
cards.note: Never the mean: Google, AWS (a vendor), Microsoft (a vendor). Prometheus warns only against averaging quantiles; OpenTelemetry is a definition page
cards.rule: Define latency SLOs and alerts on high percentiles, never on the mean.
cards.why: A mean can look healthy while 1 request in 100 takes seconds, and those are the users who leave. Averaging per-instance quantiles is also wrong: quantiles do not add, so compute the percentile from a histogram, the one form that aggregates correctly across replicas.
cards.counterpoint: "Percentiles are noisy at low traffic." They are, so set a minimum request count before the alert fires, or alert on the error budget burn rate. Pick bucket edges around the objective, or the percentile will be a guess between two wide buckets.

cards.applies_when: A new service, a new feature with its own traffic, or a large architecture change is about to launch.
cards.tool_gate: Load-test job with thresholds (k6, Gatling) in the release pipeline.
cards.rule: Load test before launch, past the expected peak, with pass and fail thresholds written down.
cards.why: Overload behaviour is hard to predict from code, and launch traffic often beats the estimate. Test the whole workload on production-like infrastructure: testing one component, on smaller machines, or only up to the expected load misses the queue that fills first. Run the test as a pipeline step too, so a later change cannot slip under the thresholds.
cards.counterpoint: "A production-sized test environment costs too much." Size the test to the risk. A scaled-down environment is acceptable for a non-critical workload, and skipping the test is low risk for a small one. For a launch that could take down a shared dependency, the test is cheaper than the outage. Roll out in stages either way ([[prod-canary-staged-rollout]]).

cards.applies_when: A service records aggregated metrics (counters, histograms, gauges) with labels or dimensions.
cards.tool_gate: A cardinality limit on the metrics backend; a lint that rejects labels named user_id, request_id or raw path.
cards.note: Prometheus (no user IDs, email addresses or other unbounded sets), Microsoft Azure Monitor (never a constantly changing value; timestamp as the example) and Micrometer (normalize and bound user-supplied tag values; the 404 URI example)
cards.rule: Give a metric label only a bounded set of values; never a user id, request id, email, timestamp or raw URL path.
cards.why: Every distinct label value creates a new time series. An unbounded label multiplies storage and query cost until the backend drops data or the bill arrives. User-supplied values are the usual cause, and a request path that includes ids or random 404 URLs is the sneakiest. Put per-request detail in a log line, span or event instead.
cards.counterpoint: "We need per-user numbers." Aggregated metrics are the wrong store for that. Wide-event and log stores are built for high-cardinality fields, so write the user id there and keep the metric label to the route and status class. A small, known set such as tenant tier or region is fine.

cards.why: Test environments rarely match production load, so the hot path in a test run is often not the hot path in production. cards.applies_when: Reads, writes, or a pipeline's traffic move from an old system to a new one, such as a new data store, a database upgrade, or a rewritten service.
cards.note: Netflix (ran the old and new ad-event pipelines in parallel and diffed their output on live traffic), Stripe (compared point-in-time snapshots of source and target shards before the traffic switch), Airbnb (replayed captured production queries on MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 and diffed the results), GitHub (a Scientist experiment ran a candidate code block beside the control and compared results and timing); Cabify checks for zero replication lag before a swap, which is a precondition and not a diff, so it is not cited
cards.rule: Before you move traffic to a new system, run it beside the old one on live or captured production traffic, diff the results, and cut over only when every mismatch is fixed or explained.
cards.why: Fixtures cover the cases someone thought of, and production holds the rest. Airbnb's replay of real queries against MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 found queries whose row order was never fixed, and an application that sent the same cacheable query over and over. Neither shows up in a test suite. A diff on real traffic finds these while the old system still answers users, so a mismatch costs a log line instead of an incident. Then shift traffic in steps with a way back; see [[prod-canary-staged-rollout]] and [[prod-kill-switch-fallback]].
cards.counterpoint: "Running both is slow and doubles the load." It is slower than a flag-day switch, and Netflix says that is the reason it trusts the result. Keep the cost down: shadow a sample, call the new system off the request path, and never shadow a call with side effects such as a charge or an email. For writes, compare data snapshots after replication, as Stripe does, instead of sending each write twice. A refactor inside one process needs a characterization test, not production traffic. See [[chg-refactor-has-behaviour-pin]].

cards.applies_when: The service links a federated identity to an existing account, or looks up an account by an email or profile claim.
cards.note: the practical gate is an integration test: a local account with an unverified email, then an IdP sign-in asserting the same address, must not merge without proof of control of the local account
cards.rule: Link a federated identity to an existing account only after proving control of both, and key the link on the pair `iss` and `sub`, never on an unverified email or another profile claim.
cards.why: An attacker who registers a victim's address first can wait for the victim to press "Sign in with Google" and inherit the account through an automatic merge. The same bug appears when an IdP asserts an address it never verified, or one that changed owner since it did. An authenticated session on the existing account, plus a freshly authenticated federated identity, proves both sides. `iss` and `sub` together are the only stable key; email, `preferred_username` and name can be reused or reassigned, so they are a lookup hint at best. Each `iss` and `sub` pair belongs to one local account only.
cards.counterpoint: "Users expect the Google button to find the account with their email." Find it by a verified address if you like, then stop and require the password or an authenticated session before linking. A verified flag is not always present, and an address verified at signup can belong to someone else today, so verify it yourself when the IdP does not. Treating the match as proof is what the attack needs. Google says that where it is authoritative for the address (a `@gmail.com` address, or `email_verified` with `hd` set) you may skip a password challenge. That settles who owns the address, not who controls the local account, so an IdP that is authoritative for the domain may be trusted for the lookup, and the merge still needs the authenticated local session when the local address was never verified.

cards.applies_when: A service returns responses that a browser, CDN, gateway or client library may cache.
cards.tool_gate: Integration test or header lint that rejects a 200 GET without `Cache-Control`.
cards.note: do not let an edge rule override the origin header - PortSwigger, AWS, Google and Microsoft; decide cacheability by Content-Type - PortSwigger, Cloudflare and Google; "the origin and the cache read the path the same way" has PortSwigger only, so it is in Why
cards.rule: Set an explicit `Cache-Control` on every response a cache may store, use `private` or `no-store` for user-specific data, add `Vary` for any request header that changes the body, keep the origin's `Cache-Control` authoritative at the edge (no minimum TTL or force-cache override), and decide cacheability by the response `Content-Type`, not the URL extension.
cards.why: With no directive, a cache may guess a lifetime from `Last-Modified`. A shared cache may then serve one user's response to another, or serve stale data for hours after a write. A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with `Authorization` unless the response says `public`, `must-revalidate` or `s-maxage`. `private` still lets the browser keep a copy, so use `no-store` for sensitive data. At the edge, cache only responses that do not depend on the user. A dynamic page requested at `/account/x.css` is the same failure from the cache side: a rule that decides by extension stores a private page, and an edge rule that overrides `no-store` keeps it. The origin and the cache must also read the path the same way. When they do not, a path the origin treats as private can look like a static file to the cache.
cards.counterpoint: "Our CDN bypasses the cache for logged-in users." That config is a second place to get wrong, and it does not cover the browser. A cache rule that sets a minimum TTL, or a force-cache mode, can still beat the origin header. Check the specific policy value, and keep secrets out of cacheable URLs even when the header is right.

(no Cache-Control, no Vary; body differs per Authorization)

cards.applies_when: Two callers can update the same resource through PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
cards.tool_gate: Integration test that sends a write with a stale `If-Match` and expects 412.
cards.rule: Return an `ETag` on reads and honour `If-Match` on writes, answering 412 when the entity tag is stale.
cards.why: A read-modify-write over HTTP is a race. The second writer overwrites the first without knowing it, and no error appears anywhere. A DELETE races the same way: without the check it removes an update made after the read. After a 412 the client reads the resource again and retries on the fresh copy.
cards.counterpoint: "Last write wins is fine here." For a log or a counter it is; say so in the spec. For a document, a profile or a config that two people edit, it loses work. The card applies to shared resources that people edit.

fail.code:
GET /docs/4  -> 200 {title: "A"}
PUT /docs/4  {title: "B"}   -> 200   # overwrites a change made after the GET

pass.code:
GET /docs/4  -> 200  ETag: "v7"
PUT /docs/4  If-Match: "v7"  -> 200  ETag: "v8"
PUT /docs/4  If-Match: "v7"  -> 412 Precondition Failed

cards.applies_when: A service calls, or is called by, another service owned by a different team or deployed on its own schedule.
cards.tool_gate: Contract test run in CI for both sides, and a gate that blocks deploy when a consumer's contract fails against the provider.
cards.note: the Pact page read does not describe provider verification or the broker; those steps are not asserted here
cards.rule: Run a contract test for each cross-service call, derived from the consumer's real requests, and fail the provider's build when it breaks one.
cards.why: A provider's own tests check what the provider thinks callers need. A spec check says what could happen, not what the consumer relies on. Only a check built from the consumer's usage catches the removed field before deploy, without a full-system end-to-end run.
cards.counterpoint: "End-to-end tests cover it." They are slow, need every service running, and run late. Contract tests run per service in minutes. Pact is one way; a consumer-written example set replayed against the provider also passes. For services deployed together from one repo, mark the card N/A.

fail.code:
billing calls GET /customers/{id} and reads "vat_id"
customers team removes "vat_id"; its tests pass; billing breaks in production

pass.code:
billing CI publishes a contract: GET /customers/{id} -> body has "vat_id"
customers CI verifies every published contract and fails on the removal

cards.applies_when: A service retires an endpoint, field, version or parameter that outside callers use.
cards.tool_gate: Middleware that adds both headers for routes tagged deprecated; a spec linter on `deprecated: true` without a sunset date; a dashboard counting calls that carry the headers.
cards.note: Mark deprecated: Zalando, OpenAPI, Google AIP-185 (marks deprecation in the API definition, not literally an OpenAPI document). Send both headers: IETF, Zalando, GitHub (a vendor). Sunset not before Deprecation: IETF RFC 9745 only, so it is in Why
cards.rule: Before removing an endpoint, mark it `deprecated` in the spec and send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers.
cards.why: The `Sunset` date must not be earlier than the `Deprecation` date (RFC 9745). Callers cannot read your roadmap. A removal with no signal in the responses is an outage for whoever has not read the changelog. Set the `Sunset` date well after the announcement: projects that publish a minimum keep deprecated behaviour for one to two years. Counting calls that carry the headers also tells you when removal is safe.
cards.counterpoint: "Our only callers are internal." Then the call count with the header gives you the list of owners to ask, and removal is cheap. [[chg-expand-contract]] covers the order of steps; this card covers what the response tells the caller. Both headers describe one resource, so send them on each deprecated route, not only on the API root.

fail.code:
git: delete GET /v1/orders/{id}/summary
responses before removal: no header, spec not marked deprecated

pass.code:
GET /v1/orders/9/summary -> 200
  Deprecation: @1798761600
  Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2028 00:00:00 GMT
  Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/summary-removal>; rel="deprecation"
  Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/summary-removal>; rel="sunset"
spec: deprecated: true

cards.applies_when: A service has an OpenAPI description, or callers depend on its error responses.
cards.tool_gate: Spec linter that requires 4xx and 5xx responses with a schema on every operation, and an example on each.
cards.note: OpenAPI requires only one response per operation; the stricter rule comes from Zalando rule 151
cards.rule: Document every error status each operation can return, with a schema and one example.
cards.why: Callers write error handling from the spec. An operation that lists only 200 teaches them nothing about 404, 409, 422 or 429, so they find out in production. Give the errors one shared schema, such as RFC 9457 problem details, so each carries a status, a title and a type URI that callers can match on.
cards.counterpoint: "A shared `default` response covers everything." OpenAPI allows `default`, but it hides which codes carry which meaning. List the codes a caller must act on and use `default` for the rest.

fail.code:
/orders/{id}:
  get:
    responses:
      "200": {description: ok}

cards.applies_when: Callers of an HTTP or RPC API branch on the kind of error.
cards.tool_gate: Spec linter that requires an enumerated error `type` or `reason` per operation; a test that pins the codes.
cards.note: RFC 9457 and Google AIP-193 describe the mechanism; the rule never to reword a published code is inference from both
cards.rule: Give each error a stable machine-readable code that callers branch on, and never make them parse the message text.
cards.why: Message text gets reworded, translated and fixed. A client that matches on "already exists" breaks on the first edit. A published code is a contract, and one code names one kind of error: reusing it for a different error breaks callers who branch on it.
cards.counterpoint: "The HTTP status is enough." It is too coarse: two different 409 conflicts need different handling. Add a code only where callers act differently; do not mint one for every branch.

fail.code:
if "already exists" in response.json()["detail"]:   # client
    handle_conflict()

pass.code:
if response.json()["type"] == "https://api.example.com/problems/order-exists":   # client
    handle_conflict()
# the server keeps that type value for as long as the API version lives

cards.applies_when: The service issues an API key or long-lived access token to a caller.
cards.note: exposure paths are covered by code-secret-scan, svc-no-secrets-in-url and sys-secrets-and-errors; this card covers what the issued key is allowed to do
cards.rule: Issue each API key with the narrowest scopes and a bounded lifetime, and rotate or revoke it after any exposure.
cards.why: A key with account-wide scope turns one leaked string into the whole account, and a key with no end date is still valid years after the integration was forgotten. Scopes bound what a leak can do; an expiry or a rotation bounds how long it can do it. Rotating on a schedule, as Google and Stripe advise, also shows whether you can replace the key before an incident forces the question. Review keys regularly and delete any that are no longer needed. Where the platform allows, also bind a key to the sites, IP addresses or apps that use it. Show the secret once, at creation, as AWS does.
cards.counterpoint: "Short expiry and rotation break integrations that nobody watches." That is the cost, and it is smaller than a key that never dies. Prefer a temporary credential where the platform offers one, give each integration its own key so rotation is one at a time, and keep the overlap window long enough for a deploy. A shared key with no owner cannot be rotated safely, which is the real defect.

fail.code:
key = "sk_live_..."          # full account scope, no expiry
db.insert(user_id, key)      # plaintext, returned by every read

pass.code:
key = issue(user, scopes=["orders:read"], expires_in=90 * DAY)
return key                   # shown once
# rotate on a schedule; revoke at once on exposure

cards.applies_when: A service defines JSON fields, query parameters, headers or path segments for an HTTP API.
cards.tool_gate: Spec linter with a casing rule per location.
cards.note: Zalando and Microsoft disagree on the convention, so the card checks consistency, not the choice
cards.rule: Use one casing convention per location (fields, query parameters, headers, paths) across the whole API, and state it in the API guide. Name collections and array fields as plural nouns.
cards.why: Mixed casing in one API makes callers look up each name. A client that guesses `orderId` after meeting `order_id` gets a silent null. The same goes for number: a field named `item` that holds a list reads as one value, so name collections and array fields in the plural.
cards.counterpoint: "Pick the right convention." Published guides disagree: some ask for snake_case, others for camelCase in fields. Either passes. Do not change an existing API's casing to match a guide; that is a breaking change.

fail.code: GET /orders?pageSize=20 -> {"order_id": 1, "createdAt": "...", "Total-Cents": 500, "item": [...]}

pass.code:
GET /orders?page_size=20 -> {"order_id": 1, "created_at": "...", "total_cents": 500, "items": [...]}
# snake_case everywhere, as docs/api-guide.md says

cards.applies_when: A service returns errors from an HTTP API to other services or to clients.
cards.tool_gate: Middleware that builds every error body from one problem-details type; a test that fails on an error response without the media type.
cards.rule: Return errors as `application/problem+json` with a `status` that equals the HTTP status, and leave stack traces and internal detail out.
cards.why: Callers then parse every error one way. A body that differs per endpoint, or a `status` that disagrees with the real code, makes generic client and proxy handling unreliable. A stack trace in `detail` hands an attacker the implementation.
cards.counterpoint: "We already have our own error envelope." That is fine inside one team's API, if it is one envelope and documented. The card asks for one shape everywhere; problem details is the one with a registered media type and existing client support. See [[sys-secrets-and-errors]] for what must stay out of any error.

fail.code:
HTTP/1.1 500 Content-Type: text/html 
NullPointerException at OrderRepo.java:88 ...

pass.code:
HTTP/1.1 404
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.example.com/problems/order-not-found",
 "title": "Order not found", "status": 404,
 "detail": "No order with id 7731 for this account."}

cards.applies_when: A service answers 429 or 503 to HTTP callers.
cards.tool_gate: Integration test that forces a 429 and a 503 and asserts a `Retry-After` header.
cards.note: the draft rate-limit header fields are not required here; RFC 6585 on 429 was not fetched
cards.rule: Send `Retry-After` on every 429 and 503, and set it no earlier than the time capacity returns.
cards.why: Without it, every client invents its own backoff, and a hundred of them retry in the same second. The header lets the server pace its own recovery.
cards.counterpoint: "Clients should use exponential backoff anyway." They should, and [[svc-retry-policy]] says so. A server hint narrows the guess; it does not replace the client's cap. The IETF `RateLimit` header fields are still an Internet-Draft, so the card requires only `Retry-After`, which is in the HTTP standard. The quota itself is [[svc-rate-limit-quota]].

fail.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

{"error": "slow down"}

pass.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

cards.applies_when: A service returns HTTP responses that callers or intermediaries interpret by status code.
cards.tool_gate: Integration tests asserting status and headers per operation; a spec linter for 201 and 405 responses.
cards.note: RFC 9110 sections 9.3.4, 10.2.1 and 15.3.2; section 15.5.6 on 405 was not read
cards.rule: Return the most specific status code that fits: 201 with `Location` for a create, 405 with `Allow` for a wrong method, and a 4xx or 5xx for any failure.
cards.why: Clients, proxies and monitors act on the status line. A 200 with an error in the body hides failures from retries, caches and error-rate alerts. A create that returns 200 without `Location` forces the caller to guess the new URL. A request body in a format the operation does not accept gets 415, not a 200 or a generic 400.
cards.counterpoint: "A 200 with a status field is easier for our clients." It breaks every generic tool that reads the status line, including your own dashboards. Choosing between two fitting codes is a style call; the card fails only a code that says the wrong thing.

fail.code:
POST /orders -> 200 {"error": "out of stock"}
PATCH /orders (route is read-only) -> 404, no Allow header

pass.code:
POST /orders -> 201  Location: /orders/9031
POST /orders (out of stock) -> 409 application/problem+json
PATCH /orders (not supported) -> 405  Allow: GET, POST

cards.applies_when: The code calls an HTTP API that publishes dated or numbered versions, or the service offers one.
cards.tool_gate: A shared HTTP client wrapper or gateway rule that sets the version, and a contract test that a request without one is rejected.
cards.rule: Name the API version on every request, in a header or a query parameter.
cards.why: A request with no version gets whatever the server treats as the default, and that default moves. The caller then breaks on the server's schedule, not its own. A request that names its version keeps the behaviour it was tested against until the caller moves it. Choosing the scheme and keeping a version stable are covered by [[svc-api-versioning-policy]].
cards.counterpoint: "Always sending a version is clutter, and the latest is what we want anyway." The latest is only what you want on the day you tested it. Put the version in one client wrapper so call sites stay clean, and bump it as a reviewed change.

fail.code:
GET /orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

pass.code:
GET /orders?api-version=2026-03-01 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

cards.applies_when: A service offers an HTTP API to callers you do not deploy together with it.
cards.tool_gate: Spec diff in CI that fails on a breaking change inside a published version.
cards.note: the three sources pick three different mechanisms; the card requires only that one is chosen and documented
cards.rule: Write down one versioning scheme for the API, and ship no breaking change inside a version it has published.
cards.why: Callers upgrade on their own schedule. With no stated scheme, each breaking change is a surprise, and each team invents its own v2. Additive changes, such as a new field, can ship inside the current version; only a breaking change needs a new one.
cards.counterpoint: "We will cross that bridge later." Later arrives with a customer on the old shape. The scheme can be minimal. A media type, a dated query parameter and a pinned header all work. Pick one and write it down. What counts as breaking is in [[chg-breaking-change-taxonomy]].

fail.code:
GET /orders   # renamed total -> amount_total
no version marker anywhere; README says "we try not to break things"

pass.code:
docs/api-versioning.md: dated api-version query parameter, previews last 6 months, 90 days' notice
GET /orders?api-version=2026-03-01 keeps returning "total"
the rename ships under api-version=2026-09-01

cards.applies_when: A page loads images, embeds, fonts, ads, or fetched content after the first paint.
cards.tool_gate: Lighthouse CI assertion on `cumulative-layout-shift`.
cards.note: injected content and ads are backed by Google only; cut to image dimensions the Rule has Google and Mozilla firm, while WHATWG advises width and height only on lazy-loaded images (checked 2026-10-24), so it is a partial third; Apple and NN/g on placeholders are indirect
cards.rule: Reserve the space for late-loading content with set dimensions or an aspect ratio, so nothing already on screen moves.
cards.why: A page that jumps while someone reads or taps makes them hit the wrong target. A cumulative layout shift of 0.1 or less is good, and over 0.25 is poor, measured on real users at the 75th percentile. A placeholder of the same size, such as a skeleton, fills the reserved space and reads better than a blank gap.
cards.counterpoint: "Ads vary in height." Reserve the common height, or the largest, and accept some blank space. A banner that pushes the article down is the worse trade.

cards.applies_when: The service has a login, password-reset or one-time-code endpoint.
cards.tool_gate: Rate-limit middleware on auth routes; test that known and unknown users get identical responses.
cards.rule: Limit failed attempts per account, and return the same message and status code whether or not the account exists.
cards.why: Unlimited guesses make passwords and 6-digit codes brute-forceable. Different errors for "no such user" and "wrong password" let an attacker list valid accounts first. Limit per account, since a per-IP limit is bypassed by rotating addresses. Response time leaks the same fact: if the code hashes the password only when the user exists, a fast reply means "no such user", so hash on every attempt. Registration needs its own design: give the same reply whether or not the address is taken, and email the owner of an existing account instead of creating a second one.
cards.counterpoint: "A lockout lets attackers lock out real users." Use a rising delay, not a permanent lock, and keep the recovery flow reachable. Log every lockout so abuse shows up.

fail.code:
if not user: return "No such user", 404
if not check(pw): return "Wrong password", 401      # no attempt limit

pass.code:
if too_many_failures(account_key): return "Try again later", 429   # checked before the password
ok = check(pw, user.pw_hash if user else DUMMY_HASH)              # hash runs either way
if not (user and ok): record_failure(account_key); return "Invalid credentials", 401

cards.applies_when: The service has routes that need a signed-in user next to routes that are public.
cards.tool_gate: A framework fallback that requires authentication (ASP.NET Core `FallbackPolicy`, Django `LoginRequiredMiddleware`, Spring Security `anyRequest().authenticated()`); a test that calls every route without credentials and expects 401 or a login redirect unless the route is on the public list.
cards.note: svc-authz-central-deny-default decides what a known user may do; this card decides whether an anonymous caller gets in at all (CWE-306)
cards.rule: Require authentication on every route by default, and mark each public route by name.
cards.why: When each handler opts in to authentication, the one that forgets is open to the internet, and nothing in the diff looks wrong. A global fallback flips the default: a new route is closed until someone marks it public, and that mark is a line a reviewer can question. Health checks and internal admin ports count as routes too.
cards.counterpoint: "Our gateway already checks the token." Then the service trusts every caller that can reach it without the gateway: another pod, a debug port, a misrouted path. Keep the gateway check and the fallback in the service. The fallback costs one middleware.

fail.code:
@app.get("/invoices/<id>")          # no login check; anonymous callers get the invoice
def invoice(id): ...

cards.applies_when: The service exposes routes or functions that different roles may call.
cards.tool_gate: Router that denies routes with no policy; a test that lists every route and its required role.
cards.rule: Route every request through one authorization layer that denies when no rule allows it.
cards.why: Per-handler checks drift: one admin route ships without its decorator and any user can call it. A central layer with deny as the fallback turns a forgotten check into a 403 instead of a hole.
cards.counterpoint: "A central policy is a bottleneck for feature teams." Keep the engine central and let each team own its rows. The cost of a one-line policy entry is small next to an unguarded admin route.

fail.code:
@app.route("/admin/export")        # no role check; framework default is allow
def export(): ...

cards.applies_when: The critical path of a request or a job calls a dependency whose data the product can do without, such as enrichment, recommendations, analytics, or a rate-limit control plane.
cards.note: best-effort calls - Netflix (calls to metrics, logs and other systems are best-effort; a slow dependency degrades the graph and never blocks it), Uber (rate-limit clients fail open when the control plane is down), Cabify (skips non-critical details in a driver offer when it cannot collect them fast enough); a metric and alert on each fallback - Cabify only
cards.rule: Give each call to a non-critical dependency a short budget and a default, so its failure degrades the result instead of failing the critical path, and count every fallback.
cards.why: An order page should not fail because the recommendations service is slow. Netflix makes enrichment best-effort, so a slow dependency can degrade its knowledge graph but never block it. Uber's rate-limit clients let traffic through when the control plane is down, because blocking would cause an outage of its own. Cabify drops non-critical details from a driver offer when it cannot collect them in time. It also puts metrics and alerts on every such fallback, because SLO dashboards built for critical flows miss them.
cards.counterpoint: "A silent default hides an outage." It does when nobody counts it, so the PASS needs the metric and an alert on it. Call a dependency non-critical only when the product works without its data. Authentication, payment, and authorization checks are critical, and they fail closed. Failing open on a rate limiter gives up protection to keep availability, so write that choice into the design. For the timeout itself, see [[svc-timeouts]]. To check that the fallback really runs, see [[prod-kill-switch-fallback]].

cards.applies_when: A request parameter or body sets how many records, bytes, items or operations the server handles.
cards.tool_gate: Gateway request-size limit; schema `maxLength`/`maxItems`; test with a 10 MB body and `limit=1000000`.
cards.rule: Cap every client-controlled size and count on the server: body bytes, string length, array items, page size and batch size.
cards.why: A request for `limit=10000000` or a batch of 50,000 operations lets one client exhaust memory or the bill for a paid backend. The cap has to sit in the server, since a UI limit is not one. [[svc-rate-limit-quota]] covers request rate; this card covers size.
cards.counterpoint: "Legit clients sometimes need big batches." Offer a documented bulk or export endpoint with its own quota. The default path stays capped.

fail.code:
limit = int(request.args["limit"])
rows = db.fetch(limit)                              # no ceiling
items: list[Item]                                    # schema with no maxItems

pass.code:
limit = max(1, min(int(request.args.get("limit", 50)), 100))
items: list[Item] = Field(max_length=100)            # body capped at 1 MB by the proxy

cards.applies_when: The service takes requests from callers it does not control.
cards.rule: Cap how many requests a service handles at once with an explicit concurrency limit, and reject the excess. A timeout alone does not bound it.
cards.why: Concurrency is arrival rate times latency. When a dependency slows down, in-flight requests pile up even if every one has a timeout and a retry cap, and the service runs out of threads, memory or connections. A hard limit turns that into fast 503 responses. In-flight count is also a better overload signal than requests per second, because it rises when work gets slower. This card limits inbound requests. Per-dependency limits are in [[svc-circuit-breaker-bulkhead]], background tasks in [[svc-bounded-background-tasks]], and queues in [[sys-load-shedding-bounded-queues]].
cards.counterpoint: "Autoscaling adds capacity when load rises." Scaling takes minutes and the pile-up takes seconds. The limit protects the service until new capacity arrives. Set it from a load test, not a guess, and revisit it when the service changes.

fail.code:
import asyncio

from aiohttp import web

async def handle(request):
    async with asyncio.timeout(5):          # a timeout only; any number of requests can wait here
        return web.json_response(await backend.query(request))

cards.applies_when: The code starts a task, goroutine, or thread per item, request, or message.
cards.note: Both clauses are backed by Google (the Go blog, flagged as a vendor), Cabify and AWS (a vendor). AWS states a semaphore and per-workload thread pools that limit concurrency, and its page names the same thread-pool exhaustion the Why describes. errgroup and asyncio supply the limiting tools
cards.rule: Cap how many background tasks run at once, and never spawn one per input with no limit.
cards.why: Input size is not under your control. One task per item works for ten items and exhausts memory, connections, or the downstream service at ten thousand, and the failure lands on everything else in the process. Go's `errgroup.SetLimit`, asyncio's `Semaphore` and Tokio's `Semaphore` exist for exactly this.
cards.counterpoint: "Tasks are cheap." Creating them is, but what each one holds (a socket, a buffer, a database connection) is not. A semaphore around each handler also caps concurrency, though it still creates one task object per input. This card covers work that a service starts for itself. [[sys-load-shedding-bounded-queues]] covers refusing incoming requests under load.

fail.code:
for msg in batch:                       # batch size comes from the queue
    asyncio.create_task(handle(msg))    # 50k messages -> 50k concurrent handlers

pass.code:
async def worker(queue):
    while (msg := await queue.get()) is not None:
        await handle(msg)

queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    for _ in range(32):                 # at most 32 handlers at once
        tg.create_task(worker(queue))
    for msg in batch:
        await queue.put(msg)
    for _ in range(32):
        await queue.put(None)           # one stop signal per worker

cards.applies_when: A shared cache (CDN, reverse proxy, gateway, or framework cache) stores responses the service generates.
cards.tool_gate: A test that sends an unkeyed header or a GET body and asserts the response body does not change.
cards.note: svc-api-cache-control owns Cache-Control and Vary; the key and the unkeyed inputs are this card. key completeness - AWS, Cloudflare and Fastly (the Microsoft Front Door page covers only query-string keying, so it is not a source); unkeyed input kept out of the body - Cloudflare, PortSwigger and Fastly; static-only caching has Cloudflare, PortSwigger and Google but vendors disagree, so it is in Why
cards.rule: Key every request input that can change the response, and strip any other request value before it reaches a cached body.
cards.why: A cache keeps one response per key. If the origin echoes a header, a cookie, or a GET body that the key ignores, the first request stores content that every later visitor receives. An attacker can then place content on your domain without touching the origin: a link or a form. A value that reaches the body belongs in the key, or it must not reach the body at all. Do not key on a value that varies per user or per request, such as `User-Agent` or a session cookie: it splits the cache into one entry per value, so strip it instead. Caching only static types by default narrows the surface, though CDN defaults differ.
cards.counterpoint: "We leave that header out of the key to keep the hit rate up." It does raise the hit rate, by serving one requester's variant to everyone. Strip or rewrite the value when the response does not need it, and key it when it does.

fail.code: GET /home HTTP/1.1 X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.example origin body: Account cache key: path only

pass.code:
edge: strip X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL and X-Rewrite-URL before the origin
edge: return 400 to a GET with a body, or bypass the cache for it
origin: echo a header only when it is in Vary or the cache key
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60   Vary: Accept-Language

cards.applies_when: A service calls several dependencies from shared pools, or retries a dependency that may be down.
cards.rule: Give each critical dependency its own concurrency limit.
cards.why: One shared pool lets a slow dependency use every thread and starve healthy paths. Retrying a dead dependency only adds load, so also fail fast through a breaker with limited half-open probing where retries are demonstrably harmful.
cards.counterpoint: "More moving parts than a timeout." True. Start with the timeout and the per-dependency limit, and add the breaker where retries are demonstrably harmful. Retry and breaker have opposite aims, so do not present one as a substitute for the other.

fail.code:
pool = ThreadPool(50)               # used by billing, search, email alike
breaker = None                      # retries a dead host every request

pass.code:
pools = {"billing": asyncio.Semaphore(10), "search": asyncio.Semaphore(20)}
# pseudocode: breaker logs and counts every state change; half-open allows 1 probe

cards.applies_when: A command-line tool has a command that deletes, overwrites or sends something.
cards.tool_gate: CLI test that runs the command with the preview flag and checks nothing changed.
cards.note: Preview flag backed by Kubernetes (kubectl --dry-run), Git (git clean -n) and GNU (make -n); confirmation bypass backed by GitHub (gh repo delete --yes), Microsoft (az --yes), Google (gcloud --quiet) and HashiCorp (terraform -auto-approve)
cards.rule: Give a destructive command a preview flag that changes nothing and a flag that skips the confirmation prompt.
cards.why: Without a preview, the first run is the real one. Without a bypass, a script cannot run the command at all, so people write wrappers that pipe "yes" into it.
cards.counterpoint: "A bypass flag invites accidents." The prompt stays the default for people, and the flag has to be typed on purpose. Pair it with [[svc-cli-non-interactive]].

cards.applies_when: The code ships a command-line tool that scripts or other programs may run.
cards.tool_gate: CLI test that runs a failing command and checks the exit code and that stdout is empty.
cards.note: Non-zero exit on failure backed by Google (gcloud), GitHub (gh exit codes), AWS (CLI return codes), HashiCorp (terraform plan) and The Open Group (POSIX); results on stdout and diagnostics on stderr backed by The Open Group (POSIX), Heroku (CLI style guide) and the Rust CLI working group; clig.dev is a reference
cards.rule: Exit non-zero when a command fails, and write results to stdout and errors and progress to stderr.
cards.why: Scripts branch on the exit code and pipe stdout into the next program. A failure that exits 0 reads as success, and an error line on stdout lands in the next program's input. Scripts should never parse error wording or default text, which can change between releases. Add a `--json` flag for structured results, and keep prompts out of non-terminal runs (see [[svc-cli-non-interactive]]). Where callers must tell failures apart, give each class its own documented code, such as bad usage, authentication required or a service error.
cards.counterpoint: "Some tools use exit codes for non-error results." Documented codes for states such as "differences found" are fine. The rule is that a failure never exits 0.

cards.applies_when: The code ships a command-line tool that scripts or agents may run.
cards.tool_gate: CLI test that runs every command with stdin closed.
cards.note: Rule backed by GitHub (GH_PROMPT_DISABLED, --title/--body skip the prompt), Google (gcloud --quiet), HashiCorp (terraform -input=false) and Microsoft (az core.disable_confirm_prompt); failing at once with an example call when a flag is missing has one org (clig.dev, a reference), so it sits in Why
cards.rule: Let the caller turn every prompt off with a flag or an environment variable, so the command never waits on a terminal.
cards.why: A script or an agent has no one to answer a prompt, so the command hangs until a timeout kills it. When stdin is not a terminal, the best behaviour is to fail at once with an error that names the missing flag and shows an example call, so the caller fixes it in one step.
cards.counterpoint: "Prompts are friendlier for people." Keep them. The rule only asks that the caller can switch prompts off.

cards.applies_when: The code makes many calls to an API that publishes a rate limit.
cards.rule: Pace outgoing calls to a rate-limited API on the client, at a fixed rate or with a token bucket, so the client is not throttled.
cards.why: A client that fires as fast as it can hits the limit, collects 429 responses, and spends its quota on calls that fail. Pacing to the published rate keeps the calls that count inside the budget. Retrying a 429 after backoff still has a place, as in [[svc-retry-policy]], but it is the second line.
cards.counterpoint: "The server returns 429 and Retry-After, so we can just react." Reacting means the limit is hit every time, and on some APIs repeated hits cost extra or lock the client out. Pace first and keep the 429 handling for the bursts that still get through.

fail.code:
for order in orders:
    client.post("/orders", json=order)   # thousands of calls in a tight loop; the API allows 2 per second

cards.applies_when: A change adds or edits a Kubernetes workload manifest or Helm values with containers.
cards.tool_gate: An admission policy or manifest linter that rejects a container with no CPU request, memory request or memory limit; a namespace LimitRange that supplies defaults.
cards.note: Microsoft says to set requests and limits on every pod, AWS says each container including sidecars needs its own, and Google says to give every container CPU and memory requests and to match memory requests to limits. Google advises leaving CPU limits unset, so the Rule asks for a memory limit only. The Kubernetes concepts page describes the mechanism and states no rule, so it is not counted
cards.rule: Set a CPU request, a memory request and a memory limit on every container in the manifest, sidecars included.
cards.why: The scheduler places pods by their requests. A container with none looks free, so nodes get overpacked and neighbours starve each other. A cluster with quotas can also reject the deployment. Without a memory limit, one leak takes the whole node down instead of restarting one container. A CPU limit is left out on purpose: it throttles a container that has spare node capacity, so set the CPU request to what the service needs and leave the limit off unless you have a reason. Size the numbers from measured use, not a guess copied from another service.
cards.counterpoint: "The namespace already has a LimitRange with defaults." Then the manifest can omit the block, as long as the repo shows that policy and the defaults fit the workload. Default values are one size for every container, so a service with a real profile still needs its own numbers.

containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.2
  - name: log-shipper

cards.applies_when: The service sends CORS headers and browsers send credentials or cookies to it, or the API is not meant to be public. A public bearer-key API with `*` and no credentials is outside it.
cards.tool_gate: Integration test that sends a hostile `Origin` and asserts it is not echoed.
cards.rule: Allow cross-origin access only to a fixed list of named origins, and never echo the request `Origin` header back unchecked.
cards.why: Reflecting any Origin, or allowing `*` on an endpoint that returns private data, lets a hostile page read responses. CORS also does not stop CSRF, so it is no substitute for [[svc-csrf-state-changing]]. A subdomain regex that matches `evil-example.com` is the same bug, and so is allowing the `null` origin.
cards.counterpoint: "`*` is fine for a public API." It is, for endpoints that return only public data and take no credentials. Keep it off any endpoint behind a login.

cards.applies_when: The service serves HTML pages to browsers.
cards.tool_gate: Google CSP Evaluator on the policy; a CI header check against a staging URL.
cards.note: follows OWASP, MDN and web.dev, which are stricter than the ASVS 3.4.3 minimum (that minimum still allows a host allowlist); fn-no-raw-html-sink is the first defence against XSS and CSP is the second
cards.rule: Send a `Content-Security-Policy` whose `script-src` uses a per-response nonce or script hashes, with `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`.
cards.why: When an XSS bug slips through, CSP decides whether the injected script runs. A host allowlist such as `script-src 'self' cdn.example` usually has a bypass, because some allowed host serves JSONP or an old library. A nonce or hash only lets through scripts the server marked. `'strict-dynamic'` lets those scripts load their own children. Browsers that support nonces ignore an `'unsafe-inline'` fallback placed next to one, so that fallback is safe. `'unsafe-inline'` on its own turns the policy off for inline script. Send the header on every response, not only the main page.
cards.counterpoint: "A strict CSP breaks inline handlers and third-party tags." It does at first, so roll it out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, move `onclick=` attributes into script files, and switch to enforce when the reports go quiet. A policy that never leaves report-only protects nothing, so give that step a date.

fail.code: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://cdn.example.com

pass.code:
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
<script nonce="r4nd0m" src="/app.js"></script>

cards.applies_when: The service authenticates browsers with cookies and changes state on requests.
cards.tool_gate: Framework CSRF middleware enabled; test that a POST without the token returns 403.
cards.rule: Require a CSRF token (or an equivalent header check) on every cookie-authenticated request that changes state, and never change state on GET.
cards.why: The browser attaches cookies to a cross-site request, so a hostile page can post as the user. `SameSite` helps but `Lax` still sends cookies on cross-site top-level GET, so it supports the token and does not replace it. Naive double-submit cookies fail when a sibling subdomain can set cookies.
cards.counterpoint: "Our API uses JSON, so browsers cannot forge it." A simple content type such as `text/plain` can carry a JSON body without a preflight. Reject it, or require a custom header such as `X-CSRF-Token`. Pure bearer-token APIs with no cookies are exempt.

@app.post("/transfer")                         # cookie auth, no token check

cards.applies_when: The service has a debug mode, such as Flask or Django debug, a framework debugger or verbose error pages.
cards.tool_gate: A config check that debug is false in the production settings, and a smoke test that a deliberate server error returns a plain error page with no traceback.
cards.note: The Rule covers debug mode, backed by OWASP ASVS, Django and Flask. Microsoft backs the Swagger UI point in the Why alone, so it is not part of the Rule
cards.rule: Keep debug mode off in production, and turn it on by environment so that a missing setting leaves it off.
cards.why: A debug mode prints stack traces, settings and local variables, and some frameworks serve an interactive console that runs code from the browser. Each hands an attacker a map and secrets. A docs UI such as Swagger UI is the same kind of exposure: it lists every endpoint, parameter and model, including internal ones, so serve it in development only or put it behind authentication. Make the safe state the default.
cards.counterpoint: "We need the traceback to diagnose a production bug." Send errors to a log or an error tracker, where the team can read them and visitors cannot. To reproduce a problem with debug on, run the same build in a staging environment that is not public.

app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)   # the interactive debugger is reachable wherever this runs

cards.applies_when: The code decompresses or decodes input whose size it does not control.
cards.tool_gate: Apache `DeflateInflateLimitRequestBody`; ASP.NET Core `MaxRequestBodySize`; a test that inflates a 1 MB gzip to about 1 GB and asserts the decoder stops at the cap.
cards.rule: Cap the decompressed output of every decoder, and set the cap on the output rather than the compressed input.
cards.why: A small gzip can expand a thousand-fold: DEFLATE tops out near 1030:1, so a 1 MB gzip can inflate to about 1 GB, and nested archives or other codecs can go further. A body limit on the compressed bytes does not bound that expansion, so the decoder needs its own ceiling. `Content-Length` counts the compressed stream, not the inflated body, and Apache's inflated-body directive is unset by default. In Node, the convenience methods take `maxOutputLength`, whose default is `buffer.kMaxLength`, so pass a real number. The zip entry iterator is a separate case: `zipEntry.contentIterator()` has no default `maxSize` and is not covered by the zip-wide ceiling, so pass `maxSize` on that call. Python's tar filters address paths and links, and its docs say they do not prevent every unsafe archive, so size still needs its own bound. See also [[svc-bound-client-controlled-sizes]] for the request-body cap and [[svc-upload-validate-store]] for archives in uploads.
cards.counterpoint: "The proxy already caps the request body." It caps the compressed bytes, which is the wrong number. A 1 MB gzip can still inflate to about 1 GB, and `Content-Length` says nothing about the decompressed size. Set the inflated cap at the decoder and keep the body cap. Where the platform offers a decompression limit, check that it is on: Apache's directive falls back to the post-deflation `LimitRequestBody`, and a value of `0` removes the inflated-body limit.

fail.code:
const body = zlib.gunzipSync(req.body); // no maxOutputLength
parse(body);

pass.code:
const body = zlib.gunzipSync(req.body, { maxOutputLength: 1 << 20 });
parse(body);

cards.applies_when: The code consumes from a queue or stream.
cards.tool_gate: A config check that every consumed queue has a dead-letter target (for SQS in Terraform, a `redrive_policy` with `maxReceiveCount`), and an alarm on dead-letter queue depth.
cards.note: dead-letter queue and replay backed by AWS (alarm on any message, re-process after the fix), Netflix (failed events spill into dead-letter queues, an offline job replays them), Notion (re-enqueue from the dead-letter queue is a first-class workflow) and Uber (dead-letter messages are published back into the first retry topic); the retry cap (AWS) and the depth alarm (AWS) sit in Why; Microsoft, Google and AWS back the ordered-queue clause
cards.rule: Give every consumer queue a dead-letter queue and keep a way to replay it after the fix. On an ordered queue, key the group or session to the unit that must stay ordered, so a poison message holds only its own unit.
cards.why: A poison message otherwise loops forever, uses the consumers' capacity and hides the real backlog. On an ordered queue it also holds the messages behind it: in a FIFO queue no further messages from the same group are returned until the stuck message is deleted or becomes visible again, and an unacknowledged ordering key can delay the others. Give each independent stream its own group, session or queue, so one failure stays contained. Then cap the retries, so that a failing message moves to the dead-letter queue after a few attempts. Alarm on any message in the dead-letter queue, because each one is a bug to fix. Replay has a cost on these queues: a message put back after a dead-letter loses its place in the order, so replay only where order no longer matters, or reorder downstream.
cards.counterpoint: "A dead-letter queue already stops the poison message." It stops it after the retry cap. Until then the redelivery holds its group, and in a FIFO queue that means every message behind it. Grouping and the dead-letter queue do different jobs, so keep both. Choose the group key from the unit that must stay ordered. A single group restores the head-of-line block you were trying to remove, so use one only when the whole queue must stay in strict order. On a standard queue with no ordering, there is no group to key and the second sentence of the Rule does not apply.

cards.applies_when: An endpoint or job produces a file, archive or stream of many records.
cards.tool_gate: A test that exports as a second tenant and asserts the other tenant's rows are absent.
cards.rule: Scope an export to what the requesting principal may read.
cards.why: An export is a read that returns many rows at once. The per-object check on the detail page never runs, so a `SELECT *` with no tenant or access predicate hands the caller the table. Apply the same filter the list endpoint uses, including any role or ownership predicate and not only the tenant, and apply it inside the export query rather than on rows already fetched. OWASP's examples put the tenant scope in the query itself. Test it with two tenants. A restore asks the same question in reverse: a shared backup holds several tenants and old memberships, so restore one tenant into a separate resource and re-apply current access and retention before anyone can read it. A recovered environment also needs the production controls, not the ones it had when the backup was taken.
cards.counterpoint: "Some exports deliberately include everything." Some products ship an admin XML export that includes pages the exporter cannot view. That path is an administrative backup, so gate it on an admin permission and audit it. The user-facing exports in the same products contain only what the exporter can view, which is the rule here. Check which export path the change touches before calling a missing filter a bug.

fail.code: GET /export  ->  SELECT * FROM orders; streamed to any authenticated caller

cards.applies_when: The service reads configuration for authentication, an allow-list, a safety check, or a signing secret.
cards.tool_gate: A startup check that raises on a missing or placeholder secret (Django refuses an unset `SECRET_KEY`; Pydantic Settings fields without a default); a test that boots the service with an empty environment and expects a failed start or denied requests.
cards.note: A route that forgets a login check is a separate defect; this card covers a control that is switched off, empty, or backed by a placeholder until someone configures it. sys-secrets-and-errors covers errors that continue after a failed check
cards.rule: Ship every security control switched on, with an empty allow-list denying everything.
cards.why: A control that is off until configured is off in the deployment where nobody read the setup page. An empty allow-list that means "allow all" and a built-in `changeme` key both boot cleanly, so nothing alerts anyone while the service runs open or signs tokens anyone can forge. Refuse to start when a secret is missing or still a placeholder: failing at startup moves the discovery from an incident to the first deploy.
cards.counterpoint: "Developers need to run it locally without setup." Give them a separate dev entry point or a dev-only flag that is named for what it does (`INSECURE_DEV_MODE=1`) and that production images never set. The default stays closed, and the open mode is a visible, greppable choice.

cards.applies_when: The service builds an absolute URL from the request, or reads `Host` or `X-Forwarded-*` to decide what to serve or where to send a user.
cards.tool_gate: Framework host allowlist configured (`ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `AllowedHosts`, `config.hosts`, `trustHosts`), and a test that sends a hostile `Host` and expects 400.
cards.note: fn-redirect-target-allowlist checks where a redirect points; this card checks how a URL is built and which Host values the service answers. configured base URL - PortSwigger, Fastly and Rails; allowlist - PortSwigger, Fastly, Django, Microsoft, Rails and Laravel; trusted proxy - Django, Microsoft, PortSwigger and Fastly; duplicate Host has IETF and Fastly only, so it is in Why; a `*` allowlist entry has Django and Microsoft only, so it is in Why
cards.rule: Build absolute URLs from configured values, answer only for a `Host` on an allowlist, and take `X-Forwarded-*` values only from a trusted proxy.
cards.why: A reset link built from the request `Host` carries whatever domain the attacker sent. The victim asks for a reset, the mail arrives with the attacker's host, and the token goes to the attacker when the link is opened. The same value drives routing, cache keys, and absolute redirects. A forwarded header is worse, because many stacks accept `X-Forwarded-Host` from any client and use it in place of `Host`. Two `Host` headers are a second route to the same disagreement: one component validates the first and another reads the last, so reject a request that carries more than one. A `*` entry in the allowlist admits every host, so it is no allowlist at all.
cards.counterpoint: "A reverse proxy sets `Host`, so the value can be trusted." It can only be trusted when the proxy overwrites any client-supplied value and the app accepts requests only from the proxy's address. An app that is reachable directly, or a proxy that passes the client header through, hands the value back to the attacker.

# no allowlist, and X-Forwarded-Host is honoured from any client

cards.applies_when: A non-idempotent operation (charge, create, send) can be retried by a client, a queue, or a saga.
cards.rule: Make every retryable write idempotent: the caller sends a unique key, and a retry with the same key never applies the write twice.
cards.why: A timeout does not say whether the first attempt ran. Retrying without a key charges twice or sends two emails. A common way to answer the retry is to store the first result and return it again. Reject a key that comes back with a different payload, since it is a client bug, not a retry. Where an API has side effects and offers no key, do not retry it.
cards.counterpoint: "Our retries are rare." Queues redeliver and sagas retry by design, so rare is not never. The cost is a unique key and a stored result. No standard fixes how long the server keeps a key. Pick a window and publish it.

POST /payments {amount: 10}          # retried on timeout
INSERT INTO payment(amount) VALUES (10)
