cards.applies_when: A handler takes a number, an id, a header or a body field from the caller and uses it in a query, a calculation or an encoder.
cards.tool_gate: Schema or model constraints on every field (minimum, maximum, enum, format); a test that posts a negative number, an unknown id and a non-ASCII header and expects a 4xx.
cards.note: The domain check and the reject are backed by OWASP, Google (gRPC INVALID_ARGUMENT, user code only) and Kubernetes (422). The 4xx class is backed by IETF, Microsoft, Stripe, Google and Kubernetes. A missing id answering 404 is backed by IETF, Google (NOT_FOUND) and Kubernetes. Stripe and Microsoft state the status for a bad request, not for a foreign key. Which 4xx and where the check lives are covered by other cards
cards.rule: Check each caller-supplied value against its allowed domain (range, allowed set, an id that must exist, an encoding the code can handle) at the boundary, and answer a failed check with a 4xx, never a 5xx.
cards.why: A negative quota, a limit of zero, an id with no row, or a header with a non-ASCII character is the caller's error. If it reaches the database or an `.encode("ascii")`, the user gets a 500: the caller retries, the error-rate alert fires, and a negative quota may be stored and later allow unlimited use. A schema constraint or an explicit lookup costs one line per field. [[svc-bound-client-controlled-sizes]] caps size and count; this card covers every other value.
cards.counterpoint: "The database has a CHECK and a foreign key, so the data is safe." It is, but the constraint violation surfaces as a 500 unless the code maps it. Keep the constraint as the last line and validate first, so the caller gets a message that names the field. Catching the database error and mapping it to a 4xx also meets this card when a pre-check would race.

cards.applies_when: The service exposes an endpoint or RPC that returns a collection.
cards.tool_gate: Contract test that calls the list with a huge page size and asserts the clamp or a 400.
cards.note: 5 orgs back pagination and 4 state a server-side maximum (Zalando's maximum was not seen); a clamp or a 400 are both accepted
cards.rule: Paginate every list endpoint, with a default page size and a server-side maximum.
cards.why: A list that returns everything grows with the data until one request exhausts memory or the timeout. Adding pagination later breaks clients, so start with it. Without a maximum, a caller can ask for a page as big as the table.
cards.counterpoint: "This list is always small." Say so with a bounded type or a documented limit, since data tends to outgrow its first estimate. Cursors cost more than offsets to build, but they stay stable while rows change.

cards.applies_when: A service writes plain-text (unstructured) log lines that include a value from a request, header, form or other external input.
cards.tool_gate: A formatter that escapes CR and LF in every record; a test that logs a value containing a newline and asserts a single line.
cards.note: OWASP (sanitise all event data for CR, LF and delimiters), MITRE CWE-117 (log message built from external input without neutralising special elements) and GitLab (external input not captured in logs without validation). The Python logging cookbook shows a newline-escaping formatter and is descriptive only. Structured logs ([[svc-logs-structured]]) escape newlines by construction
cards.rule: In plain-text logs, escape or strip CR, LF and delimiter characters in external input before logging it.
cards.why: A value that contains a newline lets the sender write a line of their own into the log, such as a fake "login succeeded" entry, and so hide or forge events. Anyone reading or parsing the log cannot tell the forged line from a real one.
cards.counterpoint: "We already log JSON." Then the encoder escapes the newline and this check passes by construction; the card only applies to plain-text formats. Escaping in the formatter for every record is better than at each call site, so a missed call cannot reopen the hole.

fail.code: logging.info(f"login failed for {username}")   # username = "bob\nINFO login succeeded for admin"

pass.code: logging.info("login failed for %r", username)   # %r escapes the newline: 'bob\nINFO login ...'

cards.applies_when: A service ships its logs to an aggregator or search tool and its logger supports key/value fields.
cards.tool_gate: Pylint logging-fstring-interpolation (W1203), .NET analyzer CA2254, or a logger wrapper that accepts only a constant message plus fields.
cards.note: Structured fields - Microsoft (prefer structured telemetry), Kubernetes (unstructured klog calls such as Infof are no longer recommended) and OWASP (do not use unstructured text log formats). No interpolation into the message - Kubernetes, Microsoft (avoid string interpolation in logging) and Python (log variable data as format arguments). The Go slog post describes the benefit and is descriptive only
cards.rule: Log an event as a constant message plus key/value fields; do not build the message by interpolating variable data into it.
cards.why: A formatted string can only be searched by text. Fields can be filtered, grouped and counted, and the message stays one searchable pattern however many orders fail. Interpolation also formats the string even when the level is off, and a value with a newline can forge a log line ([[svc-log-input-neutralised]]). Put the request id in the fields too.
cards.counterpoint: CLIs and small scripts print text for a person, and a service with no aggregator gains little from fields. The card covers services whose logs are searched by machine. Where the logger has no field support, a format string with arguments (`logger.error("order %s failed", order_id)`) still avoids eager formatting.

fail.code: log.Printf("order %s failed for %s: %v", orderID, userID, err)

pass.code: slog.Error("order failed", "order_id", orderID, "user_id", userID, "err", err)

cards.applies_when: The service offers multi-factor authentication, or lets a signed-in user change a password, email address, or authentication factor.
cards.note: the practical gate is an integration test: a session that passed password-only login gets a step-up challenge on every sensitive route, including factor change; svc-session-lifecycle covers timeouts, not the assurance behind the current session
cards.rule: Require a fresh authentication with an already-bound factor before sensitive actions and before adding, replacing or removing an MFA factor; an existing session alone is not enough.
cards.why: A session that passed a password check says nothing about who holds it now. Let that session enrol a new phone or replace an authenticator and an attacker with a stolen cookie keeps the account after the password is changed. The same gap covers password, email and admin-role changes. Step-up at the action asks for the factor only when it matters, and a short freshness window keeps the prompt rare. A session must not be treated as stronger than the authentication that created it. A user who lost the only factor needs a documented recovery path, such as single-use recovery codes or a temporary access pass. That path is part of the control, and it is judged as a separate recovery flow.
cards.counterpoint: "Prompting on every sensitive action annoys users, and a user who lost the only factor gets locked out." Use risk and a recent-auth window so the prompt appears only when the session is stale or the action is high risk, such as a new device or an untrusted network, and keep the recovery path described above; without it, step-up becomes a denial of service against the account's owner.

cards.applies_when: A multi-step flow, such as checkout or signup, asks for data in more than one step.
cards.tool_gate: none; a walk through the flow that lists each field asked twice.
cards.note: 3 orgs (W3C, GOV.UK, Baymard); Baymard sells research, so it is closer to a vendor. NN/g and Shneiderman back the Why (recognition over recall), not the practice
cards.rule: Do not ask for information the user already gave in the same flow. Fill it in, or let the user pick it.
cards.why: Typing the same address twice costs time and adds typos. People recognise what they gave more easily than they recall it, so show it and let them confirm it.
cards.counterpoint: "Retyping a new password confirms it." That is a fair exception. So is data that is no longer valid, and re-entry that is the point of the task, such as a memory test. Browser autofill does not count: the page itself must supply the value.

fail.code:
<!-- step 1 -->  <input name="ship_address">
<!-- step 2 -->  <input name="billing_address">   <!-- empty again -->

pass.code:
<!-- step 2 -->
<label><input type="checkbox" name="same" checked> Billing address is the same as shipping</label>
<input name="billing_address" value="12 Elm Road, Leeds" hidden>   <!-- hidden while the box is checked; shown, pre-filled, when it is unchecked -->

cards.applies_when: A service writes application or request logs.
cards.tool_gate: A redacting log filter or formatter; secret scanning over the log output of the test suite.
cards.note: OWASP (tokens, passwords, session ids, keys and connection strings are removed, masked, hashed or encrypted before logging), MITRE CWE-532 ("do not write secrets into the log files") and GitLab ("never log credentials under any circumstance"; log the credential's internal id). AWS Prescriptive Guidance repeats the OWASP list and is not counted
cards.rule: Do not log passwords, tokens, keys or session ids; log an internal id or a masked value instead.
cards.why: Logs are copied to more places and read by more people than the secret store, and they live longer. A credential in a log line stays valid for as long as the log does. Whole header maps, request bodies and config objects are the usual leak, because nobody wrote the secret into the call on purpose.
cards.counterpoint: "Debugging needs the full request." Add a redaction layer that masks known secret fields before output, and keep verbose logs on a short retention ([[sys-pii-minimise-retention]]). Identifiers such as a credential's internal id stay loggable.

fail.code:
logger.info("request headers: %s", dict(request.headers))   # includes Authorization and Cookie
logger.debug("loaded config: %s", config)                   # includes db_password

pass.code:
logger.info("request received", extra={"request_id": rid, "client_id": client.id})
logger.debug("loaded config", extra={"keys": sorted(config)})

cards.applies_when: A client or server puts an API key, session token, bearer token, password, or personal data into a URL.
cards.note: ASVS 14.2.1; a log check that rejects query keys such as `token`, `key` or `password` in access logs is the nearest gate; sys-pii-minimise-retention and code-secret-scan cover other leak paths
cards.rule: Send tokens, keys, passwords, and personal data in a header or the request body, never in the path or query string.
cards.why: A URL is copied to places nobody reviews: proxy and access logs, browser history, the `Referer` header sent to third-party scripts and images, and links pasted into chat. A token there stays readable long after the request ends. The `Authorization` header and a POST body skip all of those copies.
cards.counterpoint: "Email links have to carry the token in the URL." Make that token single-use and short-lived, have the landing page swap it for a session at once, and send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on that page. A long-lived API key has no such excuse.

fail.code:
GET /api/orders?api_key=sk_live_abc123
GET /reset?email=ana@example.com&token=9f2c

pass.code:
GET /api/orders
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_abc123

POST /reset
Content-Type: application/json

{"token": "9f2c"}

cards.applies_when: The service acts as an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect client and exchanges an authorization code for tokens.
cards.note: RFC 9700 requires the authorization server to match redirect URIs exactly, which is why the client must send the registered value (RFC 6749 section 4.1.3); the loopback port exception is only for a native app's http://127.0.0.1 redirect; fn-redirect-target-allowlist covers ?next= redirects, not the registered redirect_uri, and svc-session-lifecycle covers the session issued after login
cards.rule: Finish the authorization-code flow with PKCE and a challenge method that keeps the verifier out of the authorization request (`S256`), send the exact registered `redirect_uri` (a native app on the loopback interface may vary the port), and reject the response unless this transaction's `state` or OIDC `nonce` matches and the ID token's signature, `iss`, `aud` and `exp` check out.
cards.why: A code that is not bound to the browser in front of you can be injected into another session, and an ID token minted for a different client or issuer can be replayed at your login. PKCE makes an intercepted code useless without the verifier, and `S256` is the method that does not reveal the verifier in the request. An exact redirect URI stops the code reaching an attacker's host, and an `https` one keeps it off the network in clear (plain `http` is for a native app's loopback only). `state` or `nonce` ties the response to the login the user started. If the request carried a `nonce`, the ID token must carry it back and the value must match. The ID-token checks reject a token that another app, another issuer or an expired clock made. Compare `iss` exactly with the issuer you expect, and require `aud` to contain your own client ID.
cards.counterpoint: "The OAuth client library already handles this." It handles the protocol, not your configuration. Some libraries decode the ID token unless you pass the issuer, audience and nonce, and the state or nonce store belongs to your session code. Test with a token minted for another client and a response with no state. The loopback exception is narrow: the port may differ, the host and path may not. The card is stricter than RFC 9700, which recommends PKCE for confidential clients and lets a confidential OIDC client use `nonce` instead; a reviewer may accept that alternative when the authorization server is known to bind the code another way.

fail.code:
code = request.args["code"]
token = exchange(code, redirect_uri=request.args["redirect_uri"])
session["user"] = jwt.decode(token["id_token"], options={"verify_signature": False})["sub"]
# no PKCE, no state check, no ID-token validation, and the redirect_uri is taken from the request

pass.code:
# the authorization request carried code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256
if not secrets.compare_digest(request.args["state"], session.pop("oauth_state")):
    raise PermissionDenied
token = exchange(request.args["code"], redirect_uri=REDIRECT_URI,   # constant from config
                 code_verifier=session.pop("code_verifier"))
claims = verify_jwt(token["id_token"], jwks, iss=ISSUER, aud=CLIENT_ID,
                    nonce=session.pop("oauth_nonce"))

cards.applies_when: The service emails or texts a password-reset link or code.
cards.note: single-use - OWASP, Auth0, Django; short-lived - OWASP, Auth0, NIST; revoke sessions - MSRC, Auth0, Django, with OWASP leaving it optional. Storing only a hash of the token (OWASP and NIST for recovery codes) and revoking other outstanding reset links (OWASP, after suspected compromise) have too few sources, so they are in Why. The practical gate is a test that redeems a token twice, redeems an expired one, and then replays an old session cookie; the request endpoint's reply and rate limit belong to svc-auth-throttle-generic-errors
cards.rule: Make the reset token single-use and short-lived, and on success revoke every session.
cards.why: A reset link is a bearer password that arrives in a mailbox. If it works twice, a forwarded mail, a mail scanner or a backup keeps the access alive. If it lives for days, an attacker has days to use it. And a reset that leaves the old sessions open changes the password without evicting the intruder who already had a session. Two further habits cost little: store only a hash of the token, so a database read or a backup hands over no working links, and revoke the other outstanding reset links on success.
cards.counterpoint: "The token is random, so hashing it adds nothing." The mail, the link and every log between you and the user still carry the raw value; the hash protects the copy at rest, which is the copy an attacker reads. OWASP treats session invalidation as the user's choice in the normal flow and requires it after suspected compromise; this card asks for it every time because the reset may be the owner's answer to a stolen session. Pick the lifetime from a number the support flow can meet, not from the word "short", and send a notification after the reset so a change the owner did not make is visible.

fail.code:
token = f"{user.id}-{int(time.time())}"
user.reset_token = token             # predictable, stored in clear, usable again
send_email(link(token))

pass.code:
raw = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
db.store(sha256(raw), user=user, expires=now + 15 * MINUTE)
# the raw value exists only in the mail
consume_once(raw)
revoke_sessions(user)
revoke_other_resets(user)

cards.applies_when: A shared API or queue serves several tenants or callers.
cards.note: the per-tenant cap rests on AWS (quotas at a per-tenant or per-workload granularity), Google (a quota for each customer) and Microsoft (quota enforcement so a single tenant cannot overwhelm the system); GitHub, Shopify, AWS and Microsoft document the principal key and the window
cards.rule: Enforce a per-tenant quota on shared APIs and queues.
cards.why: Without a quota, one noisy tenant consumes shared capacity for everyone. Key the count to the identity that owns the quota, such as the tenant, account or API key, and state the window and when capacity returns. Also add a per-client rate limit over a time window, set below the tenant quota, so one client cannot spend it all at once. Also add a per-tenant concurrency cap, and return 429 for over-quota but 503 for the service's own lack of capacity, so clients do not retry quota errors as capacity problems.
cards.counterpoint: "One global rate limit is simpler." A global limit protects the service, but one tenant can use all of it, and then every other tenant gets errors. A per-tenant limit costs one key per tenant in the limiter. Some older services return 503 for quota errors, so the status code is a convention. What matters is that a client can tell a quota error from a capacity error. Shuffle sharding (per-tenant worker subsets) isolates tenants further, and this card does not require it.

fail.code:
every tenant shares one worker pool and one request budget
no per-tenant limit: one tenant's batch job starves the rest

pass.code:
limiter.check(tenant_id) -> 429 + Retry-After
per-tenant semaphore on workers

cards.applies_when: A page or app is served to browsers on screens of any size.
cards.tool_gate: axe `meta-viewport`; a rendered check at a 320 px viewport and at 200% text zoom.
cards.note: The 320 px width and no sideways scrolling are backed by W3C, WebAIM and Microsoft; WebAIM partly restates the WCAG wording but adds its own zoom test, and Microsoft states only a 320 px design floor. 200% text zoom is backed by W3C, A11y Project, Mozilla and Google. No blocked pinch-zoom is backed by Deque, A11y Project and Mozilla, and Google adds a fourth voice. The A11y Project checklist asks for zoom left on, text at 200%, and no horizontal scrolling
cards.rule: Make the page usable at 320 CSS pixels wide and at 200% text zoom, with no sideways scrolling, no clipped content, and no blocked pinch-zoom.
cards.why: Low-vision users enlarge the page instead of using a small screen. A fixed width or a clipped container hides content from exactly those users. `user-scalable=no` takes away their only tool. A 320 px width is the same test as 400% zoom on a 1280 px screen, so the layout must reflow at that size without losing content or functions. `width=device-width` in the viewport meta makes the layout follow the screen width.
cards.counterpoint: "Maps and data tables need two-way scrolling." They are exempt, but only the part that needs it. Wrap the table in its own scroll box, and keep the headings and controls around it reflowing.

fail.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, user-scalable=no, maximum-scale=1">

pass.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

cards.applies_when: The service parses HTTP requests itself, or receives them through a proxy, load balancer, or CDN.
cards.tool_gate: A test that sends one request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding and expects 400 or a closed connection.
cards.note: reject or remove one framing field - IETF, PortSwigger, Microsoft, Fastly, Envoy and Cloudflare; strict parsing - IETF, OpenJS (Node), PortSwigger, Envoy and Microsoft; the HTTP/1.1 downgrade rule has PortSwigger and Fastly only, so it is in Why
cards.rule: Reject a request that carries both `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length`, or remove one field at the first hop, and parse header framing strictly rather than with a leniency flag.
cards.why: Two hops can disagree about where a request ends. The front end reads one body length and the back end reads another, so the leftover bytes become the start of the next request on the same connection. That request skips the front end's checks: it can reach an admin route, poison a cache, or splice one user's response into another user's connection. The ambiguity comes from a second framing field, a malformed header name, or a parser that accepts what the specification rejects. A front end that downgrades HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 reopens the gap, so validate the rewritten request as well. After rejecting an ambiguous request, close the connection, because the leftover bytes still sit on it.
cards.counterpoint: "We speak HTTP/2 end to end, so there is nothing to smuggle." HTTP/2 has one framing mechanism, but many deployments still downgrade at the last hop, and compatibility flags keep the old leniency in parsers. Check both ends of every connection and the rewrite between them, not the version the client negotiated.

fail.code:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example
Content-Length: 15
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /admin

pass.code:
# front end
if both framing fields are present:
    return 400 and close the connection      # or drop Content-Length, forward, then close

# parser
insecureHTTPParser: false                    # Node
allow_chunked_length: false                  # Envoy
whitespace before a header colon: 400

cards.applies_when: The code retries a failed call, or wraps a client that retries.
cards.note: Transient errors are backed by Microsoft, Google SRE and AWS (a vendor), though AWS frames retries as the tool for transient failures rather than forbidding permanent ones. Capped attempts are backed by Microsoft, Google SRE, AWS and GitHub (a vendor). Jittered exponential backoff is backed by Google SRE, AWS and Stripe (a vendor). Google SRE gives a retry budget (about 10% of requests); the card leaves the number to the team
cards.rule: Retry only transient errors, with capped attempts and jittered exponential backoff.
cards.why: Immediate, unbounded, or synchronized retries turn a brief fault into a load spike on the struggling dependency. Retry at one layer only: three layers of three attempts is nine calls per user request. Keep one deadline for the whole call, across all attempts, not a fresh timeout per attempt. When a server sends `Retry-After`, wait that long. When the dependency keeps failing, stop retrying (a retry budget or a circuit breaker) instead of adding load. Make retried writes safe with [[svc-idempotency-key]].
cards.counterpoint: "Retries make us more reliable." Only for transient faults and only within a budget. Past that they hurt, so a non-transient error should fail at once. A retry budget (retries capped as a share of traffic) helps further. This card leaves its size to the team.

cards.applies_when: A business operation spans services, each with its own database, coordinated as a saga.
cards.rule: Make steps after the pivot idempotent and retryable, and make every compensation idempotent with a failure path.
cards.why: A crash or a lost reply makes any participant run the same step twice, so make the steps before the pivot idempotent too where you can. After the pivot there is no undo, only retry until done. A compensation can itself fail, and unhandled it leaves the system inconsistent with nobody told.
cards.counterpoint: "Use a distributed transaction." Often unavailable across services. A saga has no isolation, so also guard against reading half-done data (semantic locks, re-reading values before acting). [[svc-idempotency-key]] covers keys, and [[svc-dlq]] covers failed messages.

fail.code:
step 4 (after pivot): charge_card(order)     # retried -> double charge
compensate: release_stock(order)             # throws; exception swallowed

pass.code:
step 4: charge_card(order, idempotency_key=order.id)   # safe to retry
compensate: release_stock(order) retried; on exhaustion -> alert + manual queue

cards.applies_when: The service is a SAML 2.0 service provider and accepts a response or assertion at an assertion consumer service endpoint.
cards.note: fn-xml-no-external-entities covers the XML parser; this card covers what to check before a NameID becomes a session. For an IdP-initiated response, `InResponseTo` must be absent; keep the replay cache.
cards.rule: Verify the XML signature over the assertion you read, with the IdP's configured key rather than a key carried in the response, then require the assertion's `Audience` and its bearer `SubjectConfirmationData` `Recipient` to name this SP, the response `Destination` to be this endpoint, `InResponseTo` to match your request (absent for an IdP-initiated response), `NotOnOrAfter` to be current, and the assertion ID to be unseen. These are one step, verify the assertion, and each check is cited.
cards.why: A valid signature elsewhere in the document proves nothing about the `<NameID>` your code just read. That gap is the signature-wrapping attack, and it lets an attacker choose which identity your service trusts. A lookup such as `.//NameID` is how the signed element and the read element get separated. Pinning the key to the IdP stops the document choosing its own verification key. The audience and destination checks stop an assertion minted for another SP from being posted here. `InResponseTo` catches a response injected into a browser that never started the request, and the time window (check `NotBefore` as well as `NotOnOrAfter`) plus the used-ID set stop a captured assertion from being replayed.
cards.counterpoint: "The library validates the signature, so the assertion is trustworthy." The signature vouches for the bytes it covers, not for the element your handler reads. A strict mode that validates the response but leaves an unsigned assertion in the tree still passes a wrapped `NameID`. Require the assertion to be inside the signed content, take the key from IdP metadata, and record the ID of the assertion you accepted, not the ID of its wrapper.

fail.code:
doc = etree.fromstring(base64.b64decode(form["SAMLResponse"]))
name_id = doc.find(".//NameID").text
login(name_id)      # no signature check, no audience, no replay set

cards.applies_when: The service sets a session cookie or session ID after login.
cards.tool_gate: Header test on the login response; session fixation test in the end-to-end suite.
cards.rule: Issue a new session ID at login, and set `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite` on the session cookie.
cards.why: A session ID that survives login can be planted by an attacker beforehand (fixation). Declare the old ID invalid when you issue the new one. A cookie without `HttpOnly` is readable by any injected script, and one without `Secure` travels over plain HTTP. Prefer `SameSite=Strict`, and use `Lax` only when users must stay signed in on arrival from links on other sites. Also end the session on the server at logout and clear the cookie in the browser too, because clearing only the browser cookie leaves a stolen copy valid, and enforce idle and absolute timeouts on the server. Scope the cookie to one host. With `Domain` omitted it is returned only to the host that set it, while a `Domain` set to the registrable domain sends it to every subdomain. Omitting `Domain` does not stop planting: a sibling subdomain that serves user content can still set a parent-domain cookie with the same name for the parent to accept. The `__Host-` prefix is what stops that, because the browser refuses a `__Host-` cookie that carries `Domain` or a path other than `/`. Use it on the session cookie.
cards.counterpoint: "The framework already does this." Some do: Spring Security changes the session ID at login by default, and Rails gives you `reset_session`. Hand-written login code and custom session stores often skip it, and cookie flags depend on configuration. Check the login handler and the real `Set-Cookie` header, not the framework's reputation.

fail.code:
Set-Cookie: sid=abc123
login():  keep the pre-login session id

pass.code:
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<new random>; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/   # the __Host- name is optional hardening, not a Rule clause
login():  session.regenerate()

cards.applies_when: A page action, such as a save, an upload, a search, or a page load, can take more than about a second.
cards.tool_gate: none; throttle the network and run the action.
cards.note: Showing that a slow action is under way is backed by NN/g, Apple, Microsoft and Atlassian. Showing progress when it runs long is backed by NN/g, Apple and Microsoft, and Microsoft gives the determinate and indeterminate split the PASS example uses. The 1 s and 10 s limits and the Cancel button come from NN/g, and Cancel also from Apple, so they are in Why. Norman's feedback principle is topic only, and Shneiderman's golden rules are a person's list, not an organisation
cards.rule: Show that a slow action is under way, and show its progress when it runs long.
cards.why: With no feedback, users click again, reload, or leave, and a double click can run the action twice. A bar tells them whether to wait. A message that says what is happening is better than "Loading". As a guide, show feedback after about one second. Past about ten seconds, show how much is done and offer Cancel where stopping is safe.
cards.counterpoint: "A spinner on a 200 ms call flickers." Right: below about a second, show nothing, or the placeholder just flashes. Skeleton screens suit page loads, and progress bars suit uploads and other long jobs.

fail.code: <button onClick={upload}>Upload</button>   // 40 s, nothing changes

pass.code:
{busy && } {busy && }
{message}
// "Uploading report.pdf", then "Upload complete" // aria-disabled keeps keyboard focus on the button; disabled would drop it

cards.applies_when: A table or model marks a row as deleted instead of removing it.
cards.tool_gate: A test per read path: soft-delete a row, then assert the endpoint returns 404 or leaves it out of the list.
cards.rule: Filter soft-deleted rows out of every read path by default, and make a read that includes them an explicit call.
cards.why: A soft delete sets a column. It does not remove the row, so any query that forgets the filter still returns the record. One raw query or one new endpoint is enough to expose it. Put the filter in the model's default scope, so new queries inherit it, and keep the escape hatch visible. A deletion policy has to reach caches, exports, replicas and object versions too, or the record lives on in a copy.
cards.counterpoint: "The admin console has to see deleted rows." Keep that one call explicit, name it for what it does, and check the caller is an admin. The default stays closed. Raw SQL and reporting replicas are the usual bypass, so route them through the same helper or audit them. A service that hard-deletes does not need the filter, but backups and object versions can still hold the old copy.

fail.code:
modelBuilder.Entity<Document>();                 // no HasQueryFilter
var doc = await context.Documents.FindAsync(42); // returns the soft-deleted row

cards.applies_when: The code builds a SQL query that includes request data or other untrusted input.
cards.tool_gate: Bandit B608 (`hardcoded_sql_expressions`), CodeQL `py/sql-injection`.
cards.rule: Pass untrusted data to queries as bound parameters, never by string concatenation or formatting.
cards.why: Concatenated input becomes SQL, so a value of `1 OR 1=1` reads every row and a quote ends the string early. A bound parameter travels apart from the query text, and the database never parses it as SQL.
cards.counterpoint: "An ORM makes this moot." Raw fragments still bypass it, and so do table, column and `ORDER BY` names, which cannot be bound. Map those to a fixed allowlist in code.

fail.code:
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + req.id)
db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")

pass.code:
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (req.id,))     # the placeholder style depends on the driver
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))

cards.applies_when: A handler reads, transforms, or returns a result whose size depends on the data (files, query results, response bodies).
cards.tool_gate: Memory limit in tests with a large fixture.
cards.note: Node-specific source, general claim; the unbounded-background-tasks half of the gap has no source and is covered by sys-load-shedding-bounded-queues
cards.rule: Process large results as a stream with backpressure; do not load them whole into memory.
cards.why: A fast source piles data into memory faster than a slow consumer drains it. In the Node docs' test, memory grew from about 88 MB to about 1.5 GB. Memory then scales with data size, not with the code.
cards.counterpoint: "Streaming complicates errors and retries." Yes: a failure mid-stream cannot change the status code. For small, bounded results, loading the whole result is simpler and fine; state the bound. [[sys-load-shedding-bounded-queues]] covers queue limits.

fail.code:
rows = db.execute("SELECT * FROM events").fetchall()   # 50M rows
return json.dumps(rows)

cards.applies_when: A shared log, metric or audit store holds records from more than one tenant.
cards.tool_gate: A test that writes an event for each of two tenants, then queries one tenant and asserts the other is absent.
cards.note: tenant id on tenant-scoped records backed by OWASP (server-verified tenant context in security and audit events), AWS SaaS Lens (inject tenant context into log messages and metric events) and Microsoft (a telemetry initializer injects the tenant ID into every telemetry item; the noisy-neighbor page asks for the tenant identifier in telemetry); Google GKE routes logs to a store per tenant, which is the alternative in the Counterpoint
cards.rule: Put the verified tenant id on every tenant-scoped log, metric and audit record.
cards.why: A shared store returns another tenant's activity to any query that does not filter. The id has to be written from the verified tenant context, not from a request header, and it has to be there when a batch job or a queue worker writes the record, since no request middleware runs in those paths. A centralized audit store is acceptable only when read access enforces tenant scope. Write it in one shared helper that reads the tenant from the verified token, so a service cannot leave it out or set it by hand. Metric events need the field too, or a per-tenant dashboard shows another tenant's numbers. Platform events that belong to no tenant, such as a node restart, carry no tenant id and are outside the Rule.
cards.counterpoint: "The pipeline adds the tenant from the request context." That works only for code that runs inside a request. Workers, schedulers and sidecars write records too, and a query cannot recover a field that was never written. If a shared layer injects the field, verify it with a two-tenant query, because a layer that silently skips one producer looks the same as a correct one until the query runs. Splitting logs into a store per tenant is stronger still where the operational cost is justified.

fail.code:
log.info("order %s paid", order_id)
audit.write(action="order.paid", actor=user.id)

pass.code:
log.info("order %s paid", order_id, extra={"tenant_id": tenant.id})
audit.write(action="order.paid", tenant_id=tenant.id, actor=user.id)

cards.applies_when: Several tenants share one table or database and the service reads tenant data.
cards.tool_gate: A test that reads as a second tenant and asserts the first tenant's rows are absent; Postgres FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.
cards.note: Microsoft backs the query filter, OWASP and AWS back row-level security. OWASP also asks for an authorization check at a boundary every access path crosses and treats ORM filtering as defence in depth; this card does not replace that check
cards.rule: Enforce tenant scope in the data layer by default, with a query filter or row-level security, not by a predicate at each call site.
cards.why: A tenant predicate written per query is one forgotten `WHERE` away from showing one customer another's rows. Put the scope where every query inherits it, and make the unscoped read an explicit, visible call. Set the tenant from the verified identity, not from a request field. In Postgres, `FORCE` row-level security so the table owner is filtered too.
cards.counterpoint: "A hidden filter surprises people and costs performance." The surprise is the point: a missing filter fails safe. Index the tenant column, and keep the escape hatch (`IgnoreQueryFilters()`, or a separate admin role) rare, named, and audited.

fail.code:
// Each caller must remember the tenant predicate.
var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync();   // returns every tenant's orders

pass.code:
modelBuilder.Entity<Order>()
    .HasQueryFilter(o => o.TenantId == _tenantId);   // _tenantId comes from the verified identity

var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync();          // scoped by default

cards.applies_when: The code calls a remote service over a network.
cards.note: Rule backed by AWS, Google (gRPC), and Microsoft (ASP.NET Core gRPC); deriving the timeout from the caller's deadline has 2 orgs (Google, Microsoft) and sits in Why; no source prescribes timeout numbers
cards.rule: Set an explicit timeout on every remote call.
cards.why: A call without a bound holds a thread, a connection, and a caller indefinitely, so one slow dependency becomes an outage. Many clients, gRPC and `requests` among them, set no timeout by default. Where the caller has a deadline of its own, pass the remaining time down: a per-hop timeout that ignores it keeps working for a client that already gave up, and a retry loop shares that one deadline across its attempts.
cards.counterpoint: "Defaults are fine; the library will time out eventually." Many defaults are infinite, and an eventual timeout longer than the caller's own deadline is wasted work. Configure the client's timeout once at construction, connect and read separately, then shrink it per call to what the caller has left. Pick the numbers from measured latency, such as the downstream p99.9, not folklore.

fail.code:
resp = requests.get(url)                   # no timeout: can wait forever
reply = stub.GetUser(request)              # gRPC sets no deadline by default

cards.applies_when: The service exposes an HTTP-based API.
cards.tool_gate: A scan in CI that the public API host refuses plain HTTP on port 80.
cards.rule: Serve every HTTP-based API over TLS, with no plaintext listener or fallback.
cards.why: A plaintext listener or an `http://` call lets anyone on the path read tokens and payloads, or rewrite them. A redirect from port 80 does not fix it: the first request already went out in the clear. Turn plain HTTP off for APIs instead of redirecting it, and have clients call `https://` URLs only. This card is about whether traffic is encrypted at all. Protocol versions and certificate checks are covered by [[svc-tls-modern-only]] and [[fn-tls-verify-on]].
cards.counterpoint: "Traffic between our own services never leaves the private network." A flat network means one compromised host can read all of it. Terminating TLS in a mesh or sidecar makes internal encryption cheap, so the exception costs more than it saves.

cards.applies_when: The service or its load balancer terminates TLS.
cards.tool_gate: testssl.sh or a similar scan against the public endpoint in CI; the load balancer's named security policy checked in config review.
cards.note: ASVS 12.1.1 and 12.1.2; IETF, OWASP and Microsoft back the Rule; NIST SP 800-52r2 still lets public-facing servers keep TLS 1.0 and 1.1 when necessary, so it is not counted; Microsoft advises deferring to the OS default over hardcoding a version; fn-tls-verify-on covers the client side
cards.rule: Accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 on servers.
cards.why: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 lack modern cipher suites and are deprecated by RFC 8996, and SSL 3.0 is broken outright. A server that still offers them lets an attacker on the path force a downgrade, and it fails compliance scans. Library defaults have moved to TLS 1.2, but an explicit lower setting, an old base image, or a load-balancer policy from years ago keeps the old versions alive. With TLS 1.2, prefer AEAD suites with forward secrecy. Clients and libraries that still offer TLS 1.0 or 1.1 should be updated too, so the old versions leave your own dependencies as well.
cards.counterpoint: "Some of our users have old clients." Measure first: log the negotiated version, and if old clients are a real share, serve them from a separate endpoint with an end date instead of weakening every endpoint.

fail.code:
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1

pass.code:
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2

cards.applies_when: The service issues refresh tokens, or self-contained access tokens such as JWTs, that outlive one request.
cards.note: refresh revoked at logout - Cognito, ASVS 7.4.1, Entra single sign-out (public clients only); at disable - Cognito, ASVS 7.4.2, Entra CAE; access-token window named or closed - Cognito, RFC 7009, ASVS 7.4.1, Entra CAE. Revoking on a credential change has one firm source (Entra; ASVS only offers it), so it is in Why and svc-password-reset owns the reset case. The practical gate is a test that logs out and disables an account, then replays the old refresh token and the old access token
cards.rule: Revoke the session's refresh token on the server at logout and every refresh token of the user when the account is disabled, and make access tokens expire quickly or check them against a revocation record.
cards.why: A refresh token is a long-lived credential. If logout only deletes it from the browser, a stolen copy keeps minting access tokens, and a disabled account whose refresh token still works keeps its access. The same holds after a password change, which [[svc-password-reset]] covers for a reset. A self-contained access token is valid until its `exp` unless the resource server checks something else, so revoking the refresh token alone leaves a window as long as the access lifetime. A revocation endpoint should revoke the refresh token and, where it can, the access tokens issued from it. Close the window with a lifetime of minutes, or with a denylist by `jti`, a per-user "not before" cutoff, or a per-user signing key.
cards.counterpoint: "Stateless tokens exist to avoid a lookup." Refresh already hits the store, so revoking there is free; only the access-token window needs a decision. A short lifetime accepts that window; a per-user cutoff costs one cached read per request. Name which one you chose, and do not claim revocation is immediate if it is not.

fail.code:
POST /logout        -> delete the cookie, 204
disable account     -> user.active = false; refresh tokens untouched
access token exp = 24h; resource server checks signature and exp only

pass.code:
POST /logout        -> mark this session's refresh token revoked in the store, and where the server supports it, the access tokens issued from it
disable account     -> revoke every refresh token of the user; set user.tokens_valid_after = now
access token exp = 5-15 min; resource server rejects iat < user.tokens_valid_after

cards.applies_when: The code replaces its own binary or an installed program with a new version.
cards.tool_gate: Test that makes the final step fail and checks the old version still runs.
cards.note: Backed by Microsoft (Windows Installer automatic rollback), Google (Android A/B updates keep the old slot as a fallback) and Mender (the bootloader rolls back to the previous version); go-update documents the rename-and-restore steps for a single binary and is a reference
cards.rule: When an update fails, restore the previous version instead of leaving a missing or half-written one.
cards.why: Deleting the old binary before the new one is in place leaves nothing to run if the copy fails, and the tool cannot update itself back. On Windows a running executable cannot be deleted but can be renamed, so move it aside first and restore it on failure. Keep the old version until the new one has started and passed a self-check, since a binary that installs but will not start needs the old one back.
cards.counterpoint: "Keeping a second copy costs disk space and clutter." One binary-sized file, removed once the new version has started, is cheap next to a tool that cannot start.

cards.applies_when: The code downloads and installs or runs a new version of itself or of another program, such as a self-updater or an install script.
cards.note: Backed by Sparkle (signed archive, keys kept off the web server), Sigstore (signing covers a compromised hosting site), TUF (SSL alone leaves one key to steal) and Debian (checksums are only trusted once the Release file is signed); GitHub and Google (Go checksum database) show the same practice; go-update is a reference
cards.rule: Verify a downloaded update against a signature, an attestation or a pinned key, or against a checksum that reached you by another route than the file; a checksum fetched from the same host as the file does not count.
cards.why: An attacker who controls the download host replaces the archive and its checksum file together, so the check passes and the new binary runs with the user's rights. A signature made with a key that is not on that host, or a hash from a different channel, still fails for the attacker.
cards.counterpoint: "HTTPS already protects the download, and signing needs key management." TLS protects the connection to the host, not the files on it once the host or its account is breached. Keyless signing and build attestations remove most of the key handling.

cards.applies_when: The service accepts file uploads.
cards.tool_gate: Upload tests with a renamed `.php`, an oversized file and a zip bomb.
cards.rule: Allowlist the file type, cap the size, and store each upload under a generated name where the server will not execute it.
cards.why: The client-supplied name and Content-Type are attacker text. A user-chosen name allows path tricks, and an upload served from the web root with its original extension can run as code. Count the decompressed size of archives. Storing outside the web root and serving files through a handler, or from a separate domain, keeps a file that slips past the type check from running. [[fn-confine-file-path]] covers the path check.
cards.counterpoint: "The extension check is enough." The extension is attacker text, and double extensions or parser quirks get past a check on it. The generated name and a storage place that never executes files are what make a file that slips through harmless.

fail.code:
path = f"/var/www/uploads/{file.filename}"
file.save(path)                       # any type, any size, public URL

pass.code:
if sniff_type(file.stream) not in {"image/png", "image/jpeg"} or size > 5_000_000: abort(400)   # type from the content, not the name
file.save(STORE / f"{uuid4()}.bin")   # outside web root; served by /files/<id>

cards.applies_when: The code accepts signed webhooks or signed messages from another system.
cards.tool_gate: A test that replays a captured request with the timestamp moved outside the tolerance and asserts a 4xx, and one that changes only the timestamp header and asserts a 4xx.
cards.note: tolerance on a signed creation time backed by Svix, Slack and Stripe (all three put the timestamp inside the signed content); IETF RFC 9421 permits the check and is a reference only
cards.rule: Reject an inbound signed message whose creation time is outside a short tolerance, and sign that time with the body so it cannot be swapped.
cards.why: A valid signature proves who sent the message, not when. A captured request keeps its signature and can be sent again. Put the timestamp inside the signed content, as Slack, Svix and Stripe do. A timestamp in a separate header that the signature does not cover can be replaced by the attacker. Compare the timestamp with local time before doing any work. Compute the signature over the raw, unmodified body, and compare it in constant time. Retries are normal, so also store the message id and skip an id already processed. Deduplication stops a replay inside the window. The window stops one outside it and bounds how long the id store must keep entries.
cards.counterpoint: "A tight window drops delayed deliveries and retries." It does. RFC 9421 lets an application enforce a maximum signature age and leaves the number to it, and five minutes is the default of Slack and Stripe, not a standard. Pick a tolerance from the provider's retry schedule and your clock skew, log every reject with the offset, and keep deduplication by event id so a replay inside the window still does nothing. A signature with no timestamp at all cannot be bounded this way. The receiving endpoint has to rely on deduplication and on the sender's short-lived credential.

cards.applies_when: An LLM agent can call tools, run code, or act on external systems.
cards.tool_gate: Tool registry reviewed in code; downstream credentials scoped in IAM and tested as the agent identity.
cards.note: The narrow tool set is backed by OWASP, NCSC and Microsoft. This Microsoft page is not the MSRC prompt-injection post already cited and states least privilege and least action for the tools, data and operations an agent may use
cards.rule: Give the agent only the narrow tools and the minimal credentials its task needs.
cards.why: Hallucination or an injected instruction can drive any tool the model holds. An open-ended shell or URL fetch hands over everything the service account can do. Where you can, run each tool as the requesting user rather than a shared admin identity, and let the downstream system check that user's rights on every call. A session that reads content from an untrusted party gets no privileged tools. [[sys-prompt-injection]] covers validating model output and human approval; this card covers how much the agent can reach in the first place.
cards.counterpoint: "Narrow tools make the agent less useful." Add tools when a task needs them and remove those that no task uses. A tool the model never calls is risk without benefit.

fail.code: tools = [shell(), http_fetch(any_url), db(admin_role)]       # one shared service identity

pass.code:
tools = [read_ticket(id), add_comment(id, text)]             # narrow functions
creds = user_scoped_token(user, scopes=["tickets:rw"])       # downstream checks the user

cards.applies_when: The system keeps backups of its own data, such as database dumps, snapshots or object-store copies.
cards.tool_gate: A scheduled restore job that exits non-zero when the restored data fails its checks; an alert when the job has not run for longer than its schedule.
cards.note: The three clauses (a restore on a schedule, a check on the restored data, an owner) share the evidence. AWS, Google, CISA and Microsoft state the regular restore test. AWS, Google and CISA add the integrity check. GitLab is a team's own postmortem, with the automated restore test in its fix list. Keeping a copy offline is stated by CISA and Microsoft only, so it is left out of the Rule
cards.rule: Restore every backup set on a schedule, check the restored data, and alert when the restore fails or stops running.
cards.why: A backup that has never been restored is a guess. The dump can be empty, the credentials expired, the schema changed, or the job can have failed quietly for months, and the first restore then happens during an outage. Run the restore from a job, not from a person's memory, and give the job an owner who gets the alert. A sampled restore is enough: one table, one volume, one day. Data you can rebuild from another source, and state held only in a managed service that has no backup duty, are out of scope.
cards.counterpoint: "Restore tests cost money and need a spare environment." Restore a sample into a scratch instance that lives for the length of the job. The bill is small next to finding out during an incident that the backup is unusable. Managed backup services can schedule the restore and run the checks for you, which also meets the Rule.

fail.code:
# crontab on the db host: the only backup job
0 2 * * *  pg_dump -Fc orders | aws s3 cp - s3://acme-backups/orders/$(date +\%F).dump
# nothing ever reads the dump back

pass.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# restore-check.sh: weekly job with an owner and an alert on non-zero exit
set -euo pipefail
aws s3 cp "s3://acme-backups/orders/$(date +%F).dump" /tmp/orders.dump
createdb restore_check
pg_restore --no-owner -d restore_check /tmp/orders.dump
psql -d restore_check -tAc "select count(*) from orders" | awk '$1 < 1000 { exit 1 }'
dropdb restore_check

cards.applies_when: The code adds an in-process or shared cache.
cards.note: Expiry is backed by AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud and Cloudflare. Google Cloud and Cloudflare are vendors and state their own product knobs, and Google Cloud partly restates Redis's maxmemory and TTL pair. Size is not claimed here: Redis is the only clean organisation, the Caffeine wiki is one maintainer, and Microsoft's page only gives the consequence of an unbounded cache. Invalidation has one org (IETF, HTTP only) and value versioning none, so both sit in Why
cards.rule: Bound every cache by size and give its entries an expiry.
cards.why: An unbounded cache is a memory leak that shows up only under production traffic. Redis has no memory limit by default on 64-bit builds. Choose the TTL from the staleness you can tolerate, because an arbitrary one either serves stale data or does not help. Also version the values, since old and new code read each other's entries during a rolling deploy, and give the cache hit, miss, and origin-request metrics and a way to invalidate. Invalidate on write: when a PUT, POST, or DELETE succeeds, drop the cached entry for that URI.
cards.counterpoint: "Stale data is a business risk, not a review issue." It is one when the staleness window was never chosen. The rule asks for a decision, not a number. A soft TTL (refresh in the background) under a hard TTL (must refetch) balances freshness against load.

fail.code:
CACHE = {}                         # grows forever, never expires
redis.conf: maxmemory 0            # unlimited, used as a cache

pass.code:
cache = cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=10_000, ttl=60)
redis.conf: maxmemory 2gb, maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

cards.applies_when: Many tenants, regions, or product surfaces share one cluster, control plane, or data store.
cards.note: Netflix (each Titus region is divided into independent cells that bound any one control plane), Slack (moved critical user-facing services to cells to limit the blast radius of site failures), Airbnb (moved its metrics store to multiple clusters to set up separate failure domains), Cloudflare (control-plane postmortem: test the blast radius of failures and minimise the services one failure hits); per-tenant caps are left to svc-rate-limit-quota
cards.rule: Split shared infrastructure into independent cells, each with its own control plane and storage, and route each tenant or request to one cell, so one failure stops only that cell.
cards.why: With one global cluster, every failure is global. A bad config push, an overloaded control plane, or a corrupt index stops every customer at once. Netflix divides each region into independent cells, which also caps how large any one control plane can grow. Slack moved its critical user-facing services to cells to limit the blast radius of site failures. Airbnb moved its metrics store to several clusters to get separate failure domains.
cards.counterpoint: "Cells cost more and add a routing layer." They do, with spare capacity in every cell, and a small service with one team may not earn them. Ask what one failure takes down. If one cluster outage or one bad deploy stops every customer, and that matters at your scale, mark `FAIL`. Cloudflare's postmortem asks for exactly that test of the blast radius. A per-tenant quota inside one cluster stops a noisy tenant but not a failed control plane. See [[svc-rate-limit-quota]]. Cells help only if a change reaches them one at a time. See [[prod-canary-staged-rollout]].

fail.code:
# one cluster and one control plane serve every tenant
clusters:
  - name: metrics-prod
    tenants: all

pass.code:
# each cell has its own control plane and storage; no cross-cell call on the request path
clusters:
  - name: metrics-cell-1
    tenants: [payments, search]
  - name: metrics-cell-2
    tenants: [checkout, ads]

cards.applies_when: Several screens or apps show the same action, status, or concept to the same users.
cards.tool_gate: none; list the labels and icons for one action across all screens.
cards.note: One icon is backed by W3C, GSA (USWDS) and Atlassian; Atlassian asks for existing icons to keep meanings consistent, which is softer than one icon per action. One label is backed by W3C, NN/g and GOV.UK. This card is about words and controls a user sees. It does not cover names in code or API field names.
cards.rule: Use one label and one icon for the same action and the same concept across all screens.
cards.why: When "Remove", "Delete", and "Discard" all mean the same thing, users stop trusting any of them and ask whether each one differs. Give the same control the same accessible name on each screen, so a screen reader says "Search" every time, not "Search" on one and "Find" on another. Keep the control in the same place on each screen, too. A familiar control costs no thought. A different one costs a pause, and in a destructive flow, a mistake.
cards.counterpoint: "Each team knows its users best." Consistent does not mean uniform. Differ where the job differs, and keep the wording and look of the shared actions the same. Drive the shared parts from the design-system component, so they cannot drift.

fail.code:
Orders page:    [Delete]       (trash icon, right of row)
Customers page: [Remove]       (x icon, left of row)
Invoices page:  [Discard draft](no icon, menu)

pass.code:
Orders, Customers, Invoices: [Delete] with the trash icon, last action in the row menu.
A different outcome, such as archive, gets a different label: [Archive].

cards.applies_when: A request fans out to several backends, shards, or replicas and combines the answers.
cards.note: Elastic states a per-shard deadline and Envoy a per-try deadline; AWS states a timeout on any remote call, which is the leg rule applied to a dependency but is not written about fan-out, so it only partly states the clause. A cap on fan-out width has one org (Google) and is left out of the Rule
cards.rule: Give every leg of a fan-out its own deadline, and decide in code what happens when a leg misses it: a partial result, a hedged request, or an error.
cards.why: Fan-out turns rare slowness into common slowness. If each of 100 backends is slow on 1 request in 100, about 63% of requests wait on at least one slow backend. Without a per-leg deadline the slowest leg sets the latency of every request.
cards.counterpoint: "Hedging doubles the load." Sent at once to every replica, it does. Send the hedge only after a wait past about the 95th percentile, cap the attempts, and cancel the twin, and the extra load stays near 5%. Hedge only idempotent reads. A partial result needs a product decision. The deadline does not.

fail.code: results = await gather(*[shard.search(q) for shard in shards])   # waits for the slowest shard

pass.code:
results = await asyncio.gather(
    *[asyncio.wait_for(shard.search(q), 0.08) for shard in shards],
    return_exceptions=True)
hits = [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
return merge(hits, partial=len(hits) < len(shards))

cards.applies_when: A service exposes a health endpoint used by a load balancer, an orchestrator, or auto-replacement.
cards.rule: Wire load balancers and restarters to liveness and local checks only, never to shared-dependency checks.
cards.why: Dependency status belongs in alarms. If the database blips, every host fails its check, all are removed at once, and a partial outage becomes total. Even a local check can misfire, so the automation should stop sending traffic to one bad host but keep sending it when most of the fleet fails the check.
cards.counterpoint: Readiness that reflects a dependency feels more honest. AWS accepts fail-open designs but is wary of behavior it cannot fully test, so a fail-open health policy counts as PASS only if you have actually tested it.

fail.code: GET /health -> SELECT 1 on primary db     # drives LB removal and restart

pass.code:
/live: process responds ; /ready: local init done, no shared-dependency call
dependency status -> metric + alarm only

cards.applies_when: A migration creates an index on an existing large or busy table.
cards.tool_gate: Migration linter.
cards.rule: Create indexes with `CONCURRENTLY`, outside a transaction block, and handle a failed build that leaves an INVALID index.
cards.why: A plain build blocks writes for its whole duration. A concurrent build fails inside a transaction. A concurrent build that fails leaves an invalid index that queries ignore but writes still pay for.
cards.counterpoint: "CONCURRENTLY is slower." It does two scans, waits for older transactions, and runs only one concurrent build per table at a time. That is the price of not blocking writes. For a unique index, others can see violations before a failed build is cleaned up.

fail.code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id);

cards.applies_when: Work is buffered in a queue, a channel, or a thread pool between components.
cards.tool_gate: Lint for unbounded queue constructors.
cards.note: Dropping requests that waited too long has AWS, Google SRE (CoDel and LIFO) and Uber (shedding stale work); Netflix says nothing about queue age
cards.rule: Bound every queue, reject excess work cheaply, and drop queued requests whose caller has already given up.
cards.why: An unbounded queue turns overload into minutes of latency, and by the time old items are served, callers have given up. Also keep a way to sideline old or excess messages (see PASS). When something must go, shed the lowest-priority work first.
cards.counterpoint: "Dropping work loses data." A bounded queue only makes the loss explicit and early. For work that must not be lost, spill to durable storage rather than memory. Shedding itself must be cheap. Slowing fast errors on purpose can stop a load balancer from steering more traffic at a shedding host.

fail.code:
q = Queue()                      # no maxsize
on overload: enqueue anyway; no age alarm, no spillover

pass.code:
q = Queue(maxsize=1000); if full: return 503 fast
alarm on age of oldest item; spillover queue for old deltas
drop a request that has waited past the caller's timeout

cards.applies_when: A TTL lock or lease guards a write to an external store.
cards.note: Apache Hadoop and Hazelcast state the rule; Hazelcast is a vendor and its page draws on Chubby and Kleppmann. Microsoft and AWS, both vendors, state the compare-and-set arm only. Google's Chubby paper (OSDI 2006, section 2.4) says the recipient server tests whether the sequencer is still valid. The AWS Builders Library leader-election page backs the Why only; it names the hazard and never says to check at the resource
cards.rule: Check a correctness lock on the resource side (fencing token or compare-and-set), never by lock possession alone.
cards.why: A holder can pause past its TTL, lose the lock and still write. Only the store can reject the stale writer. The holder takes the token when it gets the lock and sends it with every write.
cards.counterpoint: "Our lock library is safe, so holding the lock is enough." Whether a given algorithm such as Redlock is safe is disputed, but that a paused holder can still write is not. Locks used only for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work) may be loose. For correctness, state that it is a correctness lock and make the store reject stale writers, with a monotonically increasing token or a unique token checked by compare-and-set, whatever the lock implementation.

fail.code:
if redis.set(key, id, nx=True, px=10000):
    db.update(row)                 # pause here => two writers

pass.code:
token = lock.acquire()             # monotonically increasing
db.update(row, where fence < token, set fence = token)

cards.applies_when: A change drops, renames, or retypes a column, or mixes schema change with a data backfill.
cards.tool_gate: Migration linter for DROP/RENAME COLUMN.
cards.note: 3 orgs per clause. Batching rests on GitLab, Ecto, and CockroachDB (a database vendor). The separate migration rests on GitLab, Ecto, and Stripe, which shows it by structure and never says batches
cards.rule: Run data backfills in batches, in a migration separate from the schema change.
cards.why: A large backfill in one transaction holds locks for its whole run, and a failure halfway rolls all of it back. Batches with a pause between them keep each lock short and let the backfill resume. Page the batches by the last id processed, not with `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`, which slows down on later pages. [[chg-expand-contract]] covers the order of releases around it.
cards.counterpoint: "One `UPDATE` is simpler than a batched job." On a small table it is, and this card does not apply there. Once the update holds a lock long enough to block live traffic, batch it.

fail.code: release N: RENAME COLUMN a TO b ; UPDATE big_table SET b = ... (one tx)

pass.code: N: add b, dual-write, ignore a in code ; N+1: batched backfill ; N+2: drop a

cards.applies_when: A migration runs ALTER TABLE on a busy PostgreSQL table.
cards.tool_gate: Migration linter (e.g. flag ALTER without lock_timeout).
cards.note: lock-queue consequence is inference, not stated in the Postgres page read
cards.rule: Set `lock_timeout` for the migration session and retry on timeout.
cards.why: The default is 0, meaning wait forever, and most ALTER forms need the strongest lock. A migration stuck waiting can make later queries on that table wait behind it (inferred from how lock queues work).
cards.counterpoint: "Set it globally." The Postgres docs advise against setting it in postgresql.conf because it affects every session, so scope it to the migration. Also, with a non-zero `statement_timeout`, a larger `lock_timeout` has no effect.

fail.code: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;   -- no lock_timeout

pass.code:
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;   -- retry on timeout

cards.applies_when: Code loads related rows in a loop, or opens database connections per request.
cards.tool_gate: Query-count assertion in tests; ORM N+1 detector.
cards.note: N+1 half has 4 orgs (Django, Rails, SQLAlchemy, Microsoft); the bounded pool rests on 3 partial sources; the index clause has no source beyond topic level
cards.rule: Fetch related rows in one query or batch, never one query per row.
cards.why: A query per row multiplies latency by result size. Where the ORM offers it, make an unplanned lazy load raise in tests (strict loading, a prevent-lazy-loading switch, the `raise` loader); that catches the loop before it ships. Also back filter and join columns with an index and use a bounded connection pool: an unindexed filter turns each query into a scan, and a connection per request exhausts the database under load.
cards.counterpoint: "Measure first." Yes, for micro-optimizations, but a query inside a loop over unbounded input is a defect by shape.

fail.code:
for o in Order.objects.all():
    print(o.user.email)                              # one query per order

pass.code:
for o in Order.objects.select_related("user"):
    print(o.user.email)                              # one query with a join

cards.applies_when: The system stores, copies or logs personal or otherwise sensitive data.
cards.tool_gate: Retention jobs with a TTL on tables and buckets; a data inventory checked in CI.
cards.note: The retention period is backed by ICO and Microsoft; GDPR Art. 5 is the only other statement and it is law, not an organisation. Delete or anonymise is backed by ICO, OWASP and Microsoft. Microsoft is a vendor and its page covers Microsoft 365 content, not application tables or logs. The legal retention periods differ by jurisdiction; the source gives only the engineering principle
cards.rule: Give every store of personal or sensitive data a retention period, and delete or anonymise the data when it ends.
cards.why: Data you do not keep cannot leak. Keep only the fields the feature needs, too. Full card numbers, national IDs and raw request bodies pile up in logs, analytics tables and backups, and nobody owns their deletion. Tokenise or truncate when the full value is not needed, and encrypt what you keep. This is a technical check, not a legal opinion.
cards.counterpoint: "We might need it later." A guess is not a purpose. Keep it when a named feature or legal duty needs it, and write that reason next to the retention rule.

fail.code:
analytics.events: full email, DOB and phone, no TTL

cards.applies_when: An LLM reads untrusted text (user input, web pages, documents) and can call tools or produce output that code acts on.
cards.rule: Validate model output deterministically before code acts on it.
cards.why: Injected instructions in retrieved text can steer tool calls. No known prevention is fool-proof, and RAG or fine-tuning do not fully fix it, so the goal is to limit what a fooled model can make the code do. Treat retrieved text and tool output as untrusted input, and block known leak paths, such as rendering external URLs, in code rather than in the prompt. Also keep credentials in code, not in the model, and require human approval for high-risk actions.
cards.counterpoint: "Guardrail prompts block it." They reduce risk but are not a boundary. The permission model has to hold even when the model is fooled.

cards.applies_when: The code handles credentials, logs data, or returns errors to clients.
cards.tool_gate: Secret scanner in CI; log-redaction tests.
cards.note: Fail closed is backed by OWASP, MITRE (CWE-636 and CWE-209) and Microsoft, whose page states it only for certificate-validation errors. RFC 9457 backs the no-internals half. Secrets in source rest on 12factor and OWASP only, so they stay in the Why
cards.rule: Fail closed: a validation or auth error must deny, never continue, and an error response must not carry internals such as stack traces, SQL or tokens.
cards.why: A catch-and-continue around a validation step grants access when the check crashes. Stack traces and SQL in a response show an attacker how the system is built, and a token there can be reused. Keep secrets out of source and logs too: read them from the environment or a secrets manager.
cards.counterpoint: "A broad `except Exception` breaks the specific-exceptions rule." At a security boundary, fail-closed wins: catch broadly, log redacted, deny, and never use a bare `except:`. "We need detail to debug." Log it server-side with a correlation id.

cards.applies_when: Many tenants share a pool of workers or nodes, and one tenant's traffic or bug can take a worker down.
cards.note: AWS describes the technique, Airbnb and Grafana Labs (Mimir) each run it on a shared tenant pool. Airbnb's wording on the technique matches the Mimir page, so the two may not be fully independent
cards.rule: Assign each tenant a shuffled subset of shared workers, so one tenant's fault reaches only a few other tenants.
cards.why: If every tenant can use every worker, one bad tenant can exhaust all of them. With a random subset per tenant, two tenants rarely share all their workers, so one bad tenant leaves most others a healthy worker.
cards.counterpoint: "Separate cells isolate better." They do, and they cost whole copies of the stack. Shuffle sharding runs on one shared pool and still leaves most tenants unaffected. Use cells for hard boundaries and this for the shared pool inside one.

cards.applies_when: The server fetches a URL that a user or external data supplies.
cards.tool_gate: CodeQL `py/full-ssrf`; an egress proxy or firewall allowlist.
cards.rule: Fetch a user-supplied URL only when its host matches a server-side allowlist.
cards.why: The server can reach networks that the attacker cannot, such as internal services and the cloud metadata address, and an open fetch lets the attacker read them. A hostname allowlist alone does not stop DNS rebinding, so also check that the resolved address is not private and connect to that address. Validate and sanitise every user value that goes into the URL, not only the host. Turn off redirect following, or check each redirect target the same way.
cards.counterpoint: "Blocklisting private ranges is enough." Alternate IP forms, URL parser tricks and open redirects get past a blocklist. An allowlist fails closed when someone finds a new trick.

cards.applies_when: The change was written fully or partly by an AI agent.
cards.tool_gate: Compiler, type checker and dependency-resolution in CI catch non-existent imports and calls.
cards.rule: Verify that every import and external call the agent wrote exists with that signature.
cards.why: Agents invent plausible APIs and rewrite nearby utilities without searching. A study of 16 code models found that at least about 5% of the packages they suggested (about 22% for open-source models) did not exist, and an attacker can publish a malicious package under a name that models keep inventing. A green build proves only what the compiler sees. [[chg-reuse-before-write]] covers re-implemented helpers. The author must also be able to explain each hunk; see [[chg-agent-independent-review]].
cards.counterpoint: "Humans make the same mistakes." True, but agents make them fluently and at volume, and disclosure alone does not catch them. Kubernetes requires disclosure and an author who can explain the change. A compiler and a dependency check catch the mechanical part, so use this card for calls that resolve but behave differently than assumed.

cards.note: a person's sign-off on agent-written changes has Stripe and Dropbox (firm) and Uber (maintenance tasks only); Kubernetes covers AI-assisted PRs with a human author; Spotify auto-merges some agent PRs; nobody backs a fresh agent as the sign-off (Cloudflare's separate-session AI reviewers review engineer-written code)

cards.why: The same context repeats the same blind spots and assumptions. An approval without real reading is a rubber stamp. The person who submits the change must also be able to explain each hunk. A human author's own approval does not count either: most review tools can bar it.

cards.applies_when: The diff changes or deletes a migration file that is already on the main branch.
cards.tool_gate: Flyway `validate` or a Liquibase checksum check in CI; a CI step that fails when a file under the migrations directory that exists on main is modified or removed.
cards.note: Flyway scopes the rule to a permanent downstream environment, and Rails allows editing a migration that has not left your machine, so the scope here is merged or deployed. Liquibase's stored checksum is a mechanism, not a stated rule, and is not counted
cards.rule: Do not edit or delete a migration that has already run in a shared environment; add a new migration that makes the change.
cards.why: A database records which migrations it has applied. If you change one afterwards, environments that ran the old version never run the new one, so staging, production and each developer's copy drift apart with no error. Migration tools that store a checksum fail on the edited file instead. A new migration reaches every environment the same way. A migration that has run only on your own machine can still be edited.
cards.counterpoint: "The migration is broken, and fixing it in place is cheaper." That holds while only your machine has run it. Once any shared environment has, the fix goes in a new migration, because the old file has already done its work there and will not run again.

cards.applies_when: A review approval or verification result exists and the branch has been pushed or rebased since.
cards.tool_gate: Branch protection that dismisses stale approvals on new commits.
cards.note: GitLab and Prow drop approvals on any new commit by default; one vendor's engineering guidance (opinion), from poteto-mode/playbooks/shipping.md; patch-id comparison is the source's method; Anthropic (a vendor) adds "A PR approval is only good for one commit" with reapproval after an untrusted commit, but no patch-id carve-outs
cards.rule: Treat an approval or verification verdict as current only if the patch is unchanged: compare `git patch-id` at the verdict commit with the current head. If the patches differ only in tests, docs, or lint config, the verdict can stand when the built output is the same; any other difference needs a fresh check.
cards.why: A verdict covers one patch. After a push or rebase the reviewer approved code that no longer exists.

A rebase that keeps the patch id does not void the verdict, and neither does a change to tests, docs, or lint config that leaves the built output the same. Branch protection can enforce this without human effort. Many review tools drop approvals on any new commit by default, so the exemptions above are the tuned case, not the baseline.
