cards.applies_when: The change alters anything a caller can observe, documented or not.
cards.tool_gate: Contract tests and API-diff tooling.
cards.note: Google AIP-180, Microsoft and Kubernetes cover observable behaviour and defaults. Python PEP 387 names return values, side effects and raised exceptions; OpenJDK treats a changed thrown error as a compatibility issue. The consumer check has AWS (contract tests on every producer change), Pact (can-i-deploy against known consumers; a vendor) and Spring Cloud Contract (a vendor). The Python devguide states nothing on this and does not count. Ordering and timing have no support, and Microsoft allows performance changes
cards.rule: Treat any change that callers can observe in a signature, return values, error types, defaults, or side effects as breaking until a consumer check says otherwise.
cards.why: With enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on, so "undocumented" does not mean "safe to change". Result ordering and timing can break callers too, but no published guide treats them as breaking, so weigh them case by case.
cards.counterpoint: Treating everything as breaking freezes the code. Weigh each change by known consumers and blast radius, and use a staged rollout instead of a ban. Optional parameters with defaults are the safe way to add.

cards.applies_when: The project keeps a changelog, and the change adds, removes or changes a feature.
cards.note: Django, Python, GitLab, Kubernetes and Apache Spark state it; Kubernetes and Spark call it a release note or migration-guide entry. USGS and Rails also state it. Ansible and Grafana ask for an entry on bug fixes too, which the Counterpoint leaves to the project
cards.rule: Add a changelog entry to each change that adds, removes or changes a feature.
cards.why: Users and release managers read the changelog, not the diff. A feature change with no entry reaches the release notes late or never, and a removal with no entry surprises whoever depended on it.
cards.counterpoint: "Every fix needs an entry too, or the log is incomplete." Bug fixes, refactors and test changes carry no user-visible feature change, and entries for them bury the ones that matter. Add an entry for a fix only when users must act on it.

cards.applies_when: The change removes, rewrites or "simplifies" odd-looking existing code, or rewrites a module.
cards.rule: Add a characterization test before rewriting code you do not understand.
cards.why: Strange code often carries a fix for a bug that is no longer visible. Removing it re-ships the bug. Check the history first (blame, the PR that added it, tickets, postmortems); defensive code such as null checks, retries and timeouts usually answers a real incident. cards.applies_when: The change renames, removes or reshapes a column, API field, message, config key or exported symbol that other code reads.
cards.tool_gate: Schema or API diff tools (breaking-change detectors) in CI.
cards.note: GitLab and Stripe state migrating every consumer before the old path goes; Microsoft's six-phase post states expand, move writes, data and reads, validate, then contract. Exception: when producer and consumers deploy atomically from one repo, or the table is small enough to alter in one safe step, a one-step change is fine. Say so in the description. cards.applies_when: The change adds or edits code behind a feature flag.
cards.tool_gate: Test helper that runs the flagged suite once per flag state, or a CI job that fails when a flag has tests for one state only.
cards.note: GitLab (both states should be fully functional while the flag exists), GrowthBook (CI exercises the enabled and disabled behaviour of release flags) and Unleash (test both code paths while the flag is active). The vendors state advice to the reader, so they count under docs/PROMOTION.md rule 3. Martin Fowler's toggles article is a person's reference and not counted
cards.rule: Test the flagged behaviour with the flag on and with the flag off for as long as the flag exists.
cards.why: The off path is the one production runs until rollout, and the one it falls back to when the flag is turned off in an incident. A suite that sets the flag on leaves that path unchecked, and it breaks unseen. See [[chg-tests-ship-with-change]] for the general rule.
cards.counterpoint: "Two states double the test cost, and many flags multiply it." Test each flag in both states on its own, with the others at their defaults, rather than every combination. Remove the flag soon after rollout and the second state goes with it.

cards.applies_when: The change evaluates a feature flag or kill switch in code.
cards.note: ConfigCat (the flag description says what the safe default is if evaluation fails), GrowthBook (every evaluation needs an explicit fallback and false is not universally safe), PostHog (per-flag safe defaults so a cold start in an outage returns usable values) and LaunchDarkly (test the fallback values of permanent flags periodically). The vendors state advice to the reader, so they count under docs/PROMOTION.md rule 3. The OpenFeature default-value argument is an API shape, not counted
cards.rule: Pass each flag evaluation a fallback chosen for the outcome if the flag service fails, and do not assume `false`.
cards.why: When the flag service is down, the SDK returns the fallback. For a switch that disables a payment path or a safeguard, `false` turns off the thing you need most. A fallback that nobody chose is a decision made by the default argument. For tests of the fallback path, see [[prod-kill-switch-fallback]].
cards.counterpoint: "Ship new features off." That holds for a release flag, where the fallback is the old behaviour. It is a choice made per flag, and it is wrong for a flag whose off state removes a safeguard or a required path.

cards.applies_when: The change adds a feature flag or renames one.
cards.tool_gate: Flag registry linter that checks each key against the documented pattern and rejects a key that was deleted before.
cards.note: Documented convention - Unleash (enforce unique naming conventions), LaunchDarkly (organisation-wide naming conventions), ConfigCat (a pattern with team, type and function), Flagsmith (create a naming convention upfront) and GrowthBook (a convention that shows domain and purpose). No reuse of a deleted key - Unleash (unique names prevent reuse of old names), GrowthBook (do not reuse a deleted key for unrelated behaviour), ConfigCat (one purpose per flag, a new purpose gets a new flag) and LaunchDarkly (a new flag with a deleted flag's key can be picked up by old code). The vendors state advice to the reader, so they count under docs/PROMOTION.md rule 3. The exact pattern differs by source and the card does not pick one
cards.rule: Name each new flag by the team's written convention, and never give a deleted flag's key to different behaviour.
cards.why: Names such as `test2` or `new_thing` hide what a flag does and who owns it, so nobody dares to remove it. A key that comes back with a new meaning can match old code, caches or telemetry that still refer to the earlier flag and switch on behaviour nobody meant to enable.
cards.counterpoint: "The pattern is bikeshedding." The exact pattern does matter little; sources disagree on it. What is checked is that one written pattern exists, the new key follows it, and retired keys are not reused. A lint over the registry makes that cheap.

cards.applies_when: The change adds a feature flag, kill switch or config toggle.
cards.tool_gate: Flag registry linter that requires owner and expiry fields.
cards.note: Removal after rollout - Chromium, GitLab, Unleash, LaunchDarkly, Statsig, Flagsmith, Harness, Optimizely, FeatBit and GrowthBook. Owner - Dropbox (every experiment and feature gate has a clear owner), Unleash, LaunchDarkly (a named maintainer per set of flags), Harness (one owning team), GrowthBook (a team, not just the author), ConfigCat, Optimizely and FeatBit. Expiry date or removal condition - Chromium (flag expiry metadata), Unleash, Optimizely, FeatBit, ConfigCat, GrowthBook and Harness. Removal ticket at creation - Statsig, Unleash and GrowthBook. Permanent flags marked as such - LaunchDarkly (temporary or permanent), GitLab (a type with a maximum lifespan) and ConfigCat (flag type and longevity). The vendors state advice to the reader, so they count under docs/PROMOTION.md rule 3. A default of off has GitLab only, and GrowthBook says false is not universally safe as a fallback, so it left the card; the fallback sits in chg-flag-fallback-chosen
cards.rule: Give every new flag an owner, a removal condition or date and a removal ticket, mark flags meant to stay as permanent, and remove the others and their dead branches once rollout ends.
cards.why: A flag without an owner becomes a permanent fork of behaviour that nobody dares delete and that multiplies test paths. Opening the removal ticket with the flag, while the context is fresh, schedules the removal before the rollout starts. The off state of a flag is not always the safe one when evaluation fails; see [[chg-flag-fallback-chosen]].
cards.counterpoint: Some flags are permanent, such as kill switches and entitlements. Label them as permanent, with an owner, and skip the removal condition. The check is that the intent is explicit.

cards.applies_when: The change adds code that solves a problem the codebase already solves somewhere.
cards.tool_gate: Repeated style nits mean a missing linter or formatter rule; add the gate instead of commenting.
cards.note: Rule backed by Google (eng-practices standard), PEP 8, and the Microsoft engineering playbook; the Orosz post is inferred support only
cards.rule: Follow the established pattern nearby.
cards.why: A silent second way to do the same thing doubles what every later reader must learn. Equally, copying a bad pattern forever freezes it in place.
cards.counterpoint: "Consistency preserves bugs." Consistency is a tie-breaker, not a reason to copy something that breaks a rule or hurts code health, so a reviewer must not demand matching code that makes things worse. When the nearby pattern is bad, keep to the local style in this change, file a ticket, and propose the new standard in its own change, improving what you touch. A second pattern slipped into a feature change without a word is the failure.

cards.applies_when: A migration adds a column to a large PostgreSQL table.
cards.tool_gate: Migration linter that flags volatile defaults, stored generated columns and identity columns on ADD COLUMN.
cards.rule: Add the column nullable or with a constant default, then fill volatile, computed, or identity values in batches.
cards.why: A constant or NULL default is a metadata change. A volatile default, a stored generated column, or an identity column rewrites the whole table, and the default lock (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) blocks every query on it for the duration.
cards.counterpoint: "The table is small." Then the rewrite is cheap and the one-step form is fine. State the row count in the description. [[sys-migration-lock-timeout]] covers locking and timeouts.

cards.tool_gate: SAST and dependency scanning in CI catch the mechanical part.
cards.note: thin sourcing: routing to a qualified reviewer and crypto randomness only; the rest is synthesis
cards.rule: List any new attack surface in the description.
cards.why: A generalist reviewing a diff will not spot an exposed route the author never mentioned. A new input, trust boundary, credential, or dependency counts, and security-relevant changes go to a qualified reviewer.
cards.counterpoint: Naming threats on every PR is theatre. Only changes that add one of the listed surfaces need the section, and most PRs write "none".

cards.applies_when: The change adds a third-party package, library or vendored source tree.
cards.tool_gate: A PR template or CI check that asks for the reason when a manifest gains a dependency.
cards.note: Chromium and the Google SWE book (motivation, alternatives considered, who keeps it up to date; one organisation), the Kubernetes dependency checklist (is a similar dependency already present, is the licence compatible) and the OpenSSF evaluation guide (every new dependency is a possible supply-chain or support problem, so eliminate unnecessary ones)
cards.rule: When a change adds a dependency, say why it is needed and which existing dependency or own code was considered instead.
cards.why: Every dependency is code the team did not write and must keep updating, a licence to satisfy and a new route for a supply-chain attack. A package added for one helper function keeps costing for years. A reviewer can only weigh the cost if the change names the need, and it also helps to name the licence and who maintains the package. See [[chg-reuse-before-write]] for reuse inside the codebase and [[code-dependency-licence-sbom]] for the licence check.
cards.counterpoint: "A one-line justification for a small utility is review friction." Scale it by risk: a dev-only tool needs a sentence, a runtime or security-sensitive package needs the full note. The check is that a reason exists, not that every package gets an essay.

cards.applies_when: A change adds a tracked file under an editor or IDE project directory.
cards.tool_gate: A CI step that fails when `git ls-files | rg '(^|/)(\.idea/workspace\.xml|\.idea/shelf/|xcuserdata/)|\.xcuserstate$'` prints a path. `git ls-files -ci --exclude-standard` lists only tracked files that already match an ignore entry, so it misses a repository with no entry.
cards.note: GitHub and Git describe the repository ignore file and the machine-wide excludes; JetBrains and Microsoft separate shared project settings from per-user state; Apple requires shared Xcode schemes for CI
cards.rule: Do not commit a file that holds one developer's editor or IDE state; ignore those paths in the repository or a machine-wide exclude file. An ignore entry does not untrack a file already committed: remove it from the index with `git rm --cached`.
cards.why: Per-user state changes on every IDE session and every machine, so it adds diff noise and merge conflicts. The shared files are the ones a teammate or CI needs. JetBrains says `.idea` holds both user-specific settings that "should not be placed under version control" and project settings "normally shared among developers". Microsoft says workspace settings in `.vscode` are "shared by all users of that project". Git and GitHub offer the repository `.gitignore` for paths everyone hits and a machine-wide exclude for a path only one developer has.
cards.counterpoint: "A blanket ignore throws away the run configurations and schemes the team shares." Those live in shared locations: `.idea/runConfigurations/`, `.vscode/launch.json`, `xcshareddata/xcschemes/`. Commit those and ignore `workspace.xml` and `xcuserdata`. In a one-developer repository, put the path in the machine-wide exclude instead of the shared ignore file.

cards.applies_when: The diff adds a suppression (lint ignore, type ignore, skipped test, swallowed error) or deletes a failing check.
cards.tool_gate: Linter rule that requires a reason and ticket on each suppression.
cards.note: Palantir URL returned 403 and was not verified; extends Palantir (TODO without issue, red checks) and Go (discarded errors) to suppressions
cards.rule: Name the rule, the reason, and a ticket on every suppression; a swallowed error, skipped test, or disabled check is a FAIL unless justified.
cards.why: Silencing a diagnostic hides the problem it reports and removes the safety net for the next author. An exception with an expiry date fails the check again when it lapses, so it cannot stay forever.
cards.counterpoint: Sometimes a warning is a false positive. Then suppress narrowly with a reason and an expiry date, which keeps the gate useful. A suppression of a rule that guards correctness or safety should be removed, not documented. Palantir's list covers TODOs without issue references and merging with checks red. The Go list covers discarded errors. This card extends both to suppressions.

cards.applies_when: The change adds a conditional, flag or nullable mode to code that serves more than one feature.
cards.tool_gate: Microsoft CA1502 (cyclomatic complexity, default 25) or PMD CognitiveComplexity (default 15) on the shared function.
cards.note: own function or type - Linux kernel (factor the conditional into a helper function), Effective Go (a type switch, a switch for an if-else chain), Shopify (move the branch onto the item); cap on branches - Microsoft CA1502, PMD CognitiveComplexity; Cursor review rubric is the origin
cards.rule: Put a new case behind its own function or type; do not add a one-off branch to a shared flow.
cards.why: Each special case in a shared path is a condition that every later reader and every other feature must reason about. The cases accumulate until nobody can say what the path does.
cards.counterpoint: "It is one line; an abstraction is overkill." One is fine. The second and third special case are the signal. See [[mod-yagni]] for when not to extract yet..

cards.applies_when: Every change.
cards.tool_gate: A CI check can label or warn on file count and diff size.
cards.rule: Make each change do one logical thing; if the description needs "and" between unrelated outcomes, split it.
cards.why: Reviewers can only judge intent and risk of a single concern. Mixed changes hide the risky part, cannot be reverted alone, and break bisect.
cards.counterpoint: Splitting adds overhead, and stacked diffs need tooling and cost rebasing pain. The rule is one concern, not a line count: as small as possible, but no smaller. A single concern that is legitimately large (a generated migration) is fine if the description says so.

cards.applies_when: The change or its description claims a speed, throughput, memory or cost improvement.
cards.note: the kernel, Phabricator and GitLab (measure again after deploy, report percentiles) back the Rule (numbers for an optimisation claim); the run count, spread and limiter in the Why come from benchmark-checklist/SKILL.md
cards.rule: Back a performance claim with measured before-and-after numbers.
cards.why: A single fast run can measure noise, a cached result, an error path that returns early, or a step that is a tenth of the total. A piece that is 10% of the run caps the gain near 11% however well it is tuned. So a useful number comes with the run count, the spread, the resource that limits further gain, and a check that errors were counted and the work ran inside the timed region.
cards.counterpoint: "A micro-optimisation needs no benchmark ceremony." A claim in prose does. If the description makes no performance claim, mark `N/A`.

cards.applies_when: The diff changes an existing field's type, default, label or name in a `.proto` file.
cards.tool_gate: `buf breaking` with the wire and JSON rule sets.
cards.rule: Never change the type of a protobuf field, switch it between repeated and scalar, or rename it while any consumer reads JSON or text format; add a new field instead.
cards.why: The wire format carries numbers and types, not names, so a type change is read as garbage by anything not yet redeployed. The JSON and text formats carry names, so a rename breaks those readers.
cards.counterpoint: "Both ends deploy together." A rolling deploy runs both versions at once, and stored data does not redeploy. If the message never leaves one binary, mark the card N/A.

cards.applies_when: The diff deletes a field or enum value from a `.proto` message or enum.
cards.tool_gate: `buf breaking` or an equivalent descriptor diff in CI.
cards.rule: When you delete a protobuf field or enum value, add `reserved` for its number and name in the same change, and never reuse a number.
cards.why: Old data and old clients still carry the number. A new field that takes it is read as the old type, and the failure is silent corruption, not an error. Renumbering a live field breaks old data the same way.
cards.counterpoint: "Nobody sends field 4 any more." Stored messages, queued messages and a client on last month's build do. Reserving costs one line and cannot be undone by accident.

cards.applies_when: The change restructures code and claims to keep its behaviour.
cards.tool_gate: Snapshot or golden-file tests in CI.
cards.note: Sonar and JetBrains (vendors) say to add tests that describe current behaviour, or characterization tests, before refactoring; Apache Flex says never to refactor without tests. Rule also backed by cursor/plugins (refactoring playbook), GitHub (existing visual regression snapshots matched before and after the CSS Modules move) and Stripe (a tool diffed parse trees across files rubyfmt formatted)
cards.rule: Pin current behaviour with a characterization test, snapshot or equivalence check before the refactor moves any structure.
cards.why: A type check and a linter pass on code that now does something else. Without a pin, "no behaviour change" is a claim nobody ran.
cards.counterpoint: "The code is already well tested." Then name the test that covers the moved paths. If you cannot, the pin is missing. See [[chg-refactor-separate]] for keeping the refactor apart from behaviour changes.

cards.applies_when: The change both restructures or reformats code and changes behaviour, or moves code between files.
cards.tool_gate: A formatter check in CI removes the reformatting case.
cards.note: Reformatting in its own commit is backed by Google, Apache Flink and LLVM, and the Python devguide also backs it. Renames rest on Google and Apache Flink; LLVM does not mention them. The kernel says one logical change per patch, which covers refactors only by extension
cards.rule: Put refactors, renames, and reformatting in their own commit or PR, apart from behaviour changes.
cards.why: A reviewer can verify a pure refactor by "tests unchanged" and a pure move by diff. Mixed in with logic, neither check works and a real bug hides in noise. Never edit moved code in the same patch as the move.
cards.counterpoint: Separate PRs cost review round trips, and untangling a mixed branch after the fact is work. Separate commits in one PR are an acceptable compromise, but separate PRs are ideal. A tidy that exists only to enable the behaviour change in hand may ship with it if the commits stay apart.

cards.applies_when: The change adds a helper, util, type or constant.
cards.tool_gate: Clone-detection in CI (jscpd, PMD CPD, or similar) can flag near-duplicate blocks.
cards.note: GitHub (reviewer repo search for each new helper), Cursor (explore before changing, since the agent may create a utility that exists) and Google's Gemini CLI team (review-duplication skill) back the search; the kernel style guide backs only "use the existing helper"; Ousterhout and refactoring.guru back the Why; "author names where they searched" had no source, so it left the Rule
cards.rule: Do not add a helper that duplicates one already in the repo; search for it first.
cards.why: Reviewers see only the diff, so a reimplementation of a helper a few files away looks fine in isolation. Two copies then drift and get fixed once.
cards.counterpoint: "Searching costs more than writing ten lines." For tiny code that is true. Then the duplicate is tolerable and `mod-yagni` governs extraction. The cost flips once the logic holds a rule (parsing, money, auth) that must stay in one place.

cards.applies_when: A reviewer is deciding what to comment on.
cards.tool_gate: Formatter, linter and type checker own style and mechanical rules.
cards.note: Microsoft says linters absorb part of review so humans focus on correctness and design. Anthropic (a vendor) backs only the tool-owned clause: its reviewer filters out findings that are only style, diagnostics or cleanup; not a counted third org and not the taste clause
cards.rule: Do not spend review comments on what a tool enforces or on minor style points; spend them on the findings that matter.
cards.why: Noise buries the real defects and trains authors to dismiss review. Prefer a few high-conviction comments, and when a first pass turns up many, talk to the author instead of posting a long list; both are common advice but have fewer than three organisations behind them, and a style point outside the written guide is the reviewer's taste. A rubber-stamp approval is just as harmful: an approval must reflect real reading.
cards.counterpoint: Limiting comments risks missing issues. The cap applies to opinion, not to defects, so every real defect is still raised. The written style guide or the formatter settles style, and repeated nits mean a missing gate.

cards.applies_when: Async code catches exceptions around awaits or uses asyncio.timeout.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff BLE001 / S110 for broad swallow; lint for CancelledError needs custom rule.
cards.rule: Re-raise `CancelledError` (do not catch it via bare `except` or `BaseException`), and catch `TimeoutError` outside the `asyncio.timeout()` block.
cards.why: TaskGroup and timeouts are built on cancellation, so swallowing it makes shutdown hang and timeouts silently not fire. The conversion to `TimeoutError` happens at context exit, so a handler inside the block never sees it.
cards.counterpoint: "Cleanup code must run even on cancel." Clean up in `finally`, then re-raise, and never suppress. `uncancel()` is task bookkeeping, not permission to swallow.

cards.applies_when: A Python class has no state, only static methods, or a `Protocol` with one implementation.
cards.tool_gate: ruff PLR6301 (partial), Pylint R0903 (min-public-methods=2, dataclasses exempt; it counts public methods, not state, so a static-only class with two methods passes)
cards.note: Go review guide and the creator's Python guide back the rule; Refactoring.Guru and Pylint add the class half. Pylint's threshold is 2 and it exempts dataclasses, so treat it as a prompt, not a hard gate
cards.rule: Give a class real state or a collaborator; otherwise write a module function.
cards.why: A static-only class is a module with extra typing. A `Protocol` with one implementation is a speculative interface. A `Protocol` needs two or more real implementations swapped at runtime; see [[mod-yagni]]. Every class costs time to understand and maintain, so one that does too little should become a function. A class kept to mark future work is the same speculation: delete it, or name the plan and its owner. Pylint flags a class with too few public methods and shows a dataclass plus a function, or a larger API, as the fixes.
cards.counterpoint: "Protocols make testing easy." A fake of a concrete class in tests works with duck typing too. Declare an interface where it is consumed, and avoid speculative ones.

cards.rule: Pass an explicit `httpx.Timeout` to every `httpx` client.
cards.why: Core rules: [[svc-timeouts]], [[mod-pooled-clients-built-once]]. `read=None` disables the read timeout. Build the client once in the app lifespan and reuse it.
cards.counterpoint: "httpx defaults are fine." They are (5s), but set the value explicitly so that a library change cannot silently change behaviour.

cards.applies_when: A Python module has imports.
cards.tool_gate: ruff I, TID252, PLC0415
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Put imports at module top, absolute only.
cards.why: Local imports hide dependencies and cycles. Relative imports break when files move. Importing a private name couples you to something its owner may change without notice. Never import a `_`-prefixed name from another module, and use `__all__` only in a re-export `__init__.py`.
cards.counterpoint: "Import inside the function avoids a cycle." It hides the cycle instead of fixing it, and the design needs a third module or a dependency inversion. A lazy import for a heavy optional dependency is the one defensible exception; document it with a reason. Some guides tolerate explicit relative imports and a function-level import to break a cycle; this pack chooses absolute imports because they survive moving files, and keeps the local import as a last resort.

cards.applies_when: Annotations use `typing` aliases such as `Optional` or `Union`.

cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Write `X | None` and builtin generics, not `typing` aliases.
cards.why: A tool decides these, so a human comment is waste. Check that the gate exists, and gate new code with `mypy --strict` and pyright.
cards.counterpoint: "Two type checkers is overkill." They disagree on edge cases, so running both on new code catches different mistakes. Pick at least one as a hard gate.

cards.applies_when: Code calls `typing.cast(...)`.
cards.tool_gate: ruff TID251 (banned-api)
cards.note: from the author's own Python review guide
cards.rule: Do not use `cast()`; parse the boundary into a typed model, or narrow with `isinstance`.
cards.why: `cast` is a promise to the type checker that nothing verifies at runtime. When the promise is wrong, the type checker's output is a lie that spreads.
cards.counterpoint: "Sometimes the checker is wrong." Then fix the stub or narrow with `isinstance` or `assert`, which check at runtime. A justified `type: ignore[code]` with a reason is more honest than a cast, because it stays visible.

cards.why: A cwd-relative path works from the repo root and fails from CI, an IDE, or an installed package.

cards.applies_when: A pytest or unittest suite builds a database, a container, a client or a model in a fixture that many tests use.
cards.tool_gate: pytest --durations=10 --durations-min=1.0 to find the fixture, and a CI job timeout to hold the line.
cards.note: scope - pytest (module-scoped smtp_connection runs "as quick as a single one"; dynamic scope for slow setups like docker containers), Python (setUpClass for an expensive connection); cached database plus rollback and --reuse-db - pytest-django; the SQLAlchemy recipe for a rolled-back Session - SQLAlchemy
cards.rule: Give an expensive pytest fixture `scope="session"` or `"module"` and isolate each test with a rollback, never a schema build or a seed load inside a function-scoped fixture.
cards.why: pytest destroys a function-scoped fixture after every test, and function scope is the default, so an expensive fixture pays its full cost for each test. A module or session scope pays it once. unittest has the same trade: `setUpClass` builds once per class, `setUp` once per test.
cards.counterpoint: "A session fixture is shared, so one test can leak state into the next." That holds for mutable objects, which is why the PASS keeps the engine shared and gives each test its own rolled-back session. A fixture that cannot be reset stays at function scope. Python's own docs warn that shared fixtures break isolation and parallelism, so build the shared part read-only. A test that must commit needs a transactional fixture, which clears the database after each test, so that test must repopulate its data every time.

cards.applies_when: Tests differ only in inputs and expected values.
cards.tool_gate: ruff PT006/PT007 (style only)
cards.note: Go (copy-paste a test, use a table), Microsoft (parameterized tests) and Vodafone (three tests that are one test with different inputs) state the practice; pytest documents the tool
cards.rule: Write tests that differ only in inputs and expected values as one `@pytest.mark.parametrize` test.
cards.why: Copy-pasted tests drift, and an empty parametrization silently runs nothing. Assert that a computed parameter list is not empty first.
cards.counterpoint: "Separate tests give clearer failures." Parametrize ids give one failure per case, with its inputs. For a computed list, `assert cases` before parametrising.

cards.applies_when: Python code calls asyncio.create_task or ensure_future.
cards.tool_gate: Ruff RUF006 (asyncio-dangling-task).
cards.rule: Never discard the result of `create_task`; keep a reference and surface its exceptions, preferably through a `TaskGroup`.
cards.why: The event loop holds only weak references, so an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected mid-run. A task that nobody awaits also loses its exception ("never retrieved").
cards.counterpoint: "The set-and-discard recipe from the docs is enough." It keeps the task alive but still never retrieves the exception, and the docs point to TaskGroup for that. The same reference rule applies to tasks passed to `asyncio.shield`.

fail.code: asyncio.create_task(send_email(user))   # fire and forget

pass.code:
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tg.create_task(send_email(user))
# or: t = create_task(...); bg.add(t); t.add_done_callback(bg.discard)

cards.applies_when: A Python unit test touches the network, the shared filesystem, the database or the real clock. A per-test temporary directory (pytest `tmp_path`) is not the shared filesystem.
cards.tool_gate: pytest-socket (`--disable-socket`), plus a unit-test CI job with no database service and no network credentials
cards.note: Google (small tests cannot reach the network or disk), Microsoft (a unit test has no file system or database and controls DateTime.Now), Spring (stub repositories, no runtime infrastructure), GitLab (mock outgoing requests, fake timers), Django (SimpleTestCase blocks database queries), Rails (travel_to, system tests in a separate CI step), Laravel (Unit tests cannot reach the database; most tests should be feature tests)
cards.rule: Keep unit tests off external I/O (the network, the shared filesystem and the database) and off the real clock, and run tests that need them in a separate, slower tier.
cards.why: A test that reaches the network, the disk or the database is slow and fails for reasons outside the code: an offline CI runner, a schema change, a clock at midnight. Those dependencies belong in an integration tier, where the failure is about the integration. Google's small tests cannot reach the network or disk; Microsoft's unit tests have no file system or database and control the clock through a seam; Django's `SimpleTestCase` blocks database queries by default. pytest-django fails a test that touches the database unless it opts in with a mark. Each test also builds and tears down its own state, so none depends on another's result or order.
cards.counterpoint: "Most tests should hit the real stack, and mocking every collaborator hides real failures." Many teams keep most tests at the feature level and prefer real dependencies where they can keep them. Both hold: the rule is about the network, disk, database and clock boundary, not about doubling every collaborator. A feature or system test that boots the app belongs in the slower tier, and a team can run that tier on every merge. The unit tier stays fast and deterministic.

cards.applies_when: A pytest suite runs in parallel with pytest-xdist (`-n`) and its tests use a database or another shared resource.
cards.note: session fixtures run once per worker - pytest-xdist; each xdist process gets its own database by default - pytest-django; PyPI's suite hit cross-test contamination after -n auto and fixed it with a database per worker (191 s to 63 s) - Trail of Bits
cards.rule: Under pytest-xdist, give each worker its own database or other mutable resource, keyed by `worker_id`, and build an expensive shared one once with a lock file.
cards.why: Each xdist worker collects its own tests, so a `session` fixture runs once per worker and not once per run. Workers that share one mutable database corrupt each other's tests, and the failures look random. PyPI's suite found this the moment it moved to `-n auto`; per-worker databases fixed it, and execution time fell from 191 s to 63 s.
cards.counterpoint: "Building a database per worker multiplies the setup cost." It does, by the number of workers, which is still far less than the number of tests. When one build is too slow even per worker, build it once under a file lock, as the xdist documentation shows, and copy it for each worker with a database template.
